LOVE'S WAYS. r Two paths hath Love for entering lovers' feet, , And one is broad and fair and very svieet, And-every grace of song and flower hath ; . ' The other is a straight and narrow path ' Where stones and brambles choke the bitter way, And songs it bath, but never one is gay- ' And some who enter are with roses bound, And ,some with thorns, but none may go uncrowned 7 •., .
And yet, both ways are thronged with eager feet, And voices, gay and sad, chant—Love is sweet. EIHNR/ETTA CHRISTIAN WRIGHT.

THE MAN IN THE MOON. Oh, the Man in the Moon has a crick in his back ; Whee ! _

Whimm ! Ain't you sorry for him? And a mole on his nose that is purple and black; Aid his eyes are so weak that they water and run, If be dares to dream when he looks at the sun; So he just dreams of stars, as the doctors advise. My!

Eyes! But isn't he wise! To just dream of stars as the doctors advise. ' And the Man in the Moon has a boil on his ear, Whee ! Whing ! What a singular thing! know! but these facts are authentic, my dear— There's a boil on his ear, and a corn on his chin— He calls it a dime. but dimple stick in; Yet it might be a dimple turned over, you know; Wham..' ! •
Why, certainly so! ' It might be a dimple turned over you kale. And the Man in the Moon has a rheumatic knee, Gee! _
Whizz!
What a pity that is ! And his to have worked round where his heels ought
to be; So wheneverhe wants to go north'be goes south, And comes back with the porridge crumbs all 'round his
Mouth; And he brushes them off with a Japanese fan ; „) • Whing ! a ' Warn! _

As useless•if it goes as if it stands. We every day and every hour say things of another that we might more properly say of ourselves.—Mon- taigne. , The comparative value or worthlessness of anything is not determined by its bearing on this world, but on the next. Life is girt all round with a zodiac of sciences, the contribution of men who have perished to add their point of light to our sky. Every thought, work, and occupation should be, like a Rembrandt picture, ahaded with a blending of the darkness of this world and the light of the next. The aid we have from others is mechanical compared with the discoveries of Nature in us. What is ahus learned is delightful in the doing' and the effect remains. It seems to me that the, real reason why reformers and some philanthropists are unpopular is, that they disturb our serenity and make us conscious of our own shortcomings. Look not into the qualities thou mayst possess which are wanting to others; but look to those which others possess and which are wanting to thee, that thou mayst acquire them. There is one peculiar imperfection connected with our want of correct information, which we should particu- larly guard against, that of being positive in proportion to our ignorance.-11. Balton. "How many lodges did you say your husband belonged to ? " she suddenly asked. "Fifteen." "Mercy on me! But think of a man being out fifteen nights a week! I am really glad that I am a widow." A punctual Minnesota maiden lately married a casual acquaintance, who happened to meet her in the church, rather than be kept waiting for her original intended, who was a quarter of an hour beyond his appointed time. Wife, looking over bill: "Do you remember, my dear, how many trout you caught last Saturday?" Husband: "There were just twelve of 'em—all beauties! Why?" Wife : "The fishmonger has made a mistake. He charges only for half a dozen." An honest Welsh carpenter, coming out of Cardigan- shire, got work in Bristol, where in a fevs months, he had saved, besides his expenses, about twelve shillings; and with this prodigious sum of money returning into his own country, when he came upon Mile Hill he looked back on the town: " Ah, poor Pristow," said he, "if one or two more of hur countrymen were to give hur such another shake as hur has done, it would be poor Pristow inieed." . MONEY AS CAPITAT,.—Younz men are apt to estimate money alone as capital. One of their number who has inherited money is, they think, better equipped for the struggle of life than any other. They should look into the comparative commercial value of money and of knowledge and skill before they decide. Figures prove that of late years money has decreased in value as a money-getter, while human ability has increased. That is, the income from money invested at interest has diminished, while the compensation for service rendered has become larger. LOVE OF CRILDREN.—No doubt all persons think they love children, and many of them are vastly mistaken in thinking so. Do you want a test? Choose one of these. Could you spend a morning in cutting out a boat for a boy, or tell for the tenth, even the twentieth, time a familiar but ravishing story to eager little ears, or con- sent to be a Newfoundland dog for very short I sto .1. ride (it need not be done in Pall Mall), or carry a ut a restless infant through the long midnight hours, thout an overweening sense of self-righteousness? Love always and everywhere implies a great faculty of aking trouble.--The Bishop of Rochester in Good Words. A smart lawyer in White Plains, Westghester County, United States, had the misfortune to lose a suit for a client,who had every reason to expect success. The client, a plain old farmer, was astonished by the long bill of costs, and, hastening to the lawyer, said, "I thought You told me you should certainly gain that suit? " aSo I did," answered the lawyer," but you see when I brought it before the judge, they said It was a quorwm non judice." "Well, if they said it was as bad as that," replied the obi farmer, "I don't wonder we lost it," and he paid the costs and a big fee besides without another murmur. A 3 a Scottish minister and an English lawyer were -riding together, said the minister to his fnend, "Sir, do you ever make mistakes in your pleadings ? " "I do," says the lawyer. "An' what do ye do wi mistakes?" was the question. "Why, sir, if large ones, I mend them; if small ones I let them go. And pray, sir, do you ever make mistakes in preaching?" "Aye, sir, I have dune sae." "And what do you do with your mistakes?" "Oh, I dispense with them in the same manner as ye du yoursel'. I rectify the lairge, an' let go the sma' anes. No lang since, as I-was preachin', I meant to observe that the devil was the father o' a' liars, but made a mistake, an' said 'the father o' a' lawyers.' But the mistake was so sma' that I let it go." SHORT SlOHT.—Short sight is very much on the in- crease. The human eyes were not meant to pore by the hour together on a white page, and to race across it hundreds and thousands of times at a sitting. More and more, it is said, adapt themselves to this work every year and lose aptitude for distant things. . . . After admitting that very many people are short-sighted, and that none of the senses vary so much in range as that of I sight, I think it may be allowed that a person who can see a thing when it has been pointed out, and detect a 1 difference In size and tint between one little bird and another when both are Many yards off, is not: short- sighted. The truly .short-sighted in general do the best they can with their eyes; when features are out of range they discrim ri inate faces by coloung ; he figures are blurred by distance they often distinguish by peculiarities of gait and movement. It is quite another thing which is the matter with many eyes that only fancy they are short-sighted.—Good Words. MADE HEROES BY ApvsusrrY.—The noblest and most characteristic volcanoes, whether we class them by the - energy of their explosions or the volume of their ejec- tions, are found in Iceland and in the Malayan Archi- pelago. In Iceland the volcano of Skaptar in the single eruption of 1783, poured out a tide of lava exceeding in bulk all that has flowed from Vesuvius and /Etna com- bined since the eruption of Pliny. It has been com- puted that the volume of lava which flowed from skaptar in that year was greater than the mass of Mont Blanc. The gas-eruption which attended this molten tide was proportionally great; the clouds of fine cinders floated over Europe and so darkened the sky as to occa- sion fears of some great calamity. Although Iceland is a thinly-peopled country, this catastrophe was extremely destructive to human life; nearly a fifth of the popula- tion perished in the villages which were overwhelmed by the eruption, from the famine which came from the loss of the year's crops, and the frightening of the fish from the neighbouring sea. The thousand years of struggle which the Icelanders have had with polar cold and central fire is one of the most pathetic incidents in the history of our race. Almost every generation on that island has borne a.heavy burden from earthquake shocks or volcanic explosions, and yet this people have managed, by labour and thrift, to develop and maintain a well-ordered civilisation. For centuries the social order has been more secure, education more general, and the moral quality purer than in the happier parts of the world. Everywhere else save in this marvellous island we find that man is degraded in spirit from a hopeless contest with physical ills.—Seribner's Magazine. Ma. div.head: GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
div.p: A GIRL IN A THOUSAND.
BY JEAN MIDDLEMASS, Author of "Lady Muriel's Secret," "The Spider axl the Fly," "Poisoned /Arrows," "Wild Gebrgie," &c., &c. •
, - CHAPTER IV. MINE. Olt MS.

At the bottom of the lane which ran at the back of Simon Knight's yard, about ten minutes' walk from the railway-station, there was a Stile on the other side of 'which lay some meadows overhung with May trees, and rich in blossoming spring-tide, with golden buttercups and ox-eyed daisies all athwart them like a brilliant sheet. On this stile was seated a man of about five-arid- twenty, of a decidedly aristocratic type, though thine was , nothing muscular or athletic about him. At public school and college he had joined in sports like the rest, but only from compulsion, for all out- of-door exercisa was quite against his habits. His comrades, of course' called him a " muff ; " but it is out of " muffs " like Geoffrey Stanhope that not unfrequently great men are fabricated. He ,had received from his birth-star just the flash of genius ; which in a poor man would have yielded him renown; but in a rich- one gave him the name of eccentric and dilettante. Strange how in some families favours seem almost unequally divided. Among the Stanhopes, Geoffrey had all the talent, Ferdinand the physical force and go, and Irene the ' sweetness and beauty. Not that Geoffrey as he ' sits swinoinf on the style is wanting in good looks. His features are decidedly well-formed, his eyes clear and bright, and his • dark hair and moustache silky and thick; but it is in charm of manner that Geoffrey Stanhope's prestige lies. He is invariably courteous and urbane, with but .little of the irritability which marks Most poets and painters. His sister worships him; She is worshipping him now. , as he stands by the stile looking at -him and talking to him in a dreamy sort of way about the 'ex-eeed i ing beauty of the land- scape, as t is bathed in spring verdure before them. For they are lounging them facing the meadow with their backs to the road ; nor is it tiff a very rapid footstep is heard approaching them that Geoffrey looks round and lifts his hat, while a slight colour conies into his usually pale face. "How late you are!' cried Irene. • "I was nearly coming qn to the house to inquire after you." The new comer was Phyllis, looking even more radiantly beautiful titan isnal. Either the delight of meeting her friends or.the swift'raee along the. lane had given her cheeks an extra tinge of carmine, making her dark hair and eyes seem even darker and more Striking than usnal, while a- erimscin cotton gown, fitting with .a nicety that always made Phyllis Nniglit's dresses the wonder Of her acquaintances, was so in unison with he: colouring Pat it appealed at once to Geoffrefs artistic eye.' "- Lady Fedora had decided that Geoffrey was unim- pressionable, becausemit of his art he maintained a stolid indifference to all surrouriding objects; in his art, however, where, by the way, Lady Fedora but seldom penetrated, he was ttioroUgly susceptible; and within the pale of Geoffrey Stanhope's art was Phyllis Knight. He thought her more beautiful than any , woman he had ever seen before, and, -while dreaming as an artist of her beauty, he had lately become ' aware that he rejoiced in it as a man, and that to be separated from Phyllis Knight would be the. heaviest punishment that could be laid on him, for he had learnt to love the sweet maiden with the deep absorbing love of a man awakened to a sense of the tender passion for the first time in his life. It was only quite lately that Geoffrey had acknowledged to himself that his feeling for Phyllis amounted in strength to what the word love conveys to a man of Geoffrey Stanhope's tendencies,but Irene, quicker than he to jump at a conclusion, more ready with her woman's /clear sightedness to read hearts, had long ago settled that Geoffrey was in love; nor, with her want of knowledge of the world, did she judge it strange or out of course that such a thing should be. Phyllis:---poor Phyllis— Geoffrey's as yet unspoken love Made her miser- able, utterly and perfectly miserable ; at the same time that the instinctive knowledge she had of it-was the very pride and joy of her heart. Much though she had been the companion of Irene Stanhope, she had been btought up in a far rougher school,' and, from her position as a daughter of the people, • knew far more than Irene did of the workings of life. ,1 She knew full well with what opposition apy love Geoffrey might evince for her would, be met, not only ' by Lady Fedora and Mr. Stanhope, but by her-own ,[ father, who, from his point of view, objected quite as ninch to the mingling of classes as the Stanhopes • could do.

Geoffrey, too; himself,—the aristocratic Geoffrey— much though he might love her, would he ever make up his mind to contract rhat his friends would call a "low marriage ? Phyllis doubted it—doubted, too, even if he were ever induced by the force of his love to go so far, whether he would be happy married to one like her. ,
th,,

to bring it about if he wishes it ; and Irene feels very sure, though he has never acknowledged it to her, that he really loves ; but watching them carefully, as she is doing now, how can it be otherwise, she decides. "Geoffrey never looks like that at anyone else. Phyllis is never quiet and) subdued except when Geoffrey's eyes are upon • her. Heigh° ! Will she herself cease her prattle and be shy and downeat under the influence of a pair of eyes r The idea makes her burst out laughing' and thus interrupt the sort of dream in which her two com- panions are talking softly of absolutely nothing, while they revel in the sense of each 'other's' pre- sence. "What is it, Irene? What has amused you?" asked Geoffrey. "Nothing. I was only thinking about my own eclairs. Don't mind me, lam nobody." " Nobody " had, however, succeeded in breaking up the conclave, for Geoffrey looked at his watch. "Ten minutes to seven," he said. "Do you think we have the most remote chance of being back in ' Eaton-square, and dressed for dinner by eight ?" •" No, cried Irene, "we shall never do it, and papa will be angry. Nothing upsets his equilibrium like unpunctuality. Good-bye, Phyllis. Good-bye, little woman. You'll come on Saturday without fail. Now then, Geoffrey, a Jun to the station, ten minutes' ; train, a hansom, and home." But Geoffrey did not seem in such dread of a scold- ing from Mr. Stanhope as Irene did. It is all right, all right," he said. Don't excite yourself. Phyllis will walk with us to the station, won't you, Phyllis? There is no train till 7.15." "Good gracious, Geoff. I. shall have to get old Marks to put the clocks back, as I did last week." ‘.‘ You will have Mrs. Purvis find that out some of these days," said Phyllis, laughing, as they all three set off to walk to the station. " And if she (toes I wouldn't give much for your chance of escape. "No," No," 'answered Irene' "she would have us all up before a high tribunaL She would put all the clocks in the parish back for Ferdinand, though." "Funny what an infatuation Purvis has for Ferdinand," remarked Geoffrey, "and I don't think he cares particularly for her—rather snubs her, in fact." ' "'Does Ferdinand care for anyone," inquired Irene, "except his elect self ?" "Irene, that is severe," Geoffrey suggested. But she only curled her lip. It was evident that Irene's sisterly love for Ferdinand would not induce her to have clocks put on or back on his account, and yet the probability is that on his march through life -he will want that sort of help far more than Geoffrey will—aye, even be glad of assistance from the old housekeeper—Purvis—whom he now seems to sn‘b. No more about Ferdinand, however, does the little party, hurrying to tlip station, talk or think. A bell rings—a train is heard approaching; they will miss it after all if they do not accelerate their speed ; so off they set at a brisk pace and arrive in the station just in time to find it is a down train instead of the up one, which will not arrive for another 10 minutes.. ' "What foolish people we are !" cries Irene, sinking down on a clumz of wood outside the station.," giving • way to impressions inseead of looking calmly at our watches." "Come over the bridge and met there; then you will be on the right platform," suggested Geoffrey, "and can sit quietly till the train comes in." • "I won't move for three minutes—we will fccitirael- tically by time now. Oh, I am so warm." So evidently was Phyllis, for the hue of her face at this moment tvas that of the peony. Geoffrey had noted its suddenness, and not ascribing it to the heat he looked round to see the cause.

A man who had just emerged from the station was standing looking at them. Geoffrey felt inclined to ask him what he meant by staring, and was just advancing for the purpose, when Phyllis, who had now lost her colour altogether Sad was as white as death, called out, "Good evening, Tom. You will find father up at the house if you go up." "Who is this—this man?" asked Geoffrey, his brow. contracting. ' "Tom Chilton," she answered; "he has just come backfrom America." "Tom Chilton. Purvis's cousin's son that she used to talk so much about?" asked Irene. Phyllis nodded her head. "He used to be a lover of yours, wasn't he, Phyllis? "this rather mischievously from Irene. Back came the colour with a rush into Phyllis's face, and she answered in a very low lone, "He has been in America: for two years." Meantime Tom Chilton did not pass on his way, but inquired if Phyllia was coming—back home. "Yes, directly," she said,." when I have seen Miss 'lrene off; but don't you wait—father is going out early this evening." • As for Geoffrey, he never uttered one word, but led the way across the bridge to the opposite platform, the two girls following him, lxith wondering of what he was thinking. The train was already signalled, they were stand- ing together waiting for it. Irene was reading a strik- ing advertisement which had attracted her on the wall. Geoffrey at last broke his silence and seized Phyllis a little roughly by the wrist. "Tell me the truth, do you or do you not love that man?' "Love him—no," she answered, with a hysterical laugh. "Remember, Phyllis, I cannot be crossed in my love. I can brook no ri'valry from a man like that —that Chilton. You must decide between us so that there shall be no chance of his making any claim. Mine or his?' "Yours, Mr. Geoffrey, yours," she said, as the train came puffing into the station. A kiss from Irene, Geoffrey's hand taken from her arm, another minute and they were gone and she was alone there, save for the porter she had known from a child, and who busy arranging some trucks, did not heed her—alone with the recollection of Geoffrey Stanhope's impetuous wooing ringing in her ears, and making her feel faint and giddy from its strange swiftness. She struggled to retain her con- sciousness, and crept out of the station away across a field where she sat down to think. Tom Chilton was waiting on the other side to walk with her up to the house, but he might wait or go as he listed ; neither then, nor for some hours would Phyllis cross the threshold of the builder's red brick house. . .

She was thinking so at this moment, when, her hand in Geoffrey's, he held it pressed while he gazed long and ardently into her glorious eyes. Before he withdrew either pressure or gaze a shiver passed over Phyllis, for she thought of Tom Chilton, and the meeting of the preceding evening seemed to sweep across her brain, scorching it as it passed. "What is it, Phyllis? Are you ill ? " asked Geoffrey tenderly. "Ill? No, Phyllis isn't ill," answered Irene; she has run too fast down the lane, that is all. Sit down here under the hedge and rest awhile; mean- time tell us why you are so late," "It is a marvel I am here at all," said Phyllis, mastering here motion with an effort.. "Father says I am to waste no more time walking about the lanes; girls like me ought to have sonzething else th do. And I really think he means it, Miss- Irene. I am afraid we shall not have many more meetings under the May trees." And she looked very 'sad', almost as if she were going to cry, much to Irene's surprise,', for Phyllis as a rule did not know what sorrow meant. Her friend's evident dejection inspired Irene with the desire to cheer her, and she answered, laughing: "It is all right, Phyllis; we p.}tonlel have to find another place of meeting, even without your father's objection to this one, for I am coming out next week, going to my first ball, and shall not have time for these excursions, and of course you ' could, not walk about the lanes along with Geoff; it would be neither proper nor amusing," and she looked sly. "Oh, this is worse and worse," cried Phyllis, "if you are never coming down here, 'how am I to see you? I might sometimes slip out unobserved if you came." ,

Alone with the strong feelings which were stirring her even to the very depths, Phyllis forgot the flight of time or what fresh difficulties and complications the prolonged absence from her father's roof might occasion.
(To he continued.)

"Why, you foolish Phyllis,of course you'll come to London ; I shall want you .horribly: I shall never be dressed fit to be seen unless you superintend, and as it is you must come up on Saturday quite early, to go with me to order my ball dress. Geoffrey thinks no one has any taste but you, and mamma says, with her love, that you must come." Alas, alas, for Lady Fedora's stability of purpose —since this message was bona,fide, and no invention , of Irene's. If Simon Knight has no more deter- J mination than Lady Fedora, there is but ' little chance of these young people being kept apart. ' And that such a measure is absolutely necessary for their future peace there is little doubt. The parents scarcely know how necessary. They would guess, perhaps, could they see Geoffrey now, as he once more takes Phyllis's hand, and it is a shapely hand enough,though somewhat browned band hardened with work. "Of course you'll come to London little Phyllis, up into my painting-room. I have your portrait to take, you know; and when It is done I will present a copy of it to Knight, and after that he'll never say a word against your meeting's with us." • But Phyllis shook her head. She knew her father well enough to be aware that no portrait would soothe him ; on the contrary her face on canvas drawn by Geoffrey Stanhope wourd rather serve to irritate. And so the afternoon's idling to which they bad all looked forward as likely to be a pleasant and agree- able one had become clouded, no one exactly knew why, though each felt that a change had arisen, and ! that something like a crisis is their lives was ap- proaching. For a long time Geoffrey still sat perched on the stile, the two girls lounging on the grass at his feet; the group might almost have formed the subject of one of his own pictures had there been a little more sunlight in the three pensive faces, instead Of each one being more or less impressed by the tormenting thoughts to which their tongues dare scarcely give utterance. Irene is naturally the gayest. There is as yet no heart.flutter agitating her on her own account. She must wait for f hat till after the ball to 'which she is going next week ; till then it is only at second- hand she is suffering the pangs of contradicted love, for she knows now, since her conversation with her mother, almost as well as Phyllis does, that this love-. making with Geoffrey will meet with determined op- position. She sits there very silentlyfor awhile watch- mg them, and deciding, in her little rebellious mind, , that whoever tries to prevent Geoffrey from marry- ! Mg Phyllis, she will we every stratagem she know*
LOVE AND LEARNING.

A well-known, elderly nobleman, of large wealth, wooed and work, a few years ago, a young and very beautiful girl. Their life has been as happy as it is pos- sible for married life to be, when December is united to May. His lordship is distinguished in scientific circles and possesses high literary attainments. Sometime after his marriage he was foolish enough to think that his lovely wife wassnot sufficiently educated, and laid out a course of reading for her. A month later he inquired about her progress. and found that she had not opened a book. He set up his eye- brows after the manner of old husbands when their young wives have displeased them. Whereupon she looked up at him with a bewitching smile, and said: "I was made to be loved, not to be learned." She wen the day, of course. What is learning compared to the light of a sunny blue eye? Would not a husband rather be met with a smile and a kiss, than by a wife who assured him that she " knew her lesson ?" Wisdom Is all very well, but winning ways go further. BY POVERTY NOOK INTO FURTHER STRAITS. A MIGRATION OF THE WOODCOCK. BY JOHN PEERS. . (Concluded .) Rut ere leaving this long-sought haven for the open sea, we found time to use the "kind of fire- place on the counter ;" for I occupied myself in veri- fying the old adage about cooks and good meat, as I sat upon the rudder-head grilling a few chops. Our appearance from the shore would doubtless have something gipsy-like, if not otherwise pic- turesque, about it. Now,whether it was this, or the smell of the mutton chops to which we were in- debted for our visitors lam not prepared to say ; but a lady and gentleman rowed round us while we were so engaged, admiring our Well-ventilated kit- chen, and he said he had often seen the boat at New Ferry with our iron comforter perched, as then upon the stern. Notwithstanding the many deficiencies of the cook, the chops disappeared with alarming pantomimic rapidity, and things were soon in a for- ward state for our departure from these pleasant shores. There' was a nice whole-sail breeze from the east, and a sea furrowed by crisp waves, over which the boat danced merrily to music of her own. From side to side we stretched, tack upon tack, I making W's of her wake, from shore to sand bank, and from bank to shore; a bright sun overhead the while making glad the glistening waters and the pleasant wind singing Aolian melodies in the taut set cords. So, joyously we sped, across the mouth of the Sound, and beneath the wall-like side of Puffin, with only one regret—that the absent are not here to enjoy the exhilarating effects of thus bounding on the curling seas in a boat that seemed to rejoice in sympathy with its crew. Out in the open sea the tretches became longer, end the wind weaker and *eaker, until finally, at th‘... month of the Conway, it died away altogether, and again, reluctantly," them woods" had to tv re- sorted to if any progress was to be Made, or other- Wise we must "lie like a painted ship on a painted ocean." For the sea lay glistening around us like a sheet of glass, guiltless of a ripple; the pleasant breeze we had experienced incoming out being mere- ly a " fejse wind,' caused by our being carried by the rapid current from the Straits through the still air. But here, where this favouring current ceased, the wind fell as if in sympathy, and left us bereft of locomotion, save that laborious self-imparted sort, where every inch of way has to be wrought for, and slewly, but steadily won. But in this plight we were not alone. A much larger boat than ours was using these " poor substitutes for the breezes of heaven," to'get up the river to Conway, while we. rowed for the Great Orme's Head, beneath the western face of which we crept st avoid the slight ebb-tide then running, to whiN. the projecting Head gave increased strength, whilst here an eddy ' ran in a favouring direction. High above our heads a ploughman slowly plodded through the sloping fields with frequent glances down upon u% who 'were ploughing the less stable element below. The cultivatable part of the westward sloping, summit was plainly and pleasantly visible from' below. Patches of verdure, interspersed by fallow in pleas- ing variety, divided by stone walls running up and. down at some fearful .angle with the horizon. We crept along, close to the foot of the cliff, and so around the seaward face of this massive Thad, where we found three men standing at the water's edge upon the white wave-worn pebbles at the cliff's steep foot. How they got down there, and Inw they were to get back again, or what they sought as compensation for the risk to life and limb, were questions we stayed not to solve, having a problem of more personal interest to solve, viz.: —how to get the old Seolopax int 6 her old nest near the slihigles of Llandudno. Patience and perseverance, work miracles—and boats into their berths in time.. At the mouth of the Bay in a line between the two Heads, lay one of the Liverpool pilot schooners, come to assist at the Royal Jubilee illu- mination. She was too cautious to risk a deeper entrance into the lion's mouth. Here a single stretch would fetch her clear of either Head, and so escape the dangers of embavment. But we, to' whom a canal offers ample stretAing room, we hesitate not to seek the furthest depths of this, to uslittle rock-pent sea. When we had found our berth and supplied frail nature's wants, we were at liberty and in a better frame of mind to respond to the ,1 jocularitioelikthe Welsh girls and their beaux, who were rowing around the Bay this lovely evening. As the night same on my two mates professed to be much pleased by the Jubilee illuminating. I, being aware of the shortness of our stay hem and the necessity of laying in a good stock of sleep whenever an opportunity came, had stretched myself upoh a rouahly extemporised couch to snatch some fitful slumbers iI could. These, in the early part of the night, were light and often bro- ken by the watch on deck, who were determined to let none of. this Jubilee illumination run to.,waste, if they could help it. They certainly intercepted as much of it as they could, and occasionally I was called from the arms of Morpheus—(isn't it, he of naps I mean ?)—to witness some extra burst of pyrotechic grandeur. In my eyes the shore illuminations had much the ap- pearance and all the artistic effects of illuminated fac- tories. It was with great reluctance that I relinquished even the poor substitute for a bed on which I lay and the chance of prefacing the all too short night's rest by some anti-midnight slumbers—to admire this celebration of the fact that Englishmen afe not considered fit for self-government—although they have been belauding themselves for this very virtue for the last fifty years. They have also for that number of years meekly borne the yoke of a Sovereign Ruler of the self-governing peo- ple and now Jubilating on this prolonged stultification. That we are a nation of shopkeepers the first Napoleon told us; and we have a modern information of the fact in thie Jubilee business, for nine-tenths of these illuminations and decoration were tainted by some form of business advertisement, and the rest the result of the imperious dictation of that mysterious im- personation whom everybody derides and everybody obeys; by name Mrs. Grundy. Brown and Jones do it because Robinson has done it. and Robinson did it be- cause he thought Brown and Jones would do it. This sheepish following ef a leader and jumping over every straw where he does, must surely be a remnant Evolu- tion has left unchanged and allowed still to show itself in our natures. In this way, and no other, can we account for the propensity men have for herding together, and their slavish copying of each other's actions. With them a thing is not done because it is right and reasourble, but because someone else has done or is doing it. Great and powerful must be the Grundian Inquisition which com- pels men to do these things even against their inclina- tion.

- All things must come to an end, even these injubilant jubilations, but which in this case died out first deponent sayeth not, but this I can 'vouch for—that they, MY mates, not the illuminations--did come creeping in ere yet the eastern streaks of early morn appeared. By a happy provision of nature the wakefulness of the even- ing was, as usual, amply compensated for by the sleepi- ness of the morning. Even the claims of appetite were scarcely strong enough to draw us from our couches to the morning meal. However, we did breakfast, and got away from our anchorage before flood tide—six a.m. The early morning was still very calm with a just per- ceptible wind from S.W. With this light impelment we left the bay, preceded by the open boat we noticed the evening before going up Conway, and which had just turned off from the Pilot steamer at the mouth of the bay, and taken a course for Liverpool. Our little light wind carried us from under the shadow of the cliffs' but ere we got within sight of the Constable Buoy, it, hav- ing, like other" base deceivers" deluded us by false I promises, left us to inotfrn the faithlessness of so promis- ing a friend. Again by Compulsion we had to call into requisition our old friend the "wooden wind." Beneath a glowing sun and o'er a glassy sea slowly we rowed, endeavouring to " ovetrun the constable." Now like many others in, or lately out of, straits we found this a matter mere difficult than delightful in its accom- plishment; for that obstinate buoy persisted in obtrud- ing its unwelcome presence. First a little ahead, slowly coming abreast, and far, far to slowly passing astern. Like his namesake ashorehe wasa very ugly customer to get rid of; but at length—too long drawn out—" distance lent enchantment to the view,' and, finally, the haze of a calm summer's day gradually resoltredit into invisibility. Soon after this, we spoke our companion in misery, he also had to "work Ins woods." Away on the right Rhyll gradually passed astern and still we pulled, '!spell and spell about," on a course for the Horse Channel; but now the sun was high in the heavens and the tide must be nearly spent. The prospect of rowing against ' the ebb was not a pleasant one. In vain we looked around for the welcome indications of a breeze! A black hulled screw passed us about a mile away and left a long train of smoke behind, him, but no consolation for us. Nature and art alike had left us tqabenefit by our own exertions. For fear of the ebb we thought best to get into sound- ings as soon as possible, so the course was altered for Chester Bar. On this coursawe fondle a favouring tide setting to the south. Off the W. Hoyle Buoy two ves- sels, a barque and a schooner, lay at anclw becalmed, their crews lazily interchanging ideas to while away the time. "Slow by degrees and beautifully less" became 'the distance between us and our old friend the dumpy Bell Buoy, and then our next points of attainment were the Dee lightship and the Point of Ayr. Here the "spell" at the oars had fallen upon Al!. and myself, and Simon overcome by his loyalty of the previous evening, had succumbed to the solicitations of Somnus and lay stretched on a seat in happy oblivion of passing events, even to the little breeze now fanning our cheeks and fil- ling our hitherto idle sails with its welcome breath. This breeze which we bad now rowed into was from the N., a seabreeze, and gradually strengthened into a nice whole-sail puff, which spun us along through the Welshman's gut, round the south end of W. Hoyle Bank, across Hilbre Swash, and into the channel between Hilbre Island and East Hoyle, thenthrough the channel of many windings into Eloylake.

And here, once more upon the familiar cockle-beds, practically ended our very pleasant summer's outing. And very pleasant indeed it had been, despite the too frequent lapses bf the old element—the circumambient —from the path of duty—said duty being, in eur eyes, to aid navigators to overcome the other old element— the 'circumfluent—and the unwelcome iteration of the try "To oars, to oars." But, as difficulties are merely something to be overcome, we overcome them, and were, I doubt not, all the better for the struggle ; for rowing, even if compulsory, is grand exercise, and I am sure we had a full benefit of that. Indeed this world appears to be so constituted that what, to our imperfect kno:vledge, seems to be evil and •disastrous, often turns out to be benefits and blessings. And these "blessings in dis- guise" very frequently fall to the lot of "they that go down to the sea in ships," but perhaps by the benefi- cience of the "sweet little cherub that sits up aloft." " Jack " often comes out of these trials the better armed for those to come; and, in the meantime, who is merrier than he? To put it nautically and antithetically, he is never "hove down" except when "hard up," and if he meets a friend with a "shot in the locker" too often gets, with him, "three sheets in the wind,"eis "taken aback" and has to "cut and run." Now here are a few sea-phrases, many of them in common use ashore, and by people who know as little of their mean- ing anclorigin as • Jack" himself would of the verbiage ofa legal document. tome of these sea-terms have, I believe, been puzzling the philologists not a little; whereas a slight knowledge of " Jack's ' business renders them plain and easily understood. It is one of the benefits of yatching that it not only brings into play faculities, as a rule, unused ashore, but makk us acquainted—if not with strange bed-fdllows—and it is like poverty in that respect some- times—at least with strange phrases. Now, when a ship is "hove down "—that is careered—laid over ot her side

There was another gentleman to whom, if they would allow him; he should like to refer—he had mentioned hinThefore in that hall at the election of 1886—that was Mr. R. W. Murray, of Belfast. (Hisses.) Mr. Murray had written a letter about- his (Mr. Crosfield's) speech in that hall at the large meeting he had alluded to. Mr; Murray said he (Mr. Crosfield) was not a statesihn. Well, he never pretended to be a statesman. (Laughter.) tAnd Mr. Murray said he was not going to be guided by him. He should be very sorry to hold the same opinions as 111 r. Murray. (Applause.) Mr. Murray said he claimed to be a Liberal, but he (Mr. Crosfield) said he was not a Liberal. (Hear, hear.) They discridned Mr. Murray as a member of the Liberal Party- if he ever was a Liberal, he was a deserter. (Laughter and applause.) He was not a Liberal either in mind or in pocket. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Murray lived 15 years in Warrington, and amassed a large fortune. He (Mr. Croslield) was the treasurer of the Liberal party during the whole of that time, and gave hundreds off: pounds out of his own pocket to maintain the party— ' (applause)—but this Mr. Murray, who called himself a Liberal, never gave him one shilling. (A Voice: He is a false Liberal.) Then as to Mr. Murray's antecedents. He fought in the Confederate army • he fought ger slavery against freedom, and he was fighting for it now. • (Hear, hear, and applause.) Last week he (Mr. Cros-' field) bad the great privilege of being present in the Free Trlde Hall, and heard that splendid speech of that noble man, Lord Spencer—(applause)—and he was.very much struck with one portion of the speech. Let them remem- ber this, that Lord Spencer was the Lord Lieutenant of Ireland for nine years, a longer time than any Lord Lieutenant living m the. past or in the present, and probably there was no 2-Mtn, no Englishman at l events, that knew better the merits of that • Irish question than Lord Spencer did. (Hear, hear.) , Lord Spencer referred to the injustice which is being perpetrated in Ireland. , This measure, Which was a Coercion Bill, was obtained —don't h r .3-et this—by fraud. (Hear, hear.) That• was a serious accusation to make, but it was per- lectly true. The Tories at the last election took care not to let electors know anything about the introduction of that so-called Crimes Bill, which was a coercion bill. They kept that in the dark. If the people of England had known what that abominable Tory Government was going to do the Tory members now in the House of Com- mons would not have been there—they would never have been elected. The English are a people that are fond of justice and freedom, and not of injustice and cruelty. There were people they might have heard of that were called resident magistrates, and these people had it in their power and at their own discretion and their own judgment of sending patriots like Sullivan and O'Brien to prison. ("Shame.") Yet, as Lord Spencer said these men were not condemned according to 'law; they were condemned according to the will of a resident magistrate. And who were these resident magistrates ?, They were ex-captains of the army, they were fellows who had broken down on the turf--(laughter and ap- plause)—or brieftess barristers like Mr. Robert Pierpoint —(loud laughter)—or silly; childish, bigoted Tories like Harry Appleton. (Renewed laughter.) That class of Tories that he had mentioned would do admirably to administer injustice in Ireland, and he should recommend this Tory Government at once to send the two gentlemen he had named over to that country. (Laughter and applause) He should like to.refer to that splendid meetingteld in Leinster Hall, Dublin' at which. Mr. Jbhn Morley and Lord Ripon were present. (Loud applause.) That was a red-letter day in the history of Ireland; it marked the progress of time, and the future historian would not forget to'record the visit of those two great statesmen which carried peace to Ireland. 'Alley ware met by thousands of the people; the streets were crowded; and it was such a reception ES no two ministers from England ever received before. (Hear, hear.) But *liat did the "Times " newspaper Say? It said they were met by a lot of rabble. Yes, the3r.were all rabble, and he was part of the rabble, according to the "Times." But just let him remark this—that the " Times " newspaper was the biggest liar in England. (Loud laughter and applause.) He wished the editor Of that newspaper was there on that platform, and hewould tell him so to his face. (Laughter.) The " Times " news- paper ever since he could remember, and he could go back nearly forty years in his political life, had opposed everything in this country that had been for the gpod of the people. It had opposed everything and it had al- ways been defeated, and it would be defeated again. (Applause.) There was a great contrast between the classes of people who met Lord Ripon and Mr. Morley, and those who. met Lord flartington and Mr. Goscheri. (Hear, hear.) In the former case they had the heart of Lire nation. They had the Mayors of every town in Ire- land except two—Belfast and Londonderry. (Laughter. What did they think of that? Did it not speak the voice of the nation when they had the Mayor of nearly every town? (Hear, hear.) Bow many Mayors were there to meet Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen,he should like to know? (" None. ) They got a lot of felloivs, magnates as they called them, with money bags in their pockets, but these men did not make a nation : it was the people who made the nation. (Applause.) They did not care whether they had the dukes and the lords or net; England was ruled by the people .and for the people, and when the next general election ca.methey would show those Tories whether it was not so. (Ap— plause.) The dark cloud that had been over Ireland so long had got,a silver lining, and if the life of their great leader was spared he would lead them on to victory, and peace, contentment, and prosperity would spread over both England and Ireland. (Loud applause.) He had plea- sure in moving the following resolution :—" That the Liberals of Warrington desire to express their heartiest sympathy with the Irish nation and their leaders and , representatives in Parliament in the present crisis,/ and ' while condemning the cruel and unjustifiable manner in vihith the Coercion Act is being administered, are at the same time resolved to support by every legitimate means the demands of the people of Ireland for the concession to them of ?he right of self-government." (Loud ap- plause.) The Rev. E. MOORE, who was cordially received, se- conded the resolation. He believed, he said, that the way in which that so-called Crimes Bill, which was a brutal Coercion Act, was being administered in Ireland, was utterly repugnant to English feeling. (Hear, hear.) They did not see why men should I;ie Rut in prison for' doing that in Irtland which was nd crime whatever in England. (Hear, hear.) Not only that, but they found that the present administration of the Coercion Act by Mr. Balfour was utterly useless, and when the Govern- ment met, they would, if they spoke the truth, have nothing but a record of miserable failure to lay before it. (Loud applause.) Mr. F. Loocarmir, who was received with loud ap- plause, supported the proposal. It had often occurred to bnn, he said, to ask himself during the past few months of the reign of ,terror in Ireland, what had come over their people. When some morning, on taking up his paper, he read of some brutal act that had been per- petrated on some of the leaders of their people—when, for instance, he read of the stripping of the clothes from Mr. O'Brien and others—he remembered the words of their national poet,. Moore, that vengeance is sweet, but that vengeance on the tyrant was sweetest of all. (Ap- plause.) He had asked if his people had degenerated, for they all remembered the time when they would have struck blow for blow, yet to-day it appeared as thoug,h all the life had been crushed out of them. But he would not charge them with cowardice, for what re- 'strained them was the knowledge that to-day they had 'what they never had before—the sympathy of a great portion of the English people. ' (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) That enabled them to bear the troubles under which they suffered to-day. And what was it that induced the Irish people,to give two Englishmen who went over :to Dublin thd other day such an unexampled reception, but that they recognised them to be the ambassadors of the great Liberal party of this country, who, he might say, were now really and truly the friends of Ireland. ;(Loud applause.) • Mr. A. CROSFIELD, who met with a cordial reception, in supporting the re.sointion referred to the .hopeless nature of coercion as a policy for dealing with the Irish question. It was argued, he remarked, that if the Irish were told they could not have Home Rule they would ' cease to ask for it, but those who had read anything of the history of Ireland could scarcely think that the Irish people were likely to give up what they now asked for merely at the bidding of Lord Salisbury and Mr. Bal- four. (Hear, hear.) These who thought they would had very considerably underestimated the strength of the feeling in Ireland, and had forgotten that the love of country and the spirit of Irishmen were every whit as strong as the spirit and love of country of Englishmen. (Loud applause.) The resolution was then put to the Meeting, and cars tied unanimously by acclamation. -

for repairs—she is in " Jaek's " eyes on the sick list and symbolical of melancholy. Ashore, when you have neither money, goods, nor friends, you are hard up" and cannot "pay away." Afloat, whenthe master wants his ships head to "pay away," he orders the helm to be jammed' hardup "aweather, and it is hence at its most effective point, beyond which it cannot go. So that alike afloat and ashore to be "hard up" is to be at the end of your resources, so far as the pocket or the rudder I, are concerned. To have "three sheets in the wittd "is the marine equivalent of being unsteadily drunk. This lis a " square-rigged " expression. The square sails of ships are confined at their lower corners by " tacks " and "sheets." These terms ate interchangeable and depend upon the position of the vessel in regard to the wind. The "tack" is always on the windward lower corner of the sail and the "sheet" on the opposite or leeward one. Now, if by csreless steering or a sudden shift of wind happening before the sails can be " braced"' round, what was ' the "sheet" becomes the "tack " and the sails which before were "drawing" are now "backing ;" the ship is hence said to be "taken aback," staggers about like a drunken man, and, for the time being, all control of her is lost; to "cut and run" is a term some- what on a par with "slipping the cable," though sea- men often use this latter to express the paynient of the last sad debt of mortality. The phrase to "cut and run" has come down to us from the old days of hempen cables when, if ship at anchor got into trouble—elemental or otherwise—and had not time to recover her anchor and cable by the usual but slow method of the windlass or capstan, she "cut her cable and ran." Chain cables have abolished "cutting," while steam winces have rendered it unnerstcsary, the phrase itself fast becoming obsolete and incomprehensible, andis passing away—as is my too prolix one—" like a tale that is told."
GREAT LIBERAL MEETING' . AT WARRINGTON. SPEECHES BY. ME MAHONEY M.P., ALDER-
MAN DROSFIELD, AND OTHERS.

On Wednesday evening a mass meeting of the Liberals of Warrington was held in the Public Ffall, Rylands-street. The chair was taken by Councillor P. A. Roberts, and amongst those on a crowded plat- form were Mr. Pierce Mahoney, M.P., Alderman John Crosfield, Mr. C, M. Percy (Wigan), Mrs. Mahoney, Mrs. F. A, Roberts, and Miss Dickinson. The attend- ance was very large, the hall being completely filled, and the proceedings were of the most enthusiastic character.
The CHAIRMAN called upon Mr. H. Roberts to read some letters of apology. ' Mr. HENRY ROBERTS said the president of their asoociation, Mr. McMinnies, sent the following letter:—

"Summer House, Warrington, 7th February.—My dear sir,—l regret that lam not able to attend your meeting to-morrow evening. I think that Englishmen should take an especial interest in the wrongs of their Irish brethren. When inquisition shall be made into the cruelty and inius'ice of the policy of the present Govern- mentin the sister country, Ireland, Scotland; and Wales I will be found free from blame. The policy which you are meeting to condemn is supported really, and almost entirely, by the English people. At the next general election they will have the opportunity of reversing their previous judgment. Meanwhile they can only manifest their opposition to the proceedings in Ireland by meetings called publicly to condemn them. I hope you will have a successful and enthusiastic meeting.—l am, yours faithfully, J. G. MCMINNIES. Their chairman of that night had made a special and very nearly successful effort to get Mr. Jacob I Bright to be present. (Applause.) Mr. Bright, however, found it impossilde to come, and sent the following letter ;- 31, St. James' Place, S.W., January 24, 1888.—Dear Mr. Frank Roberts,—l regret not to be able to come to your meeting, but am full of engagsAments at that time. lam glad you are moving in politics. Warrington ought to send a member to support a Liberal Government. We know not how soon an election may come, and every possible preparation should be made.—Wishing you every success, believe me, yours very truly, JACOB BRIGHT.

Other apologies had been received from the Rev. John Yonge, who was out of town, the Rev. G. E. Young, the Bev. W. Brooks, Councillors J. Platt and J. Brown, who were both, unfortunately, unwell; Councillor W. Pierpoint, who was in Ireland; and Messrs. C. H. Broadbent and J. .P. Rylands, who sent their hearty wishes for the success of the meeting. Mr. Ziba, Armit- age wrote that he was sorry to be unable to attend the meeting to testify his increasing distrust of the present Government, both in their administration of Irish affairs and their ideas of domestic legislation; and Alderman Holmes, in apologising for his absence, wrote that so long as he had a Tote in Warrington he intended that it should be given on the Radical side. The CHAIRMAN, who was warmly applauded, said that perhaps they could not have chosen a better tiffie for that meeting than the eve of the meeting of Parliament, but unfortunately for them it happened that that was a bad night in Warrington. In Warrington, they always recognised that Wednesday was,given up to trade, but they were unable to make otheill arrangements, and he hoped they would be forgiven for having chosen a Wed- nesday night for their meeting. (Hear, hear.) They were met that night more especially to discuss—and they should have to discuss ,it again and again—the Irish question, and they were all favoured that night, not only by its being the eve of the opening of Parlia- ment, but also by having their platform grac,ed by the presence of an Irish lady. (Loud applause.) He was sure they would show Mrs. Mahoney the esteem in which her husband and his colleagues were held by the Liberal party in Warrington, and that they recognised the arduous work they had undertaken. (Loud ap- plause.)

Alderman JOHN CnosFELD was received with loud and continued cheering. At their last meeting, he said, in that hall, when they had the pleasure of listening to Lord Ripon—(applause)—he made a few remarks about Mr. John White. (Laughter and applause.). He had not done with Mr. John White yet. (Laughter.) He (Mr.' Crosfleld) told them that he thought Mr. White was a very appropriate man to be the chairman of a Nair Trade meeting, and that he advocated the laying of a 10s duty upon, corn imported into this country, the effect of which would be to raise the price of bread, to raise the rent of the farmer, to put money into the landlords' pockets, and to raise the " screw " of the agent. (Laughter and hear, hear.). It seemed to have touched his friend Mr. John White pretty deeply, for he (Mr. Crosiield) read afterwards in the paper that at a meeting held in Latchford, he attempted to reply to the speech made in that hall. But he could not deny that the lay, jug of a'duty on corn would not raise the price of bread, he could not deny that it would 'raise the • rent of the farmer, and he could not deny that it would put money into the landlords' pockets. All Mr. White said was that it would not affect him—John White—because he was paid by salary and not by commission. (Laughter.) He wanted them particularly to observe that Mr. John White could not deny what he stated, because what he stated was the truth. (Hear, hear.) He supposed that there were other agents in England, Ireland, and Scotland, besides Mr. John White. Mr. White might be a very big man, but he was not the only agent in the whole kingdom, and he (Mr. Crosfield) would venture to say that there were plenty of agents in England, Scotland, and Ireland, who, that day were receiving tess of what he called " screw " than they did ten years ago. • (Hear, hear.) Well, he thought that was enough for Mr. John White.. (Laughter.) But he would just remark that Mr. John White was very fortunate in being the agent of a very kind and excellent landlord— Lord Winmarleigh—and Lord Winmarleigh's property in Warrington had, as they must know, between Sankey- street and Wilson Patten-street, increased enormously in value during the last ten years. (Hear, hear.) Why had i it increased n value? Because of the increase of manu- factures in Warrington causing the necessity for houses to be built for people to live in. Therefore, Lord Win- marleigh. i was n a very comfortable positioit, and was not dependent upon the price of corn imported into this country, and he was quite able to continue Mr. Jbhn Whites salary. Lord Winmarleigh was perhaps now getting £l,OOO whew he used to get £lOO. (Hear, hear.)

Mr. MAHONY, M.P., who vas received with loud cheers, said that the very kind reception which they ac- corded himin Warrington nearly a year ago had made him feel that night as though he were going to address old friends (cheersl. They had passed a resolution that evening expressiig sympathy with him, with his coil leagues, and with the Irish people. Had they thought what they were doing? His opponehts said that he was a separatist, and that by passing that resolution those present were also separatists. (A Voice: They tell lies). He had not intended to give expression to his opinions in such very plain Saxon, but he was bound to admit that that remark had absolutely conveyed his opinion. He said that a meetinKlike the present, where they exprewd sympathy with thd.lr Irish brethren, and a meeting like that he attended in Dublin only a few days ago (Cheers) —where such a splendid reception was given to two of the English leaders—he said these facts proved that they Iwere not separatists (Cheers). These things proved that they were on _the right and on the only way that lead to a true union of the peoples (Cheers). He found that a great English statesman, and one of whom he wished to speak with all respect, as long ago as 1849 gave an accurate description of the Tory policy in Ireland. He was sorry to say that in 1849 it was also the policy of the Liberal party, but the Liberal party was one that was willing to learn and that was willing to acknowledge that it had gone wrong (Cheers). This was the description i of English policy n Ireland which Mr. Bright gave in 1849. Mr. Bright said that the "treatment of this Irish malady remains ever the same. We have nothing for it still but force and arms. You have an armed force there of 50,000 men to keep the people quiet. I presume that

t nreenattbeay trsoais is easy, ie mgoavyernm snore sold eandfifight tt that t keep he civilthe peace. That was a corzct description of the government of Ireland to-day. liey had an armed force holdin. down the Irish people and theonly remedy h • w the Tories noW propose—because local self-government was not going to be given to Ireland—was force and bribery. (Hear, hear). Exactly what Mr. Bright said so long ago, , was going to be done by th e Tory Government now. They proposed to bribe the Trish people by voting them large sums of money out of the pockets of the British ' taxpayer, to be squandered and wasted in Ireland—as they had always done in the past—to be squandered' and wasted because the Irish people were to have no control over the expenditure, to be squandered and wasted by a pack Of officials who gloried in spending and wasting it. They were trying in this way to bribe the Irish people. It was not only bad for the British taxpayers to have their money wasted in this way, b'ut it did not do one atom of good to the Irish people. It only demoralised them, and N. did them an infinite amount of harm. There was only one way in which public money could be satisfactorily spent in any Country, and that was when it was spent by the people themselves, under the control of the people and when the people felt that they had an interest in having it properly spent, because they would have to contribute towards it out of their own pockets (Hear, hear). There was one point, however, in which the description was not true, and he thanked God for it. Once "the civil power might snore at ease while soldiers fought to keep the peace," but now, thank God, they could not snore at ease any longer (Cheers). And why could not they? Because an appeal could now be made to the working classes in this country. Because they ,knew what was going on in Ireland now, and because before long they would, have an opportunity of pronouncing their Judgment upon it. They would have an opportunity of, either accepting those principles as their own, making them their own, and being respon- sible for them, or they would have an opportunity of repudiating them, of following all the best and most glorious traditions of their country, of striking a blow for freedom and for liberty and against tyranny and in- -justice (Cheers). But Mr. Bright was terribly shocked at the idea of ministers in England being hand-in-hand with the representatives of the Irish people. He said in a letter the other day—"lmagine what would be the position in which her Majesty would be placed if she had to ask one of those Irish members. to be one of her ministers." Well, he was old enough to remember when Mr. Bright was not regarded with any peculiar regard or affection by those gentlemen with whom he now associate& He remembered the day when Mr. Bright was regarded by what are commonly known as the upper classes, just in the same way as he (the speaker) and his colleagues were regarded at the present moment. Not only that, but he found a great friend of Mr. Bright's—the late Mr. •Richard Cobden—was once spoken of by the Times in very much the same manner that Mr. Parnell was spoken of not long ago. Things had changed with Mr. Bright, and they all regretted it, because in his old age, and when his powers were failing, he could not keep up the strong Liberalism of his youth. But, although they might regret it, that was no reason why they should follow Mr Bright. He (Mr Mahony) came there that night as an Irish Protestant. They were told that the life of a Protestant in Ireland would not be safe if they had Home Rule. He lived in a district of the country where the whole of the people were Roman Catholics. There was not another Protestdrit, except one of his own servants, living within three or four miles. He was living five miles from a town, and five miles from a police bar- racks. (Laughter.) He was, therefore, completely at the mercy es his Roman Catholic fellow countrymen, but when he came over to England he could leave his wife in the midst of that population without one single scruple or one single thought that she was in any danger. tlis wife and children were as safe there as in an Eng- lish town. He then gave statistics to prove that it was not the Roman Catholics that showed bigotry and intol- erance „ in Ireland. A Roman Catholic constituency sentf him to Parliament to represent it. They knewthat there were a number of people in the North of Ireland who were opposed to Home Rule, but they must not go away with the idea that the whole of Ulster was opposed to Home Rule. The majority, 17 out of 33, were in favour ' of Horne Rule. Ulster too, in a constitutional manner, had expressed her voice in favour of Home Rule. Those ' who were against Home Rule wanted to maintain privi- leges and ascendancy. Those who 'were in favour of it wanted to set up in Ireland a government before which all classes and all creeds should stand equal in the sight of the law. (Cheers.) They wanted no injustice; they only wanted equality. • He considered it an insult to Protestantism to say that it depended for its support in Ireland on British bayonets. He had more faith in Irish Protdlitantism than that. He asked them to give their fiupport, not to the privileged classes, but to the vast mass of the Irish people. They wanted to set up a Government that should do justice between all sections of the Irish people—a Government that should take the control over all purely Irish business. As regarded Im- perial inatters, they were perfectly content that they shouldibe managed by the Imperial Parl4ament-at-West/0: minster. They believed that then they would' be able to develop to the fullest possible extent their national in- terests and their national life, and as regarded the Empire at large they were perfectly willing to sink their nation- ality on equal terms with England and Scotland and Waless (Cheers.) People talked about the difficulties of the Home Rule scheme. Those difficulties were fast dis- appearing, and the reason of that was that the two peo- ples were being brought closer and closer together ; and what appeared to be great difficulties a few years ago would be found now to be as a mere nothing. The peo- ples would soon be able to approach one amother not with feelings of dissatisfaction, but as tried and trusted friends who had fought a grand battle for liberty shoulder to shoulder, and not only fought,but won. Refer- ring to the land question, Mr. Mahosty pointed out that the Irish tenant had an interest in his land, was in fact a joint owner, and that very often a plot of land repre- sented the savings not only of one man, but of his father and grandfather before him. If he was turned out because the rent was too high he could not take his property with him. 'Thus they would see what evictionmeant, and why it was such a terrible matter to the Irish tenant. He contended from his own know- ledge that the Irish tenants were asked to pay impossible rents, and proceeded to remark that their opponents said the Coercion Act created no new scheme, and only altered the procedure. But procedure was an important point, upon which much depended. Trial by jury was only a matter of 'procedure, and in Ireland they had re- sident magistrates instead, paid by the Government to do certain work. The suppression of meetings, and the Prosecution of newspaper proprietors and printers for publishing reports of proclaimed meetings were other instances. Since last he met them, Mr. Mahony con- tinued, many things had happened. Many cruelties had been perpetrated in the name of the law in Ireland, and they could now see plainly the policy of the Tory Government. There was no concealment of that policy, for Lord Salisbury gloried in it. If the Tory Government did succeed, what then? Their policy was strictly limited by the shores of Ireland—but there was a greater Ireland beyond the sea that they could not hold down. (Cheers). Mr. C. M. PERCY, who had a good reception, next ad- dressed the meeting. He said that there had never been a great question before the cosmtry, but that sotee weak- backed and weak-kneed Liberals made it an opportu- nity for leaving the party. They had the satisfaction of knowing, however, that if they had lost some of their old friends they had formed a new alliance—a perman- ent alliance between the deinocracies of England and Ire- land. (Cheers.) They had also had an opportunity of parting with some Menwho were drags upon the Liberal party, who held office in a Liberal Government, but who , were always Tory at heart. Under those circumstances he felt no very great grief that some of their-friends had gone to the camp which, perhaps, they should havegone to Many years ago. He was sorry that they had lost Such men as Mr. Bright and Mr. Chamberlain, and he was hopeful enough to believe that the day would come when they should see these men clothed again, and in their right minds. They were always ready to forget and forgive in politics. He was not sorry that men like Lord Hartington and Mr. Goschen had left them. Mr.Goschen never had an ounce of Liberalism in his whole system. Their opponents were very fond of saying that all the intellect of the Liberal party had left the Liberal ranks. But the Liberal party was not short of talent and ability, They had in the House of Lords men like Lords Ripon, Rosebery, Aberdeen, Granville, and Spencer— (cheers)—and in the House of Common there was no scarcity of talent amongst the Liberal party. If they did Mr. Crosfield the honour to send him to Parliament for Warrington, and some friendly constituency would send him (Mr. Percy), they would do their best to main- 'tamn the party in the House of Commons. (Laughter and cheers ) They had in the leader of the Liberal party alone a mighty host. (Cheers,) England refused to grant Home Rule to America, with the result that America ' fought for and gained independency. To othet colonies they granted Home Rule, and the result was that in the hour of danger these colonies would rush to the assistance ef the mother country. The Irish people asked for Home Rule, and they were entitled to. it. (Cheers.) England had tried for generations to govern Ireland, and what was the state of affairs to-day? They could not hold Ireland for a single hour without the aid of thousands of soldiers and armed constabulary. The members of the Irish party were called criminals •and rebels, but there was really not much difference be- tween patriots and rebels. A rebel was a man who failed; a patriot was a man who succeeded. Their cause would triumph, and the Irish members who were now rebels wouldebecome patriots in spite of all. The result of elections that had taken place during the past year was an indication of the feeling of the country. Even in the Tory party itself feelings of disgust at the policy of the Goveriament were on the increase. (Cheers). The meeting was then brought ti a conclusion by the passing of votes of thanks to the speakers and the chair- man.

THE EUROPEAN SITUATION. SECRET TREATIES.—WARNING TO RUSSIA AND PRANCE. SPEECE[ BY PRINCE BIS- MARCK. . . %nun, Stawaa.—lii well-informed circles bereft, is believed that there also exists an Italo-German treat) With regard to France of exactly the same 'kind an the li Austro-German one affecting Russia, providing, that is to say, for combined military action by Germany ami Italy in the event of one of these Powers being. attacke:. .. by France. and if this actually be the case, it is difficult tO imagine what better precautions could have been taken to presorve the peace of Europe whether threatened on the Rhine or on the Danube, or both these rivers at once. • ROME, SUNDAY Nicirr. —The publication of the Austro-, German treaty has made a very deep imptession here. Several politicians here expressed the opinion that it is an ultimatum, under a veiled form, and that it shows the determination of Prince ' Bismarck and Count .Ralnoky to put an end to the present 'equivocal state of things. , Prince Bismarck delivered a lengthy and iniportant sPeech in the German Parliamentaon Monday, on the Motion for first reading of the Military Loan Bill for fourteen millions sterling. The housivaa filled toeiver- flowing. The Chancellor said his object was to speak i'm the general situation in "Europe. Beginning 'with France, he said that Last year war with her was feared. but a peace-loving President had been elected, and Pacific tendencies prevailed. Turning to Russia, the Chancellor remarked that the situation mist not be judged by the comments of the press. The 'Russian newspapers he 'did not believe, but lid accepted abso- lutely the word of the Czar. He saw no cause 'for wnr in the concentration of Russian troops on the frontiers. Indeed, he went so far in his confidence as to say that even a war with France would not necessitat; a war with Russia, although the latter eventually Would involve the former. Russia, no - doubt, intended to make her voice heard at the next European crisis, and 'therefore she was 'bent ,on securing a good military position. The -next crisis is clearly that which will arise out of the Bulgarian' question, and the Chancellor remarked that Germany, a' all events, was only concerned in the Eastern Question in a secondary manner. He reviewed the services he had rendered to Russia. and went on to say that the German armaments were necessitated by the movements of Russia and France, "The pike in France and Russia comPelled the Germans to become carp?' The bill would enable the Government to supply the 'best (Weapons to the fathers of families who might' be called up under the new Military Bill, and the effect of the combined Measures would be that Germany wotild be able to place a million good soldiers on each of her frontiers and behinsl "hem would be the reserves. This was an achievemeni beyond the power of any other nation. "We Germans," concluded the Chancellor, "place our reliance in Oa •strength of our army. We fear God, and nothing else in the world." • . Beaux, MONDAY.—The Kreuz Zetivirg learns that the Russian frontier towns in the neighbourhood of •Ronigs. --7'berg have, during the last few days; each received ai garrison, consisting of one regiment of infantry, in addi- tion to the troops already stationed there. The fortifica- tions near Kovno are now completed, and afford room a - for 300,000. men. , Roars, Moanar.—Orders have .been issued from the ' ' War Office to push on with the greatest alacrity the. 'transformation of tho Wetherley into a repeating rifle • -It is the intention of the Minister to arm in-stew-month- ' not only the active army but the reserves likewise with ' he new rifle. Information received from Naples con- firms the news that rifles and ammunition will be Wit to King Menelek. • AMERICA AND CANADA.--LABOUR RIOTS. • -COTTON STRIKES. limy YORK, SUNDAY.—Telegrams• from Shenandoah state that the riotous scenes ef Friday were re-enacted last night. The police again intervened, and many shots were exchanged between them and • the rioters, ont• Policeman being wounded. A despatch from 'Pittsbuic States that the Knights of Labour at that place made an attack last evening upon the coloured workmen at the Solar Ironworks, Whereupon the negroes, having pro- vided themselves with arms, retaliated and wounded several of the Knights, some fatally. Tile strikes and , labour troubles are everywhere giving'riseto aniiety for tlie future." , TORONTO, SUNDAY.—The operatives of the Canada Cotton and the Stormont Cotton Companies of Corn- wall, Ontario, have struck work against a reduction 01 15 per cent in their wages. The number of persons thus thrown out of employment is 1,500. these mills being vv. largest in Canada. All efforts to effect a compromise . ' have proved fruitless, and large numbers of the men are !taring the town. • WRECK OF A BRITISH 'BARQUE.-21 LIVES LOS': ._ Maw Vont, TUESDAY MORNING.— Information ha- reached here that a barque, supposed to be the Aber- corn, belonging to Glasgow. was wrecked off the coa.a Washington territory) during the severe gale of Febru- =-, ' • ,Ary lst. The captain and 20 men perished, three seamen alone managing to save themselves by clinging to piedes . , ot the wreckage. tit _DESPERATE RIOTING IN SPAIN-el 5 PEOPLE KILLED. X , ADRID, SUNDAY NlGHT.—rhe men employed at the 4ire., 11-known Rio Tinto Copper Mines refused to work free days ago, and, uniting with the country folk, u.etnonstrated menacingly against the imactice of open rUr calcinations. Yesterday, the civil governor of Rlielva, accompanied by two companies of troops and ',cane civil guards, proceeded to Rio Tinto. He found tneostreets of the town occupied by an indignant and threatening crowd, numbering from '12,000 to 14,030 People. It was in vain that the governor tried to pro- 'serve order. He addressed the people from the balcony of the municipal buildings,•urging them to disperse in quietude. The crowd, however, responded by firini. • Pistols and exploding dynamite cartridges, all the whil,‘ reciting their grievances in a .shrieking tone. . TJ•e• soldiers then fired upon them; killing ten and woundin 2 Many, five of whom succumbed to •their injuries. fall of the leaders had a sobering effect upon. the agil•i tem and they gradually dispersed. Two of the .Soldici- were wounded. , OPERATION ON THE . CROWN NONCE..
