• Sir George Chetwynd, acting upon the advice of eoun- . sel, has determined to issue a writ against Lord Durham for libel in connection with the turf. SITE LIFE OFFICE .—The Sun Life Office, established so 1 Aig ego as 1810, has recently surpassed itself in declar- ing a larger cash and bonus than in any other previous division of profits. As much as 196 per cent of the an- nual premium (nearly two premiums) are now being Raid in cash. These rem arkable results justify the asset,. non that a profit policy opened with the Sun Life QIC9 can, be had at considerably less them cost price.
•( A'i

The Duchess of Westminster was safely delivered 9f a daughter at Eaton Hall on Sunday morning. TIM *UTLEY DOUBLE MURDER.—Dr. Forbes Wilmslow, having examined the man Taylor, who shot his son arid a police-inspector, at Otley, in November, believes him to be of unsound niind. More than 2,000 electric lamps are now in use in the coal mines of this country, and it is stated that miners are in favour of the change, as they benefit considerably by the increased illumination. At Newcastle-on-Tyne tenders were invited for £125,000, for which the Corporation only offered per cent. The response was remarkable. Tenders for be- tween five and six times the amount of the issue was received, and the Corporation obtained on the average a premium of £2 3s. Bd. per £lOO stock. VILLAGES ETTRIETI UNDER SNOW.—Abnormal snow- storms hare caused great devastations in Vol'hynia. Besides a great loss of life, 'numerous villages are literally buried under the snow, and traffic of any kind has becomeimpossible. In Galicia it has been snowing without interruption for the last two days. By the death of Mr. William West, at the age of 93, the theatrical world loses one of its oldest members. His first appearance dates back to 1802, when he played Cupid in*" Rollo." He was lessee of Drury-lane Theatre in 120, and, Sb conjunction with Elliston, he produced "Der Freischiitz " for the first time in England. A sad drowning case occurred at Matlock on Mon- day morning. Late on Sunday night Eli Frost, 20 years of age, a musician, was standing outside the Boathouse Hotel, waiting for some friends, and when leaning on the wall he fell through a broken part of the embankment into the river Derwent. As he was being carried down by the stream cries for help Were herd, but no assist- ance could be rendered. The body was recovered on Monday. At a meeting of the Governors and friends of Liver- pool University College, on Monday, promised donations were announced of £l,OOO each from Lord Derby, Messrs. Geo. Holt, A. Booth, end Henry Tate teltriards the fund for the extension of the University buildings. A letter was read from the Mar of Liverpool intinaating that he would give. alhousana-guineas, and Mr. E. K. Mits- pratt promised £l,OOO. The sum required for the exten- sion is £35,000. SUFFOCATED By A HEATFRO VURNACE.—ShortIy before midnight on Saturday, a sad fatal accident occurred at Brighton. Two brothers. Joseph and Alfred Trill, left home to attend to the furnaces of St. Matthew's Church, .RemptoWn. , tbey remained away longer than usual, two of their relatives went in search of them. On 'enter- ing thq furnace crypt they were almost overcome bythe fumes. Alfred Trill was found lying Close to the entrance in an insensible condition and his brother Joseph was lying on his back quite dead.

WIFE MURDER NEAR STOURBRIEGE.—A ShOekitlg' wife murder was committed at a cottage at Old Swniford, near Stourbridge, on Monday mbrnizig. Harriet Pearsall, wife of George Pearsall, a. talier was found m bed with her skull battered in: Her hViaband was afterwards arrested and charged with murdering her. The accused is seventy-nine years of age, and the deceased seventy- seven. She was last seep alive by her eon, James-Pear- sall, and was then asleep An bed with her husband. Later in the morning the latter was seen with his face 14e- sprinkled with blood. A heavy 'iron instrument was found under the bed with blood stains on it.

CArrourso A "GHOST." —For the past fortnight the inhabitants of ivvillage on the outskirts of Shrewsbury have been nightly terrified by the dangerous pranks of a "ghost." Late on Sunday inght,lowever, 50 villagers set out with sticks and missiles and succeeded in effect; log a capture. It wio discovered that the offender was a Welsh farmer who had recently gone to reside in the locality. His captors chastised him severely, and had it not been for timely interference he would probably have been lynched. He had a very narrow escape, and was otaly released on handing over £5 to the Salop Infirmary in payment for his folly. MR. SPURGEON AND THE BAPTTST UNION.—DY. Dale preached, on Sunday night, en the differences between Mr. Spurgeon and the Baptist,Union. His profound respect and affection for Mr. Spurgeon prevolated him from be- coming his critic, and as far as 'Congregationalists were concerned, the question was set at rest by the opinion taken by the Union in 1878. /Co change had taken place since that time to cause alarm. Speaking of the doctrine of the plenary inspiration of the Holy Scriptures, he said there were large nurnbersof Congregational pastors who had given up the doctrine, but who still found God in the Old and New Testament. As to the, doctrine of universal suffering, he and many others believed in the second death of all that were not in Christ. 'lle dealt at length with the other charges made by Mr. Spurgeon, and said he could see clearly that they might do great harm if they led to he Church indulging in suspicious criticisms of their pastors, instead of caring supremely for their personal loyalty to Christ. THE TURF SCANDAL: MEETTNG•OP THE JOCKEY CLUB.—L A meeting of the Jockey Club, called to consider the dispute between the Earl of Durham and 'Sir Geo. Chet- wynd. was held, on Tuesday, at the residence of Lorl Hastings, London, A considerable crowd assembled to watch the arrival of the members, a large number of whom attended, including Earl ado-, gan, Mr. Leopold di Rothschild, the Duke of Rich. mond, the Earl of Portsmouth, Lord Alington' Mr. Jas. Lowther, Lord Cork, Sir J.,Astley, the Earl of Durham, Sir George Chetwynd, Sir Henry Hawkins, Mr. Gerard, the Hon. Mr. Lambton, Lord Falmouth, Mr. Henry Chaplin, the Duke of St. Albans. Lord Rosslyn, and the Earl of Rosebery.—Lord astings, who presided, said the Stewards desired that the matter in dispute should be investigated by tvcourt of law: with a view to abitrki- tion.—Sir George Chetwynd said he understood from his legal advisers that he had no ground for action at law. —On the motion of the Duke of Richmond, seconded by Mr. Chaplin, a resolution was carried unanimously, to the effect that the dispute be taken to a court of law, with a view to arbitration.

&fowls* MURDER AT ALDERSItOT.—A murder of a most deliberate and cold-bloocind character was cern- mitted on Monday' morningat Aldershot, the perpetrator being George Ciarke. landlord of the Prince Albert public-house, who cut the throat -of his stepdaughter, Annie Vaughan, aged 18. Clarke was a bootmaker by trade, having a shop next door to the.public-hoitse, but last September he gave up his trade and took the public- house. He formerly served 22 yeafs'4n the army, and was in receipt of a pension. Latterly he behaved vio- lently towards his wife. Early on -Monday morning, Clarke went downstairs more than once to get drink. He afterwards got out of bed again, but instead of going downstairs, went to the room where , the deceased slept. There were three children in the same room.' He cut the deceksed's throat, it is supposed, while she was sleeping. On rdturning to his room, his wife, suspecting soinething was wrong, got up and went tsitlie stepdaughter's room. Clarke followed her, but she managed to lock the door against him. Finding the girl was •dead, Mrs. Clarke communicated with a neighbour from the win- dow, and Clarke, who had decamped, was pursued and captured. He was brought up at the police-court during the day, and formally remanded. . _

ARISTOCRATIC ASSAULT CASR.—At Westminster Police Court, on Saturday, Major Burrowes, 11th Flussars,, was charged with having assaulted his brother-in-law, Lord Howard dd Walden. It was stated in evidence that. Lady Howard vraa'scriously ill, and required the greatest quietude. Her husband attempted to force his wt into her bedroom while drunk, making a great noise in so doing, and Major Burrowes thereupon prevented him. A police constable said he was called to the house at three o'clock on Saturday morning by cries of "Police," and there found a gentleman bleeding from the face, with his head out of the dining-roont window: He complained of being assaulted, and pointed .to Major Burrowes, who was standing at the street door, as his assailant. The gentle- man, who said he was Lord Howard•de Walden, charged the defendant, and went to the station in ,a, cab. His lordship had been drinking.—Major Burrowes admitted the assault, and explained that 'his slater-in-law, Lady Howard de Walden, was lying seriously ill at the house, and the doctors advised the only possibility of saving her life was to keep her absolutely quiet. Her husband had been asked to keep away from her, but he got drunk in the house and made a noise. The major said Lord Howard attempted to force his way into his wife's room, and that he determined to prevent him, the result being that a collision occurred. Lord HOward seemed to be recovering from the effects of drink.—Dr. Thomas Dick- inson deposed that Lady Howard de Walden was suffer- Mg from peritonitis, and her life had been hanging on a thread.—Mr. Partridge adjourned the case, the defendant to enter to recognisances meanwhile. MURDER OF A DAUGIIITER. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE. et terrible crime was committed at Monk Bretton, about two miles from Barnsley, on Saturday night, Dr. Burke, a local medical practitioner, shooting dead his daughter Aileen and attempting to take his own life. It appears that about noon Dr. Burke went to the Neiman IniVand, with the exception of two or three short intervals, remained there bearly the whole of he' afternoon. About 10 o'clock he had apparently made up his mind to go to Barnsley with his wife and daughter, the latter aged 9 years, and with this intention he went to his residence and had his carriage got ready: Coming by the Norman Inn the three alighted, and remained in the parlour until the clock struck 1L At that hour Mrs. Burke saw her husband pull a revolver from his pocket. She screamed and rushed out of the room. She was met by Police-constable Emslie, who, hearing a shot, entered the room. He found the child dead, and SSW Dr. Burke droo the revolver on the hearthrug. and stagger to the side of the room, where he lay down on the seat. It was then discovered that in addition to shooting the child he had attempted to kill himself by firing at his breast with the same revolver, a six-chambered one. The bullet entered the left breast. Superintendent Kane, Inspector Ounn, and Dr. Sadler, were quickly on the spot. Dr. Burke was taken to the hospitiat at Barnsley, where the bullet was extracted on Sffiday morning.—An inquest was held on Monday, at the Norman Inn. Mrs. Burke said that late on Satur- day night her husbatid insisted on taking her and the child to Barnsley. On the road they stopped at the Nor- man Inn, where Burke called for a bottle of champagne. Witness, finding he had a revolver in his pocket, ran out for a policeman. She afterwards heard two shots fired. Police-constable Elnaslie "aid that I3urke first shot the girl dead, and then fired at bis own breast. A verdict of wilful murder against tlurke was returned. He is pro- gressing favourably, -

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 'll, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 'll, 1888.
DISASTROUS Fl S.-ENQRtOUS LOSSES.-SERIOGS ACCrtIENTS.

Shortly before one o'clock on Saturday morning, a tire broke out in the rifstishmentrrnom of the Oxford-road ltallway Station, Manchester. The City Brigade were promptly in attendance, but it was only after an hour's hard work that they succeeded in getting the flames -under. Between five and six o'clock, a fire occurred at Messrs. Baddeley's tea warehouse, a large building in The centre of the city. The names were extinguished in about an hour after the arrival of the brigade. Great damage was done in both eases. A terrible fire broke outon Saturday night on the wooden vessel Thomas Reed, nearly 2,000 tons burthen, lying in Bramley Moore Dock, Liverpool.. For several hours the flames baffled the efforts of the fire brigade, who on their arrival at the dock, were for a short time prevented getting access to the vessel owing to her being located some distance from the quay. The damage is estimated at £30,000, and the vessel was partly insured.

An alarming fire broke out about half-past one o'clock, on Saturday morning, in Upper Thames- street, London, at the rear of 145, Queen Vic- toria-street, in a large four-storied building, extend- ing between the two streets, and tenanted by Messrs. John Russell and Co., iron tube makers; Sutton, Sharpe, and Co., printers; Ryder and Davies, accoun- tants; and others. and used principally as offices. 'the fire burstoutin the casement and second floor, and spreadfrom the baelc to the front with great rapidity. A number of fire engines arrived, and a copious supply of water was poured on the building from steamers on both sides. For some time, however, this seemed to have little effect, as the fire had evidently got a firm hold of the basement, and was spreading with alarming speed to the upper floors. Engine after engine kept arriving, until about 'fifteen were at work. The damage, on the whole, will be enormous. The cause of the fire is unknown, and no person was on the premises when it .broke out.

On Monday night, just before 11 o'clock, the clothing factory of Messrs. Buckley and Son, which extends nearly the whole length of Greek-street and Bedford- , street, Leeds, suddenly broke into a mass of flame. Having started in a section of the extensive structure devoted to the making of hats and caps, the flames spread with startling rapidity, rendering all efforts to check them perfectly futile. By the time all the brigades in the town arrived this division of the building was enveloped in'fire from basement to roof. About a dozen jets played on 'both sides of the burning struoture, and the efforts of the firemen were directed to severing the flames from the next portion of the factory. The conflagration, however, continued its ravages withent any apparent check until after midnight. The whole centre of the town was illuminated by the flames, and from twenty to thirty thousand people assertibled., Buckley's premises are in the heart of a thickly-built warehouse district near the Town Flall, and the sur- rounding property, including the East-parade Congre- gational Chapel, was for some time in danger, so great was the heat and so risky the clouds of burning embers., Property and stock worth over NE20,000 was destroyed. The closing scene of the fire was marked by an accident, of a serious, but, fortunately, not of a fatal character. For some time a number of the people had secured a good 'view of the conflagration by clustering upon the -palisading which runs along the tide of East-parade Chapel in Greek-street. Shortly before one o'clock, the rails, for a distance pf fiftegp yards, linable any longer o stand the strain of so grldlit a crowd, gave way, and about thirty men and boys were precipitated into the area I lelow, a distance of 10 feet. Aid was soon forthcoming. i.:everal gentlemen made their way into the schoolroom •ander the chapel, and, breaking the windows, some of. the injured were lifted through. while others were raised MI the pavement. By the fall of the ironwork and masonry two men were so seriously injured that they Ind to be conveyed to the Infirmary. Fortunately, notice of the accident was given at the Infirmary, and the metnbers of the medical staff and a ntweber of nurses were in readiness to receive the injured. In all about twenty-three persons were taken to that institution to have their injuries dressed.

k T VIARRINGTQIIT .XOWN COUNCIL. I if.) . A quarterly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on, truest evening. The Mayor (Alderman T. H. Sutton) resided, and there were also present Aldermen Pickmere, Holmes, Burgess, Davies, Webster, Harrison; Councillors F. A. Roberts' Hokin, Jolley, Blackhurst, Francomb, Bolton, Fleming,9llutchinson, Platt, J. PierpoPat, Taylor, Marsh, H. Roberts, J. Shaw Green, Perci/al, Dixon, Greening, Wright; Messrs. Brook (town clerk). nWhittle (deputy town eler)r), and Chorley (borough °treasurer.)

THE TWO COMMISSIONS. - The TowN CLERK announced that a communication had been received fro ni the Crown Office, placing the names of Messrs. Richard Walker Francomb,Joseph Har- rison, and Thomas Sutton on the Crown Commission of the Peace. In answer to a question the Town Clerk said that there were two commissions, one the Duchy Commission, the other the Crown Commission. The gentlemen named had been on the Duchy Commission some time, and now they were put on the Crown Com- mission. Councillor PLATT asked what were the special pri- vileges of the Crown Commission over the Duchy. The Alavon : I don't kiTvr : it came on me as a sur- prise. Alderman Howcas said he had been told by the late town clerk that the Duchy Commission enabled the ma., gistrate to act within the Lancashire portion of the borough, and the Crown Commission enabled him to act on the Latchford side of the borough. The subject then dropped. WATCH COMMITTER. _ _ .

This Committee recommended that thedrivers of hack- ney carriages be required to wear badges in accordance with the hackney carriage bye-law, and also that cer- tain alteration be made in the bye-laws relating to the sale of articles in the streets by children. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor JOLLBY seconded, the adoption a the minu tee, which was agreed to. -

div.head: MR. BRUNNER, M.V., AT CHORLEY.
div.p: MR. BRUNNER, M.V., AT CHORLEY.

On Monday night, a Liberal rilefting was held at the Town Hall, Chorley, under the auspices of the Liberal flub. The audience assembled early, and for some time sang political songs set to popular music, concluding the series with " Auld Lang Sync 7 and the National Hymn. The'popular President of the Club, Mr. 3.. T. Thom, J.P., was received with cheers, which were 'intensified when the audience recognised Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., who was described during the evening as "The Hero of Northwich." Among those on the platform were Mr. Adam Lee, of Oldham (who,has recently made an in- structive journey through Trelancl); Mr..L'Carter. isecres tars' of the club); the Revs. P. M. 'limner, J. L. Fraser. G. Ride, T. Ashcroft, and B. Wilson; Messrs. J. Whitfield: Kellett Ashton, Sr..c. Several letters of napology from gentlemen who were unable to attend were read by the Secretary (Mr: Carter). The Rev. D. M. 13n/wan moved; "That his meeting Protests against the tyrannical administration of the Trish Coercio4 Act, whereby the liberty of 'the press and he freedom of speech are suppressed, and tenders• its hearty sympathy to the Irish people in this their hour of trial and suffering, and, in declaring its unabated con- iidence in our leader. Mr. Gladstone, and in'his policy of ,unciliation, trusts that an early opportunity .will be ziven to the constituencies of expressing their die- spproval of the policy of the present Government, and of signifying their abhorrence and detestation of the I,ersecution and ill-treatment accorded to Irish patriots ...nd the political opponents of the Government." Be held that the action of our present Government towards Ireland was directly contrary to the precepts and the ~rincjples‘of the religion they professed, and he, for one. was constrained to raise up his protest, in the name of religion, against the action of the Government. s Mr. Kettxrr ASHTON seconded the motion. ' .

'Mr. Baumann, M.P., spoke in support of the[rosolutiOn. He said it apnenred to him.that the Liberal Unionists in that town of Chorley had some power. He Was very glad to tell them that in his division of 'Northwich, in Cheshire, they did not amount to a row of pins.-(Laugh. ter.) He thought if Mr. Thom continued to appeal to tlie people of Charley in' the same 'noble spirit with which he had addressed them that - night, :he rieeo not fear the Unionists.. He Proceeded to criticise the Coercion Act, and to compare with it Acts, hap- pily repealed many years am'', against the combination of workmen in England. Under the Crimes Act, Mr. Balfour had the power to declare any association in Ireland a dangerous • association. Now, an association was defined in this Act as an assOciation of two or more persons, no matter whether they called Themselves by distinctive names or not. Mr. Balfour had the power to declare any association a dangerous association. A dan- gerous association was defined -tinder Section 6 in a good many ways. It was defined•as an association formed' or the commission of crimes." No one. would honestly object to associations formed for the commission of crimes being put down with a very strong, hand. But what was a crime ? In the latter part of the 6th section of the Act be found a crime defined as any offence punishable under the Act. He found in that same section that intimidation was an offence punishable under the Act, and it was defined in the 19th section as "includes any words calculated to [ put any person in fear of any injury to his business." An association might be two, or three, people, and if , amongst them they agreed not to trade with a particular [ shoemaker, they .used words or performed acts , ;calculated ' to put that shoemaker in fear of loss of business. 'Three , men might honestly 4ree that a particular shoemaker 'did not make iMod shoes, and thosr who suffered from corn might have strong opinions upon the subject. (Laughter.) Now,:what would they think of a law which put it in the power of Mr. Matthews, as Howe Secretary, to declare that those three people who had excited each other to co to this particular shoemaker, were a dangerous associa. don, and any one, of the members of it liable to six month's imprisonment with hard labour. The 'very first part of that. Act gave po.wer to any resident magistrate of Ireland, whenever he had reason to believe that a crime had been committed in a neighbourhood, to bold a sworn inquiry, and he was entitled to call before him anybody in We neighbour- hood, ,and oannel the person—rlietter it was man, woman, or'child—to give sworn information as to the supposed or real crime. Now that he had given them a definition .of crime, they could undershrnd what a tremendous encino of power had been put into the hands of those -reside& magistrates of Ireland. When they re- membered the ela.ss of men to whom that power had I been given, when they knew that a large proportion of I [ them were military men, and that a considerable section were broken-down betting men, and that only 14 out of 76 were men with any pretension to legal knowledge, would understand that the Irish people. were not nonvinced that they would get justice at the hands of ' inch men. Only six of the sections were discussed in the House of Commons, and when the discussion of the , 6th section had come to an end, Mr., smith. "on the p mime," as he was often described, moved' that the question be now put." The rest of the Act was pissed without discussion. How would they in England like to he put under an Act Of Parliament passed without discus- don? He claimed for the English that, having stronger backs thanthe Irish, they would send the Government that passed such an Act flying within a week. He reviewed the growth of trades unionism in England, and described its dark characteristics when under aim heel of the law. We had since acknowledged the right of the workmen to combine; we had passed an Act of Parliament legalis- ing trades unions; and the change that had come over this country in 30 years was remarkable. The leaders of their trades unions in Great Britain and, Ireland were now statemen—(hear, hear),—and when it was known that theywere about to address their fellows at the annual Trades Union Congress—no matter in what town of Britain—the whole brotherhood of labour the world over listened attentively to what they had to say. Mr. Brunner afterwards gave- a graphic description of the Mitchelstown transaction, and stated that what he had, seen there and elsewhere had caused him to C 01330 to the conclusion that as long asthe law was on the side of the Government and against the people the Government weuld uphold the law, but from the moment that the :aw was on the aide of 'the people and against the police the Government flouted the law. (Cheers.)
The resolution was carried. Mr. Adam Lee and other gentlemen afterwards ad- dressed the Fteettrig.

div.head: FINANCE,.
div.p: FINANCE,.

The following was contained in the minutes of the runenc,e Committee, viz. :—" The Committee had under consideration the resolution of the Condi of the 6th December last as to the advisability of ne Council pass- ing a resolution requiring each Committee to report quarterly to the Council the amount expended by them during the preceding three months, and showing the balance in hand of the estimated expenditure of each Committee. After discussing the return of the Borough Treasurer, showing the estimated and actual expenditure of the two principal spending Committeqs of the Town Council Sanitary Committee and Paving and Sewerage Committee for the last six years, it was resolved that, in the opinion of this Committee, such a resolution as that referred to is not necessary." Alderman LiouLes, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the Committee referred to had kept mainly. within their estimates, and he thought that on the whole' the Finance Committee had come to a right conclusion. ILast year was an exception, the Sanitary Committee having spent about £1,400 more than they estimated for. That arose largely from the fact that they, had to pay out of revenue what under ordinary circumstances would have been paid out of capital, and the same ap- plied to the Paving and Sewerage Committee which had also exceeded its estimates last year. Councillor GREENING seconded the adoption of the re- Port- Councillor F. A. Ronawrs, wfio was the mover of the resolution passed by the Council on the §th December, said he was glad to see that the resolution had caused the Sanitary Committee to go into the matter .and he thought it would do them.good. Councillor PLATT thought that the best course to take when it had expended all it had estimated for, would be to prepare a supplementary estimate and submit it to the Council before any further expenditure is incurred. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS, in replying, said the Chairman of the Finance Committee and borough treasurer were very exacting and required that the estimate of expenditure I of any Committee should be reduced within the nar- I rowest poSsible limits and they were not at all dispbsed I to listen to any argument for a slight margin being al- lowed for contingencies. It was hardly possible, there- fore to so frame the minutes of a Committee like the Sanitary Committee as to net all the emergencies that are perpetually showing themselves. In winter time, for instance, he had known an expenditure of nearly £lOO in a few days for clearing away snow from the streets. That was a kind of expenditure they could not estimate for. (Hear, hear). There was, again, the hospital. Last year it was comparatively empty, but this year he was soily to say it was too full, but they could not estimate in March for that increase; Mr. Chorley would not allow it. Alderman Hammon Mr: Chorley is a. great autocrat. (Laughter.) Alderman Bunoass : And properly so, too. (Laughter.) There are other, cogtingenties of a similar kind which could not be provided for in the estimates of the com- mittee. Alderman Burgess also referred to the expendi- ture of the Street Improvement Committee, who, he said, had "'in their wisdom or unwisdom, or something else," saddled the ratepayers with an expenditure of something like £l,OOO a year. After a few remarks by Councillors H. ROBERTS and BOLTON, Alderman Homing said he did not know why Alderman Burgess had entered into the statement he had made, because the Finance Committee had most thoroughly white-waphed the Sanitary Committee. They had tel them that from first to last they had been an exceedingly good lot of boys. (Laughter.) The minutes were then confirmed. • THE BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENT.,

Councillor Pr.wrr, in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Street Improvement Committee, referred to what had Veen said by Alderman Burgess as to the Bridge-street improvement, and said the committee would be extremely glad if they, could see their way to put a stop to the expenditure going on in connection with it. The improvement had been almost unanimously supported by the whole Council. The committ6e, how- ever, could not make the land sell \if it would no sell. (Hear, hear.) Councillor GREENING seconded the motion for the passing of the minutes. Alden:flan Dams thought it was , no reflection on the committee that they had not been able to sell the land. At tilie present time trade was not prosperous, and haci not been for the last five or six years, and it was, no doubt,owingin a, great measure to thav fact thatthe land was not sold. He was one of the few who objetted to the improvement being made' not because he did not think tt would be necessary. He only begged for time; he wanted this sad time to run over before they com- menced work. The committee must now wait patiently. The matter was in good hands. . The minutes were then agreed to. TES MINUTES OF THE SANITARY COMMITTEE.—COUNCILLOR DIXON AND tHE LONGFORD DEPoT.
haci
The minutes of-the Sanitary Committee contained recommendations for the acceptance of several small contracts.

Alderman BURGESS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he had to ask their indulgence while he read a short correspondence which reflected on a mem- ber of that Council to some extent. He was neither regular nor in order, but inasmuch as there was a mat- ter in the correspondence that reflected to some extent on a member of the Council, and as there had not been time to get it put upon the agenda paper, he thought it was better it should be discussed then rather than postponed fot a month.

The Council having decided to hear the letters read, Alderman Burgess said the first letter was dated 25th January, and was directed.to Mr Wilkinson, manager of the Sanitary Depbt, Birmingham. It was as follow: "Dear Sir,—l am directed by ,the Sanitary Committee of this borough to call your attention to certain remarks made by Mr. Councillor Dixonat the last meeting of our Town Council relative to a conversation Which he said he had with you. I'shall be glad if you will inform me whether you made use of the following expression: I am sorry to tell you that your works at Longford are anything but satisfactory,' and, if so, what your authority is for suckan expression ? I 'enclose a news- paper report of the Council nieeting."—This was the re- ply, signeil "John Wilkinson :" 6 Dear Sir,—l am in reteipt of your letter of the 25th inst. Will you oblige by informing me who Mr. Councillor Dixon is, and whether he is connected with a firm of galvanizers? If you will give me this information .I shall then, no doubt, be able to reply to your letter." The next letter read as follows :—" January 28. Dear Sir,—ln reply to your letter of yesterday's date"— Councilor Jona PIERPOINT (interrupting) : By whom is it signed ? Alderman BURGESS I would rather not say; I have reasons for it. (After a pause.) Well, it is Mr. Btook, your Town Clerk. The alderman then continued his, reading of the letter:—" In reply to yhur letter of yes- terday's date, I believe Mr. Councillor Dixon deals in speilter and galvanizing materials, and was some years ago the manager of a spelter works. He now describes lumselp as a metal merchant." -Then comes the reply of IMr. Wilkinson :—" I trust you will pardon ray asking you the question to which you have kindly replied, by 1 which I have been able to trace Mr. Dixon, and a,ble to 'say that I was 209 miles away when Mr. Dixon was at. these works, so that all I can sax is that the expression must bA one from his own imaginative brain." That is signed "John Wilkinson" so that according to Mr. Wil- kinson he has not seen lir. Dixon. He (Alderman Bur- gess) thanked them forlllowinghim thread the corms- -Ipondenee ; he thought it showed that under some con- ditions or other a stateAntmight be made which had a misleading effect. He had no doubt Mr. Dixon wouldk able to correct that in some way or other; but he should Ibe glad to be allowed to ask that the correspondence he had just read be embodied in the proceedings of the 'Council of that evening. (No, no.) If that could not be done it would come on the minutes in the ordinary

way. • councillor FRANCOME seconded the passing- of the minutes. Counallor DIXON .§aid the course he took with refer- ence to the works 'at Birmingham was this. He first wrote to the Town Hall there, and then went from Derby to Birmingham He had some time to spare, and 'he went to the Town Hall, and a gentleman gave him a note.

In addition to that he telephoned to the works, and said that he (Councillor Dixon) was about to visit them, and would someone be at the gates to take him over the I place. He went to the works. He did not know the nanie of the man he saw, but he was making a drawing for a new machine. When they were talking about the machine the remark was made that that was very differ- ent to what they had at Warrington. He (Counci)lor Dixon) thought the words quoted in the first letter were as nearly as he could remember the words that passed between the workman who went over the works with him and the man who showed him the drawings. • Alderman HARRISON: Mr. Dixon does not appear to have mentioned anyone. Councillor DIXON: I did not know the gentleman's name. Councillor Joins PisuPona : You took him to be one of the managers ? Councillor Dixox : Of course; he took me round. Councillor JOHN PIERPOIHr : I see nothing about the matter. Alderman HARRISON: I think you may make ytkur.con- science very easy, Mr. Dixon. Alderman HOLMES didn't think it was work while going into the subject any further, nor was 411 worth while to enter it on the minutes. (Hear, hear.) It might have been a lapses lingua on the part of Coun- cillor Dixon. _ _ .

Alderman BURGESS: j am now obliged to read another communication, which I did not intend to read. The lett* I am about to read is dated the 2nd February : "Dear sir,—l am instructed by my committee to thank you for your letter of the 28th ultt, which is quite satis- factory, and to state that they would be glad if you would ask the gentleman whom Mr. Dixon saw at your works whether he made use of the expression reported in the extract I sent to you?—Yours truly, W. H. BROOK." The reply is as follows :—`• Ibe to acknow- ledge the receipt of your letter of the 2nd inst., and to say that both the parties that saw Mr. Dixon deny hav- ing made any such statement. Moreover, they: had no knowledge of there being such works at Warrington.— Yours faithfully, JOHN WILKINSON. —W. H. Brook, Esq." Alderman Hkainsoic • That is rather awkward. Councillor Dram : ; one of the gentlemen said, "I have been two or three times to Warrington." He could tellme what the chairman would not tell me. _

Councillor H. ROBERTS thought it was time that this thing was put upon a proper footing. Councillor Dixon's explanation that night was a mean and contemptible ex- planation. (" Order.") It was a prevarication, and did not meet the statement which he made at the previous meeting. Councillor PLATT: I must appeal to you (the Mayor) not to allow the Council to drift into these personalities. (Hear, hear.) 1 Councillor H. ROBERTS: I think the Mayor will correct me if lam in error.
Councillor PLATT : I hope he will. you stand in need of it. _
The 3ffeYon hoped they would keep personal feeling rt of these discussions, _ _

Councillor H. ROBERTS said that this was entirely a personal matter. A member of the Council had made serious assertions based upon a statement that was proved to be untrue. ("No.") If Mr. Dixon was willing to act as an honourable man he would withdraw the statement that he made at the last meeting of the Council. Mr. Dixon had a motive in making that statement, and his motive was to damage the action of the Sanitary Com- mittee with regard to the management of Longford works, That kind of spirit should be put down. ColltleillOr JOHN PIERPOINT said that he thought it was time that this kind of discussion should be put down in the Council. Ve was surprised that a man of position like Mr. Roberts should so attempt to abuse another councillor.

_ Councillor H. ROBERTS: Call a spade a spade. Councillor JOHN PIBRPOINT said that he hoped that Mr. Dixon would be able to prove all that he had said. If he were Councillor Dixon he would make Councillor Roberts "pay for it." CouncillOr PERCIVAL said that it was time this kind Of thing should be put a stop to. He considered it very wrong indeed to introduce these personal remarks; it upset the whole meeting. Alderman PICEMERE said that it appeared to him that everything connected with the Sanitary Committee was of a very unsevoiuy character just now. He thought that the good sense of the Council would be best evinr,ed by ignoring entirely what had passed with reference to Mr. Dixon. He thought that they could afford to let the matter die out, and did not think that it should be en- tered as a record of their proceedings. Alderman BURGESS said that he introduced the ques- tion without staying anything of a severe character, con- tenting himself with reading the correspondence and asking the Council to allow it to form part of the pro- ceeding of that evening. It was nevertheless quite true that the correspondence was from that moment public property, although it might be suppressed in that cham- ber. Mr. Dixon, if he was right, would haVe an oppor- tunity of putting himself in a proper position, but he Said the manager," and there was only one manager at the works at Birmingham. The object of the Sani- tary Committee was that the statement made by Mr. Dixon, as on the authority of the manager at Birming- ham, should not go without explanation. The Sanitary Committee would go on with its work as before, and he was not afraid of the bulk of the ratepayers finding fault with them, although a small section might do so. , The MAYOR said that he hoped that in future they would be able to conduct their discussions in a more tem- perate manner. The minutes of the Committee were then passed, and it was agreed not to enter the correspondence in ques- tion as part of the record of the business.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Ten man have been summoned at Athenry, under the Crimes Act, for riot- and unlawful assembly when Mr. Blunt was being taken to gaoL Summerfield, the residence of the Ron. Mrs. Chichester, near Ballymena, was on Sunday night broken into, and a large quantity of plate and jewelry taken. Two men, named Magee and Mullein, were arrested on Sunday in Falcanagh, for taking part in on unlawful assembly on the occasion at Father, Stephen's arrest. A fire broke out, early on Saturday, at 131 and 132, Baggot-street, Dublin, a large restaurant. The 18 inmates, principally young ladies, were eafely rescued, and the fire • brigade afterwards reduced the conflagration to. harmless proportions.

At Edgrtorthtown (County Longford) Petty Sessions, on Saturday, six men charged with riot and assault on the police at the stopping of a hunting party were sen- tenced to six months' imprisonment, and one prisoner to four months. AO appealed, and were allowed out on bail. • At Clonmaesta, county Armagh, on Monday, a fisher- man received the Royal Humane Society's reward for rescuing three men from deowning, in Lough Neagh, last October. Seven men were returning from Nationalist meeting in Tyrone. when the •boat over- turned, and four of its occupants drowned. • •

At Milltown Malbay, on .saturday, several shopkeepers were prosecuted for refusing to supply bread and groceries to Mrs. Hannah Connell, who is caretaker of a Arm from which the tenant Was evicted. Two of the defendants, named Joseph O'Brien and Thady Flanagan, were each sentenced to thretraionths imprisonment with hard labour. On Saturday, the Master of the lolls dismissed the action brought against Cardinal Moran, Roman Catholic Archbishop of Sydney. Australia, and Dr. Brownrigg„ Roman Catholic Bishop of Ossory, Ireland, holding that £2,000 which Mrs. Fox gave the" Cardinal when Bishop of Ossory was given upon trust, not, specifically for the aged and infirm priests of that diocese, as she contended. but for the Diocesan Clerical Fund, and if not required for that, then for diocesan purposes generally.

. - The Mayor of Limerick and 11.. GuinanerJ.P., visiting justice, saw Mr. Cox, M.P., at Limerick Gaol, on Sunday. They found him in the infirmary, whither be was ordered on Saturday by the prison physician, Dr. Gelston. Mr. Cox stated that he had not sought the change, but, as tliedoctor found him suffering from loss of appetite, he considered it necessary to order him special medical treatment in the infirmary. Mr. Cox was in good spirits, and said hehad no complaint whatever to make.

A singular affair occurred in Belfast on Saturday. While a messenger was carrying a mail bag from a suburban branch to the General Post Office, a young man called attention to the fact. that he was losing his letters. On an examination it was discovered that a large hole had been cut or torn in the bottom of the bag, and the letters were strewn alonc,the road for a considerable distance. One containing £3O. addressed to the Postmaster, *as found opposite the residence of a local medical gentle- man. The authorities are investigating the affair. THE POPE AND. TFIE TRISH QUESTION. _ .

The Archbishop of 'roam, in openiiig the annual re- treat in Tuam Cathedral, on Tuesday, said rumours had been set about by certain newspapers .and interested persons that the Pope as oi posed to the legitimate a:- pirations of the Irish people!, but there ha 4 pever been fouler calumny invented. No heart beat with more, friendship to his people than that of Leo XIII. His high position imposed certain reserve,. but he would never turn against the legitimate aspirations of his people,
THE SULLIVAN APPEAL CASE.-THE CONVICTION
QUASIIED.

On Monday, in the Exchequer Division, Dublin, befori Chief Berm Pales, Baron Dowse, and Mr Justice Andrews the hearing was concluded of the habeas corpus at common law for the discharge of John Sullivan, who was convicted and sentenced to one month's imprison- tnent for conspiring to boycott Mrs. Curtin, whose husband was murdered by: Kerry moonlighters, the Court having decided on Monday, Baron Dowse dissent- ing, that they were entitled to look at the depositions to see if they sustained the conviction. Mr: Ronan and Mr. Cara.* for the Crown, argned that the evidence that Mrs. Curtin was partially boy- cotted, and had difficulty in getting persons to work for her, was proof of a conspiracy. The word "boycotted" was with all understood, and had been adopted into several languages. Baron Dowse: It is a recognised word. Aacording t,, a distinguished statesman, it is authorised by the Mosaic law. (Laughter.) . Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Healy, M.P., \contended that thf, evidence was insufficient, as it was proved that Hard- grin, whom Sullivan was alleged to have influenced, had previously refused to sliee horses for Mrs: Curtin. Chief Baron Pales and .Judge Andrews held that the evidence was insufficient; that it was not enough to say Mrs. Curtin was boycotted, but evidence proving a con- spiracy against her, and connecting Sullivan with it, should be given. They, therefore, ordered his discharge. The. announcement was received with cheers. Baron Dowse, dissenting, held that the Court could only look at the depositions to see had the magistrate, jurisdiction to enter, upon the inquiry. The prisoner Was liberated, and himself and his counsel were loudly cheered as they left the court. The judgment has created great consternation as being con- trary to that of the Queen's Bench, where a certiorari to bring up the conviction to be quashed. for insufficient evidence was unanimously refused.

The minutes were adopted on the motion of Alderman Horatrys, seconded by Alderman WeasTER. °Rival/Ai, PURPOSES cosourrpE. \ The minutes otthis Committee contained the follow- ing :—Resolution, that the town clerk give notice to the

Manchester Ship Canal Company, in accordance with and for the purposes of sub-section 19 of section 88 of the Manchester Ship Canal Act; 1885, that a new road is about to be constructed between The Latchford-read and the Wilderspool-causeway. Report of the sub-committee appointed to take proceedings in opposition to the pro- posal of the Corporation of Liverpool to lay the Vyrnwy Aqueduct on the bed of the Mersey, of the result of such proceedings. Report of Mr. Alderman Webster and Mr. Alderman Pickmere, that they had selected a site, and had erected a bronze tablet to mark the site of St. Aus- tin's Friary, bearing the following inscription :—" Here , stood the ancient Austin Fri, founded in the 13th . century. Excavations were me in the year 1886, and the walls and portions of the pavements of the nave and chancel of the church were discovered. This tablet is situate near the site of the west front of the church. The nave extended from this point eastwardly 89 feet, and had a breadth of 30f)eet ; the chancel extended 75 feet beyond it, with readth of 24 feet. Other remains were found to the north of the nave. This tablet is placed here by the Corporation of Warrington, with the consent of Mr. John Nunnerley, the owner of the pro- perty, to preserve the memory of the site, A.D. 1887. The MAYOR proposed the adoptioa of the report. Alderman atvirs, who seconded the motino, said that the changes in the formation of the railway caused by the continuation of the Ship Canal, would not affect the level crossing at Wilderspool-road, but from that point the railway would rise until it got to Latchford station, when it would be something like seventy feet high. He then read the report of the sub-committee with regard to the Vymwy scheme, shewing that the action of the Core poration had in that matter been very successful. Alderman Busoitss said that he thought that the Coun- cil should be congratulated on the result of the action they had taken. Councillor PLATT thought that the cost of the opposi- tion, £l2O 13s 3d, came to a large amount. He did not say that it could have been reduced, but the state of the law was such that- they • could not make applica- tions without counsPl, and without incurring other ex- penses. Councillor H. Romirrs thought the cost, when compared with the result, was infinitesimal. Alderman Davirs said that a third of the money was paid for technical evidence,which was really worth very little. The minutes were then adopted, and this being all the business, the Council rose.

THE S.ALFQ.RD TRAGEDY.-FURTHER DETAILS. RESULT OF THE POST-MORTEM EXAMINATION. /As might have been anticipated, the shocking tragedy, discovered in Salford on Friday, caused the greatest sensation not only in the district but throughout the country. On Saturday, .the house in Garfield-street. where Derby, after poisoning his wife and six children, committed suicide, was in possession of the police, one of whom was stationedrizeAde and another outside in the street in front of the house. The bodies lay precisely as they were found. Mr. D. Alexander Derby, in a further interview with a friend, says he is con- vinced that his "poor boy" (the affectionate way in which he alluded to the deceased) could not be right in his mind, because he (the father) does not receive a single shilling under the will of his late relative in Ireland, the whole of the property being left to his three sons (one of whom was the deceased) and his daughter. On the deceased's father going into the bed- room at Garfield-street, on Friday morning, he saw the box containing the will and papers, and the key was in the lock. The old gentleman was going to lock up the box and take the keys, but the constable in charge of the premises objected, and said nothing of the sort must be done. In answer to the question, "How long do you think your son and family have been dead ?" Mr. Alex. Derby said, "Well, that question I cannot deAnitely answer, but I shoultl think the deed was done on Thee- day. My reasorefor thinking so is this :—On Tuesday morning I received a letter from my other eon in Ireland saying that if 'Sam' (that is the deceased) would send back, either to him or to the lawyer in Ireland, the will and papers relating to the uncle's estate, he would do everything in his power to assist him in realising the estate and getting the money and his 'present specula- tion as to the patent,' This patent has reference to an invention which my son, the deceased, has brought out for preventing the jumping of the wheels of railway car- riages in passing. over joints of the rails. He has already patented it in England, and he required more money to patent it in Germany, Austria, France, and America. In that letter which I received from my son in Ireland he states that he has written Sam at the same time and to the same effect, so that I expect the letter would be delivered at Garfield- street on Tuesday morning. A letter has been found in the house in Garfield-street, which is dated Tuesday, and is evidently in answer to the one my eon Sam received prom his brother in Irelani. In that letter the deceased etys something to the effect that his brother's letter arrived too late, that his wife and children were gone, and that he was going too." Here the old gentleman burst into tears, and afterwards added that his son Sam was very affectionate towards his wife and family, and he never knew them to have a qualrel or " even a wrong word." Deceased was a steady man, very intelligent, and of a kindly disposition, and had been a total ab- stainer from boyhood. On Saturday morning, Mr. William Wilson, M.D., Broad-street, Pendleton, received the requisite authority from Mr. F. Price, the district coroner, to make a post- mortem examination of the bodies of the deceased. About noon, Dr. Wilson accompanied by Sergeant Wilson, the coroner's of'ficer, arrived at the house. During the afternoon a crowd gathered in front of the house, and a large number of persons were standing op- oosite on the footpath in Trafford-read, but even the 'nest humble were quiet and orderly in the extreme, And as they stood in knots of a dozen or so every face bore an expression of sorrow. Dr. Wilson. who has had long and varied experience in post-mortems, on arriv- ing in the kitchen at once proceeded to examine the body of the man Simnel Hill Derby. The body was found to be fairly well nourished, and ' there were no outward marks of violence of any kind. Dr. Wilson then began his dissection, nd opening the stomach there was emitted a strong smell of prussic acid. The examination was care- and exhaustive, and the operation occupied about two or three hours. Dr. Wilson then made an external •xatnination of thesernaining seven bodies, and came to 'li conclusion that it would not be necessary to dissect llThf them, as from ontward anpearance.s there could be no doubt death was produced by the same means in each ease, whatever that means might be. After making a. eostenortem et one of the young children, Dr. Wilson &sad his examination, and the stomachs and intestines /I the two bodies were plaoed in jars, sealed, and under his personal supervision conveyed to his surgery in 'tread-street, where the parts will be subjected to a imple analytical test, and, it is stated, there can belittle loutit that prussic acid has been the cause of death in 'ccli case. •

INQUEST AND VERDICT. The inquestion the bodies of Samuel Hill Derby, 313, knn Derby, his wife, 43, Ernest Llewe.llyn Derby, aged 13, Darold Percy Derby, 11; Frederick Cecil Derby, 9, 7111ra Elizabeth Derby, 7, Florence Helena Derby, 5, and (iladys Derby, 3, was held on Monday at Salford. ' A police-constable gave evidence of the finding of the hodies, as already described. rre found a cup on the bed where the children lay ; also the will of the deceased Mtn, and a letter addressed to" Dear Liz and Dick." Sarah Milner, a neighbour, said that on Monday last week she and her family were disturbed by a noise in Derby's house, as of furniture being mooed. A chemist named Cooper spoke of signing Derby's will m the 31st January. On that occasion Derby bought chloral. The murderer's father gave evidence as to-the excite- tuent of his son over faintly matlers, and said that the :ast time he saw his son he raised his hand to strike him. Evidence was given to show that the wife and chil- tlyen were lying murdered in the house when, on the 31st January, Derby induced his friends to sign his will, 6n which occasion he purchased syrup of chloral. The medical evidence was to the effect that 'all eight uersons died from prussic acid. Portions of 'several-. letters from the murderer were read, which indicated that he laboured under very bitter feelings as to certain members of his fanny.

Finally the jury returned a veidlOt "That the six children met their death by poison. administered by Samuel Hill Derby; that Ann Derby, his wife, was similarly rortrdered; and that Samuel Hill Derby himself committed suicide, being temporarily insane."

!THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1888.

THE Liberals of Warrington are typical of the rest of the country in showing themselves more and more earnest in their determination to secure Home Rule for Ireland. The meeting which was held in the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening, was ex- ceedingly crowded, and in the highest degree en- thusiastic. It is rare indeed that such a large assembly can be kept together until half-past ten; but, as Mr. PERCY jocularly remarked at the clone, they were ready, if need be, for a night of it. Happily, the principle of self-government is easily understood. Englishmen have pleaded for its operation at home and abroad; &Id now that the appeal is made for its application to Ireland they cannot see why this simple act of justice should , not be done. There has been a desperate attempt to raise a false issue, but it has utterly failed. The cry that Home Rule involves Separation is slot be- lieved in by those who raise it; and at Liberal meetings it is laughed at as a ridiculous bogy. The country is disgusted, too, by the perfidy of the present holders of office. As Mr. Joinv Caosirittp forcibly plait at the meeting, the Tories won the last election by means of fraud. There wr., talk on either side about coercion, except to saY that its day was past; and even the Tories and Liberal Unionists went the length of admitting that the, time had come when a large measure• of local self-government should be given to Ireland. But what happened ? As soon as Parliament met, they began to see that the Nationalists were all powerful in Ireland, that further power granted to Ireland meant further power granted to them, and would be used as lever to obtain a Home Rule Parliament. The - Ministry had convictions on the question of local self-government, but they had riot the courage of those convictions; and, instead of redeeming their pledges, they have meanly harked back to coer- cion. They did not dare to go forward; they have therefore turned back, and are inow flounder- ing as of yore in the Slough of Despond. Mr. PIERCE MAHON; M.P., drew a graphic picture of the situation in Ireland, and retorted with tell- ing effect upon the PRIMB MINISTER'S statement', that the Nationalists are a dishonest party. He reminded his audience that Lord SALISBURY had said it would be dishonest; to revise .the judicial rents; and then, when he found he could not carry , the Liberal Unionists with him, he had consented to such revision, although at the same time saying he did not believe in the proposal. Lord SAWS.' BURY had on his own showing done a dislcionest thing; and he should be, the last person to throw a stone at the Nationalist members of Parliament. Nothing could be more affective than the way in which Mr. MARONY described how he had been'affected by his experience as one of the Assistant Land Commissioners. He was not at that time a follower of Mr. PARNELL; but like General BULLER, he had a mind open to the teaching of facts; arid the knoWledge which he gained as an official convinced him that Irishmen would never have justice done to them until they could govern themselves by means of a Home Rule Parliament. As a Protestant Nationalist, elected to represent a Catholic constituency, his testimony to the tolerance of his Roman Catholic countrymen is invaluable. He proved by figures that are beyond question that the intolerance is on the side of the Orangemen of Ulster, who deliberately and systematically exclude men from office, how- ever qualified they may be, if they happen to be Roman Catholics. Altogether Mr. Mszomr's speech, moderate in tone, clear as to reasoning, and based upon indisputable facts, had a powerful effect upon the audience. It carried convietion with it, and was an assurance to his hearers that Englishmen rieed have no fear from such members as he in a Home Rule Parliament on College Green.

THE publication of the treaty of alliance between , Germany and Austria has created no little excite- ment on the continent and in this country. It is not that there is anything unexpected in the treaty; its purport has been known for some time to the great European Powers; but there is an object •in revealing it to all the world; and that object is to make it clear that if thepeace is broken it will be because Russia is the aggpasor. runs the first article of the treaty, "contrary to the hope and against the wish of both the high con- tracting parties, one of the two Empires should be attacked by Russia, then the high contracting parties bind themselves to assist each other with the entire military power of their Empires, and, accordingly, only to conclude peace by common agreement." There is nothing in the treaty of an offensive kind; its purpose is purely defensive; but , Russia is warned by it, and more especially by its being made public, that if she goes, to war with either Austria or Germany, she will be compelled , to grapple with both these powers. ; known for some time that such a treaty was in existence; but it has not prevented himmassing his troops on the Austrian frontier in a menacing ' fashion. He may have thought•that there would be a change of front if he showed himself disposed to push matters to the extreme; but in this he is -mistaken, and the treaty between Austria and Germany is published ,to let him see that he is mistaken. More than this, Prince BISMARCK, on Monday, made a speech on the question in the German Parliament which left nothing indeter- ' minate. He spoke with characteristic frankness and directness. "The warlike tendencies of France and Russia," he said, "drive us to defence." Ger- many has reason to fear that France will spring at her throat the moment she has her hands occupied by being at war with another Power. Austria has reason to believe that Russia weuld not hesitate to -seize Bulgaria, and attack her, if it were not for the fear of Germany; and thus it is that Germany - and Austria are mutually interested in helping • each other. It is natural that Russia should feel • disappointed with the result of her war with Turkey, as she counited on Bulgaria becoming, to all intents and purposes, a Russian province. It is • hateful to her to find resistance where it was so little expected, and that Austria considers that she is defending herself in standing by the treaty of Berlin. Prince BlsmAxcx is careful and courteous in his references to Russia—much more So than he is when he speaks of France. " Austria," he says, "is our natural ally in the dangers which threaten/ us from Russia and France. But there is no need to fear the hatred of Russia. No 'wars are waged from mere hatred, for otherwise France would have to be at war with Italy and the whole world." It is a sharp thrust at France to suggest that she cannot keep on good terms viith the rest of the world; but there is some ground for the accusation. Italy is in fear of France, and there is an. alliance between her and Germany and Austria. France is thus left to depend upon Russia, and what a connection it is—the most refined nation in Europe allying itself. with the most barbarous "It is not • and it cannot come to good." If France would be content to accept the inevitable, Russia would be \ effectually check-mated by Germany and Austria. As it is, there is danger even yet of Europe being set ablaze; for the CZAR is self-willed, and has a purpose to serve in pushing farther and farther south. So far as England is concerned, it is her • duty to keep her hands free and look 'calmly on. If Russia will insist in entering en a mad and wicked • war, there is no reason why we should emulate her madness and wickedness by joining in the fray. ,

THE Warrington Temperance Federation are to ' be congratulated upon the large representative meeting which, was held in the Public Iran, on Tuesday night, in support of the principles of the United Kingdom Alliance. The Rev.. Canon BARKER and Mr. J. H. RAPER attended as a depu- tation from the latter organisation, and delivered addresses, which, while strongly argumeiltative, Were admirably calculated to win their way to the • hearts of their hearers. The Federation is fortu- nate in having the Rev., S? WILKINSON as chair- • man, and the Rev. J. J. LANGHAM as _secretary.

Whilst two highly esteemed clergymen hold these important offices, it will be absurd to • say, as has sometimes been said, that the ..temperance move- ment is a Radical movement. It is a m4ter of course to admit that the Federation is political in so far as it seeks to influence _legislation on the licensing question. It would not deserve to exist 'if it failed in that respect; but it is a libel to assert

• that those who are active in the temperance move- ment are designing party men. Tie fact is, party politicians on both sides have too -long exercised an undue influence over thisir followers, with the result that the question of local option has been again and again shelved. ,If temperance men of all classes and creeds had thought less of the par- ticular party to which they happened to be attached, and more tof the mischief of the present licensing system, they would have been bound to- gether by itronger ties, and the reforms which 'they advocate would, long ago, have been placed upon the statute book. Still considerable head- way has been made, and there is good reason to believe that the cause is on the eve of victory. There is no politician of standing, be he Liberal • 'or Conservative, Nationalist or Unionist, who does not recognise that the time has come for making a great change in our licensing system. The late ' Government, as we know on the authority of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN had prepared a bill on the ques- tion; and the present Goverr,imient are pledged to introduce a measure dealing with' the question during the turrent session. The duty of Temper- ance Reformers at this moment is to be vigilant; they must see to it that they get what is really needed to effect a permanent improvemeht, namely, direct popular control of the granting of licenses. At present the great bulk of the inhabi- tants are as much shut off from any control of licenses, either by voice or vote, as if they were so many dumb driven cattle. If they sign memorials praying that no further plague spots shall be planted in their midst, the lordly people whossit on the Bench will not take the trouble, unless they happen to be in a particularly gracious mood, to read what is written. Such a remnant of serf- dom is humiliating, and requires to be swept away. Licensed houses are presumably established in a neighbourhood in the interests of the people; and it must be for thn' people to determine whether they will have them or not. Anything which stops short of this will be unsatisfactory and delusive, - and this is why, when Parliament is aboueto move In the matter, every effort should be made to see to it, not oily that it travels on the right cad, but that it goes the whole way. When striking is necessary, it is as well to strike 'Whilst the iron is hot.

LOCAL LAW CASE.—In. the High Court of Justice, Chancery, Division, on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice North, the case of Lord.Gerard—Oliphant v. Gerard, was heard. This was a summons to determine . whether certain appointments 'made by a married lady in her own favour could be supported so as to keep the appointed funds out of settlement, not- withstanding a covenant in the lady's marriage set- tlement to settle after acquired property. On the marriage of Lady Oliphant, the plaintiff in the summons, an ante-nuptial settlement was made which contained a covenant that all property com- ing to her at one time of the value of £5OO or up- wards should be settled. Her father, Lord Gerard, bequeathed her a legacy of £5,000, and bequeathed a further legacy of £4,000 in trust for such persons as she should appoint, with the expressed purpose of enabling her to deal with the fund in such way that it would not go into settlement. She executed nine appointments of the tund in her own favour; the eight bearing the earlier dates were appoint- ments of the sum of 5.450 each, part of the £4,000. The ninth referred to the eight previous appoint- ments, and dealt with the residue of the £4,000. Mr. Cozens Hardy, Q.c.. and Mr. T. C. Wright ap- peared for Lady Oliphant ; Mr. Decimus Sturges for the trustees of the will; Mr. G. Pemberton Leach for the trustees of the settlement. Mr. Justice North considered himself bound by the authority of "Bower v. Smith" (" L.R." 11, Eq. 279), decided by the late lArd Romilly, which holds that the appointed fends were excluded from the operation of the 'covenant notwithstanding the argument that doubt had been thrown on that Cage.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO:"
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO:"

- _ Lord Clanricarde has not yet filled up the cup of his iniquity. At an adjourned Quarter Sessions for Loughrea, held befoLe Judge Henn, there have been rearly 202 ejectmdfit processes applied for on his lordship's estate. Some men become famous, and some infamous.

Londoners are being invited to join in an elec- tric light supply; they can have one arc light by paying £3 for fittings, with a rental charge fofthe light of £3O per year. A modest proposal, truly Thousands of people in the metropolis have to live for a year on a less sum. The electric light is like the Divorce Court; it is open to rich and poor alike; but it is the rich only who can avail them- selves of it.

A temperance orator once described intoxicating liquor as 'liquid fire and distilled damnation." It would seem that manufacturers are determined to keep up its fiery reputation • for, on Monday, a publican named Bond was fined £l5 and costs, at Hanley, for selling gin adulterated with cayenne pepper and wate±.f The cayenne was used at the rate of four _grains per gallon; and the water was put 4, wasn't it? to neutralise the effect of the cayenne,' Very likely.

A" gentleman," said to be welfknoivn in hunt- ing circles' *has been fiqed £5 ,at Warwick, for travelling first-class in the railway with intent to defraud. He at first said he had given up his ticket, but this was found to be untrue. Ile pleaded in court that he was in liquor when the offence was committed. The old Latin proverb— en vino xeritas, was not exemplified in this in- stance; for in wine there was not truth." Perhaps the "gentleman" had been drinking beer.

The Surveyor to the Dean and Chapter of Can- terbury seems to be making an exhibition, in his drawing-room, of the supposed remains of St. Thomas of Canterbury. He does not show them to Dick, Tommy,, and Harry; but to those who have antiquarian tast9s ; and who, we presume, have spare shillings. "To such base uses may we come at last, Horatio." But is it quite lawful to go poking Lbout in graves, and carry the spoil off to ..one's drawing-room P

'The Crofters have not cried out before they were hurt. tn an aggregate of twenty-four cases the rent is reduced by the Commissioners from £323 to £l5B, or over 50 per cent; and of £824 arrears, '4616 has been cancelled, or 74 per cent. This means that those who have been paying the old rents have been plundered by their landlords, whose motto would seem to be :
Steal by night and steal by day, Doing it all in a legal way.

In Irelantl the landlords are crying out for com- pensation. They have liden pocketing Unjust rents, and now that rents are being legally reduced they would like the State to pay the clifrin-ence ! If justice were done, they would bit compelled to dis- gorge all they have obtained above the judicial rents. Their audacity is about equal to that of brewers, who, after doing their best to fill our gaols, workhouses, and lunatic asylums, have the hardi- hood to talk of compensation in case the Legisla- ture should think fit to reduce the number of licenses. These money-grubbers are rapacious.

The Sugar Bounties Conference is hlfely to bear fruit; there is every Prospect of the, bounty being removed from sugar exported from , Belgium, France, Holland, and Germany. But what of this country? Shall we be any better for the change? It may be that it will give a few sugar refiners a better chance in competition; but this advantage will be dearly purchased if the price of sugar is considerably increased. However, it is something' to know that, whichevrer way the matter goes, the change will not take place till next year. .

Meinrs. Cassell and Co. are issuing Milton's "Paradise Lost ", with the Dore illustrations— fifty in number—in monthly parts. When com- pleted, it will make a magnificient volume—one worthy, that is to say, of the great epic poem. A fund is being raised, it is interesting to note, to purchase and preserve the cottage in Chalfont St. Giles, Buck, in which Milton completed "Paradise Lost" and commenced "Paradise Regained." The Queen has contributed £2O towards the object. We have preserved Shakespeare's house; and it is fitting that loving care should be taken of this memorial of, Milton.

It is gratifying to see !low swiftly punishment has followed the crime of setting fire to and burn- ing down the Theatre Royal, Bolton. A dis- charged bill-sticker and scene-shifter named Pres- ton was, on Tuesday, sentenced to twelve years' penal servitude for the offence. He fieems to have been a drunken worthless fellow, who was rightly given the sack. He knew, however, the "ins and outs" of the Theatre, and, took his revenge by burning down the place. But when he had done the deed, he left tracks instead of making them; and now he has to pay the heavy penalty of his teriible crime. Rivenge is not sweet ;it 4s bitter.

Mules are proverbial as creatures that kick; but Peter Cawlen, a boatman, of Runcorn, -who is possessed of a mile that is said to be very wicked, 'kicks the animal instead of letting the animal kick him. He was charged with this offence on Mon- day ; but, as he gave the brute a bad character, he was let off on the payment of one shilling and costs. One of the magistrates gravely recom- mended that Cawley should take his mule to Buffalo Bill; but the boatman said, he thought it would be best to bring it to the police court and have it locked up. Mules have always been in bad repute, It was Mr. Disraeli, was it not ? who described Conservatism as "the mule of politics which engenders nothing."

Mr. Et. J. Tollemache, addressing his consti- tuents, at Frodsham, the other evening, said "the Government had passed a measure by which the agricultural labourer could now get allotments, and he believed It would be one of the most beneficial Acts ever placed on the Statute Book." There are peotle who will believe anything; it would be more to the -point if Mr. Tollemache would tell us if there is a single labourer in Cheshire who has i got an allotment under the Act. The Act is n existence certainly; but allotments under it are so fenced in as to be unapproachable. The moon is said to be made of green cheese; but what of that when it is beyond reach?

It is worthy of mention that, while there is a disposition in some quarters to vilify Mr. Brad- laugh, a Tory of Tories like Mr. Tollemache has a good word for him, He said:— He (Mr. Tollemache) wished also to allude to -the, Truck Act, which had been amended by a gentle- man whom he had many times denounced, and that was Mr. Bradlaugh. It *as owing to that gentleman's exertions that the Bill was passed; and he wished to say about that man that since he had been in the House ,of Commons—however much -they might differ from his political notions, how- ever much they might loathe and detest his religious views, still as a member of the, House of Commons Mr. Bradlaugh had been a shining example to every young inember. There was no man who had earned a bitter notoriety for obeying the rule of the House and showing courtesy to every member than Mr. Bradlaugh, and he (Mr. Tollemache) was extremely glad to say that was a true record of what he had • done.

Nar's Tic Plus, a specific in Neuralgia, Faceache, 91d. and 'l3d.; postage, ld., Of all Chemists.— Advt. IMPUDENT ,ROBBERY IN A BEERMOU:SE,—At the Prescot Pet tly Session's, on Tuesday, before Messrs. T. Pilkington and 11. R. d'A Willis, , Mary Murray, of Prescot, was charged with stealing ed,-the property of Jthne,s Doddy, a labourer, living in Tea-street. Mrs Doddy stated that on the previous night she was in the Shamrock Tavern, 'Tea-street, and dropped a sixpence on the floor. The prisoner, who was in the room, placed her foot on the sixpence, and afterwards picked it up and lefethe beer- house. Catlwring Dillon and Elizabeth Durkin, assis- tants at the Shamrock Tavern, gave corroborative evi- deuce, and added that they heard the prisoner say she had the sixpence but" divil a bit of it" would she give it back.—P.C. William Fisher apprehended the prisoner who, in reply to the charge, said "I have not got the sixpence I might be hanged for 2d."—The Bench com- mitted the prisoner for a month. ror all kinds of domestic sewing, Bagley and Wright scottoa Is the best.—Advt.
