div.head: EXAMINER, SITURDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SITURDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1888.
I I -
LOCAL NEWS.

THE RAINFORD Vicensuu.—This living has now been offered by the Vicar of Presc,ot to the Rev. John Wright Williams, Vicar of St. Mary's, Widnes, who was or- dained deacon in 1874, and priest in 1875, by the Bishop of Dowfi and Connor. Mr. Williams has held several important appointments in connection with the Irish Church. _ _ _

SCAL,DED TO DEATH AT WIDISES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, on Monday held an inquest at the Rose Sr Crown Inn, Moss Bank road, upon the body of Edith Babbitt, aged 3 years, daughter of Patrick Babbitt, labourer, of 2, Mary-street. It appeared that on Thurs- day, whilst Mrs. Babbitt was preparing dinner, the child, fell against the fender. In doing so she upset a pot of tea upon her head and breast, and was severely scalded. Dr. Nealon and Mr. Burgess were summoned and did all in their power for the sufferer, but death took place on the following morning. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. .

WIDNES Pentsn CM:MM.—The annual congregational tea party in connection with this church was held in the National Schools on Wednesday evening. About 350 persons were present. Afterwards, an entertain- ment was provided, and the room wa.scrowded. Mr. H. Wade Deadon, J.P., presided, and in his opening speech gave the history of the Church Extension Scheme, which resulted in the erection of St. Ambrose Church, at Hal- ton View, and St. Paul's Church at Anderson's Corner, at the cost of £5,153 and £5,728 respectivelY. The various details were published in this journal when the churches were constructed. The following vocalists took part in the entertainment :—Mrs. White, Miss Fogg, and Messrs. Broughton, Imison, J. Lea, Chinneck, Scott, Jones, Walker, and Bate. The chairman gave a couple of readings.—The chairman was cordially thanked for his presence, and for his labours in connection with the Church movement, Mr. Imison and the Vicar, who moved and seconded the motion, speaking in eulogistic terms of his services. A WIFE'S CLAIM FOR MAINTENANCE AT RIINCDUN.— Before Mr. C. Reynolds and MajorHazlehurst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Leah Howard applied for a maintenance order of 15s per week against her husband, William Howard, carpenter, Wellington-street. Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for the complainant, and Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared for the defendant.—Mr. Linaker ap- pliedlor an adjournment of the case, because he had not had time to collecethe evidence, as the summons was only issued on Thursday. His client had a good defence to the action, and there would be 15 or 18 witnesses to be examined.—Mr. Lake objected to an adjournment. This matter had been on the carpet since December last. On the 22nd of that month he wrote to Mr. Linaker declin- .ing an offer he had made, and stated that proceedings would be commenced. Other communications had passed between them, and last week he (Mr. Lake had an inter- view with Mr. A. Linaker, which was not satisfactory. It could not, therefore; be said that the matter had been sprung upon them.—After some further conversation, the Bench agreed to adjourn the case for a week, on Mr. Linaker undertaking to pay fmaintenance for that period should the complainant establish her,olahn.—Mt. Lake had previously pointed out that any order the Bench might make could not be retrospective. WIDNES CHEMICAL Irrists,—Messrs. Mather and Platt, of the Salford ironworks, having just now completed a well 800 feet deep for the Widnes Alkali Company, and which is' giving that company an abundant supply of water, are now engaged in preparing for the same people a Yaryan multiple evaporator fot the quick cOncentra- tion of their causticised liquor. Messrs. SulliVan and Company, Limited, are now at work, I understand, on Chance's waste recovery process; but surely all these troubles will soon become things of the past, for I hear that some genius has (at any rate, in his own fancy) dis- covered a process for making alkali waste into manure. Many years ago Mr. G. H. Bolton exhibited at the Earn- worth Agricultural Show some exceedingly fine potatoes grown by the aid of vat waste; and, again, at a meet- ing of the same society, a few years ago, Mr. F. H. Gossage recommended the farmers to follow up their grain crops by a very liberal dressing of "waste." Ctne local farmer has followed the advice more or less every year, but I belieye that two years ago he succeeded in growing" dead sea apples i " n place of potatoes through a too liberal dressing. However, if we get a British Guano Company established in Widnes to convert the presto into manure, the Leblanc manufacturer may take heart of grace," and consider that he is one step, at any rate, nearer Utopia.—Oil and Colourman's Journal. MERSEY MISSIONS TO SeemEx.—A series of special mis- sions reached their culminating point on Thursday even- ing, when, through the generosity of Mr. Henry Dodd, theworkers of the mission, numbering over 80, partook of an excellent tea. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Allen, Mrs. Cropper, Mrs. Mack, Mrs. Hulmes, Mrs. W. Littler, Mrs. Reid, Miss Garrett, Miss Bowyer, the Misses Waterworth, and Miss Allen. The subsequent proceedings were presided over by Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary, who expressed regret that the mission room was not large enough, and not in a suitable locality for the work that might be done by the staff of voluntary helpers he possessed. During the evening an interesting presentation was made to Mrs. Allen, the leadet of the Wednesday evening's Bible Class. The presents were a handsome bible, and a hymn book (Moody and Sankey), subscribed for by the members of the class; a bouquet of flowers and a book-marker from Mrs. Reid, and another book-marker from Mr. and Mrs. Wardle.—Mr. Dodd, in handing the offerings to Mrs. Allen, made a suitable speech, in which he spoke in high terms of the work accomplished 15Y Mr. Shaw and his assistants, and expressed a hope that Mrs. Allen would be long spared to continue her Christian labours.—Mrs. Allen gracefully acknowledged the gifts.—Mr. Meadow- croft, the honorary secretary, also spoke, and the cus- tomary votes of thanks brought an enjoyable eVening to a close.

HTJTCHINSON-STRIET PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF Horn, Wimses.—On Wednesday evening4o3and of Hope meeting, of a very pleasing and entertiamng character, was held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Hutchinson- street. Thera was a good attendance. Mr, Thomas Cooke, of Runcorn, presided, and in a most earnest and encouraging address, spoke of the blessings of teeto- talism, and , contrasted the misery and wretchedness caused by the excessive use of strong drink. Mr. Elijah Seddon also addressed the meeting. He said it gave him great pleasure to see Mr. Cooke occupying the position as chairman of that meeting. He remembered him some 19 years back, when, as a lad, belonging to their Band of Hope, singing and reciting for them at their meeting. Since that time he had always stood firm to Jis temperance principles. He strongly advised the young men present especially to keep firm to their pledge, as in after life they would never regret it. Duritig the even- ing a most pleasing programme was gone through, don- slating of recitations by Misses E. Lee, T. Overton, E. Smith, and J. Hill, and Messrs. R. Bellis, G. Smith, R. Pompet, C, Hill. H. Marshall, and E. Hill; song by Mr. J. Thompson; duett by Mr. J. Thompsen, and Mr. J. • Atikers, melodies by the chair, and a humorous dialogue by three young ladies. Mr. G. T. Barker, with his usual ability, acted a 4 accompanist. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, proposed by Mr. J. Thompson, seconded by Mr. W. Cooper, and supported by Mr. G. Seddon, brought what had been a most enjoyable meeting to a close. _ •

A" WICKED" MULE AT RUNCORN.—A PRIZE YOE BUFFALO BlLL.—Peter Cawley, a boatman, wae sum- moned before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday to answer a charge of cruelly illtreating a mule.—P.C. 243 said that on the 31st Jarwary he saw the defendant beat- ing a mule, at Top ,LoAs. The defendant kicked the animal on the stomach in a most shameful manper ; striking it about a dozen times. The excuse given Was that the mule was a wicked brute. The defendant said he " kicked " at the mule but did not "catch him." After being in the table for a few days it took seven or eight melt to start Ehe animal, which put, itself into all forms, and put four or five men down in a ruck. He called his daughter, who said.liier father kicked at the horse three times but did not hit it. He had had a few pints of bees and she took charge of the mule when the constable interfered. As she was taking the animal back to the stable, he jumped a wall. Mr. Reynolds said there was no doubt that mules were hard to manage, but kick- ing one in the stomach *as no way to manage the brute. In consideration that the mule was a wicked one, the defendant would only be fined is and costs, lOs As the defendant was leaving the Court, Mr. Reynolds advised the man to take the animal to Buffalo Bill at Manchester next time he had his boat there. (Loud laughter). He was really serious. If the defendant had a mule that would really make a show, Buffalo Bill would give a fair price for it. It is the best thing you can do with it. The defendant : I will bring it here and have it locked up. (Laughter). IRELAND, ITS BEAUTY AND ITS BLIGHT.—LIIIS was the title of a lecture delivered in Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, by Mr. W. Handley, secretary to the North- wich Division Liberal Association. The room wag crowded with an 'attentive and appreciative audience. • Mr. L. C. Beckett presided, and in opening the proceed- ings said the most impertant public queiston at the pre- sent time was Ireland. That night would be opened one of the most memorable sessions of the British House of Commons, and during the session the question of Ireland would be thoroughly debated. His only hope was that the question of Home Rule would, shortly be settled. They were not going to discuss Horne Rule that evening, but there seemed to be some misconception about Ireland, and it was thought that a course of illustrated lectures would induce some friends who had been doubtful on the question to come tq a right conclusion (Applause). ,The lecture consisted ot a large number of photographic and other views, thrown upon a streen by means of a oxy- hydrogen lantern, manipulated by Mr Horate Handley. Scenes of great natural beauty were shown, and appropriately described by the lecturer. The palatial mansions of ' the landlord were con- trasted with the miserable hovels of the poor, and Dublin Castle, the symbol of Deland's degra- dation, was represented. There were numerous other views represented, and in conclusion there were thrown upon the screen portraits of Mr. Parnell and. other Irish patriots, each being greeted rith cheers. Mr. Handley was a most efficient guide, and the facts of the history which he related in the course of the evening, were well chosen and admirably. delivered. The pleasure of those present was enchanced by the Irish airs performed on the piano by Mr. Ravenscroft, and by the vocal contri- .butions of Messrs. R. Moore, R. Morris, and T, Clegg. The usual votes of thanks were accorded,

LABOIJE.ERS IN TROUBLE.—At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, John Solomon and James connor were brought up on remand charged with having, on the 7th inst., been in the stack yard of Henry Ackerley, farmer, Higher Runcorn, for an unlawful purpose. They were discharged. FORTHCOMING• CONCERT AT WIDNES.—The date of the concert in aid of the Baptist Chapel, Widnes, an an- nouncement of which appears in our advertisement , columns, has been fixed for the 27th inst. Mr. Jude, the eminent musician of Liverpool, has charge of the arrangements, and, while taking a prominent part him- self, he will be assisted by vocalists of acknowledged position and ability. The concert is under the patronage of Mr. T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P. and the local gentry of all shades of political opinion, and those who attend, ' besides having a musical treat, will have the satis- faction of knowing that they are helping in a good cause.

WILFUL WASTE OF OIL AT WlDNES.—William Healey (1 a) son of a hatter living in Victoria-road, and John. Walsh (8) son of a widow with seven children, were summoned by Mr. Samuel Cowburn, contractor, for hay- mg two casks of oil on the 30th December. It appeared that the casks were placed on the Market Ground, and Walsh admitted that he had pulled out the bungs. The whole of the oil was wasted. Healey denied that he was implicated. A nunlike of boys were palled, and the. Bench de.cideld that Healey was innocent, and as Mr. Cowburn did not wish to press the case again Walsh, that boy's mother was ordered to pay the costs 13s.

Mn. Cmulexs Weae, OF. Ruecons.—The "Oil and Colourrnan's Journal" thus refers to this gentleman The retirement is now formally announced of Mr. Charles Wigg (who may be called it founder) from the firm of Wiee Bros and Steele' of Runcorn. It speaks se, • volumes for the management of that place when I in- form your readers that maey yerus ago Sir Richard Brooke, Bart.,. of Nerton Priory, obtained an injunction. to close the works of that firm pn account of. destruction of his timber and his tenants' crops; the significant fact being that it has never heeded to be enforced, and the .firm have of late turned so seriously to the production of colours as to greatly lessen any liability to the creation of offences to their neighbours. A WIDNRS.YOUTH COMHITTED FOR TRIAL.—At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, before Me. H. Wade Deacon, Ralph Goddard, aged 18 years, of 47, Mersey-road, was charged with having indecently assaulted Annie Mot- tershead, aged 13 years, daughter of ,Tames Metterebead, of 46, Cholmondeley-street. ' Mr. Knowles appeared for the defence. It appeared that the girl was domestic servant at the house of Goddard's parents, and on the 4th inst. /she was cleaning boots in the yard, when the pri- soner took her into a shed and acted in an indecent -fashion. The girl informed his Worship that the youth had on several occasions attempted to take liberties with her, but she had successfully resisted him. The prisoner was committed for the Quarter Sessions for trial. RUNCORN CO-OPED.ATITE SOCIETY.—The half-yearly meeting of the members of this society was held,,on Tues- day evening. Mr. Thomas Watson presided, and there was a gopd attendance. In their report the directors state that the total sales amount to £39,299 2s id, being an increase of £1,548 Os 10d on the previous half-year. , The profits realised after charging ' all expenses including depreciation and interest on capital, amount to £5,809 3s 10d, and after deducting the dividend paid in excess of amount provided last year and the checks purchased, the net amount disposable was £5,716 6s 514. The directors recommended a dividend of 3s in the pound on £38,298 of check 'account books brought in, which would' amount to £5,74e is, and the balance £l6 12s sed, to the reserve fund. The report and balance sheet was adopted. RUNCORN Beretax. BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. W. Littler presided, and there were present 'Messrs. Jas. Handley, J.P., R. Morris, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The Secretary reported that the interments. for the ten months ending January 25th numbered 301, correspond- ing period last year 271, increase 3Q. The fees received during the same period amounted to £312 18s 10d, last year £270 Os 2d, increase £42 18s Bd. Mr. Handley moved the adoption of the minutes of the Finance Com- mittee, who reported that the month's cash account had been examined and found correct. The fees received during the past Month amounted to £33 9s Bd, and after paying wages the sum of £25 5s 8d had been paid into bank. The sum to the credit of sinking fund account, £l5l 4s 2d, had been invested in Consols. Mr. R. Morris seconded the motion, which was carried. AMONGST POLES AT WIDNES.—A young man named Michael McCormick was brought before the Widnes ma- gistrates, on Thursday, charged with throwing a stone at Andrew Suttanavish, a Pole, who is employed at the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., and lives in Water-street. Several of the complainant's country- men were examined, and an interpreter had to be em- ployed. It was alleged that the defendant, without any provocation, had thrown a stone, whith had struck complainant on the head, and inflicted a wound. The defendant stated, and called several witnesses in corro- boration, that he was walking rapidly down Water- streef on the 23rd Jan., when the complainant tripped him, and he fell to the ground. Upon regaining his feet, he asked for the name of his assailant, when the Poles set upon him and maltreated him. The Bench dis- missed the case, on the ground that the Poles commenced the row. . THREATENING A WIDNES GROCER'S WIFE.-61 Thurs- day, at Widnes Petty Sessions, John O'Connor, a respec- table-looking man, was charged with threatening to as- sault Mrs. Gould, wife of Edward Gould, grocer, Lugs- dale-road,Widnes. Mr. Knowles was for the complainant, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the defendant.—lt was alleged that one Saturday night the defendant, who was under the influence of liquor, went into Gould's shop and throwing aweovereign on the counter told the son to take what he owed out of that. Mrs. Gould said he owed £2, and the defendant then called her foul names. Gould attempted to put him out, but the defendant seized him by the throat,but a man named McDermott pulled him of .—Mrs. Gould swore that she was in bodily fear.—For the defence it was stated defendant only owed is. 44d., and he had entered a case in the County Court for the receVery of the sovereigu Mrs. Gould had detained. It was denied that any threats were used.—After hearing the evidence, the defendant was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties of £5 each. UNLAWFULLY WOUNDED ATWIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., and H. Wade Deacon had before them another case of unlaw- fully wounding. The prisoner on this occasion is John Murthy, a middle-aged man, of 41, Cromwell-street, and the victim Patrick Malone, of Marsh-street. It appeared that late on Saturday evening the prisoner and the com- plainant, who were both labourers at Messrs. John Hutchinson and Company's works, were drinking in the Commercial Inn, when they began sparring. Afterwards they went into the works, and whilst there had some words, no doubt the outcome of the recent tussle. A man named James Riley, of West-street, who was near, soon after heard a thud, as of some one being struck, and turning round saw Malone falling to the ground. He had a large wound on his head, which was bleeding profusely, and near to lay a large piece of ore.. Riley did not see the atone thrown, but directly after he heard the noise ho *heard footsteps as of a person running away. Malone, who was afterwards attended to by Dr. Hutch- inson, now, lies in the Accident Hospital, and as he was too ill to attend on Monday, the case was remanded for a week. THE REAL OFFENDER PUNISHED AT WiDNES.—At Wid- nes Police Court on Monday, Ann Jane Wood, aged 15, of 4, Sankey-street. pleaded guilty to having, on Friday afternoon, stolen from Messrs. John Hutchinson and. Co.'s works•a quantity of ad, value about ld, the pro- perty of the firm. The defendant was seen to take the coal by P.C. Holbrook, and when asked by the officer why she committed the offence she said she wanted to put the coal on the fire at home; they had not bought any for the last three months.—Defendant's mother (on hearing this) stated that it was not true; she bought some coal only on Friday. She did not know her ichild went out to get coal. She had never brought any home and if the Bench would let her off she (the mother) I would see that it did not occur a,gain.—Mr. Gaskell (pointing to a strong iron bucket which contained the coal) : Who's bucket is that 7—Defendant's mother : It's mine, sir, but I did not kno* she had it.—lt was stateffley a representative of the firm that the company were desirous of putting a stop to the practice, not merely because of the value of the coal, but because of the nuisance.—lt was elicited by inquiries of the mother 1 that the father of the defendant was a labourer, but had I only *orked "off and on."—Mr, Gaskell, on passing sentence, told defendant's mother that if her daughter came up again she would most probably be sent to prison. It was her (the mother's) fault, and they were sorry they could not send her to prison. As it was, they would impose a fine of 20s, which she would have to pay. Rummer CIPIRCH INSTITUTE.—Under the auspices of this Institute a concert,, which was a success both as regards music and attendance, was given in the National School on Tuesday evening. The first part of the pro- gramme VS devoted to sacred pieces, and commenced with the motett "Hear my prayer" (Nfendelssohn), Miss Ward, of Liscazd,. and the Parish Church choir taking part. Miss Ward, who has a sweet, sympathetic voice, rendered the solo with much pathos and power, and the dhoir also acquitted themselves with credit. The march "Eli," for piano and harmonium, by Miss Isher- wood, Mrs. W. B. Kay, and Mr.W. Johnson, was much enjoyed; and Miss Hampson gave the solo "0 rest in the Lord" in a very pleasing manner. Mr. Garner did fairly well in the solo "Sound' an alarm." The duet, "Love divine," „feorn the "Daughter of Jairus," was rendered by Mr. -Littler and Master Hampson in vele, creditable fashion. Id the second part the choir contri- buted two choruses, and the amusing "Tickling trip," for which they were encored. An enthusiastic encore was also awarded Mr. R. Pierpoint for his clever and artistic. performance of the cornet solo, "The lost chord." A similar compliment was paid to Miss Isher- wood and Mrs. W. B. Kay, who treated the audience to fine rendeking of the pianoforte duet, " Tarentella." Is. Littler sang "The sea is England's glory" with commendable ehre and taste, and Mr. Gates'ga, rve a capital interpretation of "Down in the deep. Mr. Garner gave "The beggar's prayer," andl the concert concluded with the chorus The song of thesbrother- hood," sung by the choir by desire.
ACCIDENT AT_ A WIDNES CHEMICAL WOE/O.—Thomas

Comey, pf 5, Pitt-street, was following his employment at Messrs. Hutchinson and Co.'s works on Thursday, when he received a severe fracture to the scalp, and had, one of his hands severely crushed. He was wheeling a barrow, when a portion of it broke, and he fell heavily to the ground. He was attended to by Dr. Hutchinson. CONCHRT. It will be seen from our advertising columns that the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir have ar- ranged to give their second concert on Monday evening next, the 13th inst. The principal work is Henry Cow- ard's popular cantata "Magna Charts." The choir will be assisted on this occasibn by Miss Moulsdale, who has previously delighted Runcorn audiences and by Messrs. Thomas Allen and J. W. Maltby, who have established themselves in the principal pkovincial towns as artistes

a exceptional merit. WIDNES POLICE COURT.--YESLerday John COnnollev, Victoria-street, was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly on the previous day—Thomas Burke, of Turner-street, Warrington, was charged with having on the 9th inst. been drunk in charge of a horse and cart, and also with assaulting P.C. Messenger. • He was fined 103. and costs on each charge.---Peter Sinnott, of no address, and James Booth, of Widnes, were each sen- tenced to seven days' hard labour for sleeping in the works of Messrs. Gasket', Deacon, and Co.--For creat- ing a breach of the peace on the 28th ult. John Doyle was bound over to beof good behaviour forthreemonths. --John Henry Winstantey (11) was ordered to receive I six strokes with the birch-rod for having stolen es. from

the cupboard of his father's house. ° WIDNES. FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—The usual monthly meeting of the committee of this institution was held in the Town Hall, yesterday afternoon. Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided, and , there were also present—Dr. O'Keeffe and Messrs. J. Morrison, E. Carey, S. Sadler, and J. T. Allen, and Miss Proctor (librarian.)—The Librarian reported that there had been borrowed from the lending department ad consulted in the reference department 5,508 volumes, an increase of 23.overlast month in the lending, and a decrease of 43 in the refer- ence departments. The cash received had amounted to £3 14s sd, of which sum £2 4s 9d was for fines.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved, and Mr Sadler seconded, that the chair= man, Mr. Morrison, and Mr. S. Robinson, be authorised a sub-committee to purchase new books tothe value of about £l5O. The.number of persons who had visited the library during the month had been 13,186. PRIMROSE LEAGUE SOIREE AT RUNCORN.—The annual soiree in connection with the Runcorn Habitation of the Primrose League took place in the Runcorn Public Hall on Wednesday evening. The proceedings commenced with a tea, at which about 400 persons were prosent. Lady Brooke, the Ruling Councillor, presided over a table that was fixed upon the platform, and the re- mainder were in charge of Mesdames. Ford, Martin, Bell, Oates, Kirkham, Lightburn, Player, Pool; A. Timmins, Crosby, Barker, Rogerson, Horsefield, Gregory, C. Tim- mins, and Goodwell, and Miss Riley and Miss Lea. Aftertea. a concert was given, under the presidency of Lady Brooke, who was supported on the platform by the Misses Brook; the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., Colonel Bond, of Chepstone, the divisional agent, Mr. J. W. Lightburn, and Mr. T. H. Annett, the:secretary. Lady Brooke having made a few opening remarks, a long ad- dress was delivered by Colonel Bond. During the evening a brief programme of musical it6ms, was gone through, and subsequently the company indulged in dancing to the strains of Mr. James Woods' Quadrille , Band. The stewards were Messrs. J. J. W. Potter, Jas. Littler, W. Crosby, A. Lightburn..and N. 'Aladin. The refreshment department was ably c.arried out by Mr. 11. Jackson, of Wilson's Hotel, and the general arrange- ments wererunder the superintentience of Mr. Annett. SAD DEATH IN A FLAT AT RUNCORN.—Yesterday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest it the Burial !Board office, touching the death of Elizabeth Lunt, aged about 30 years.—William' Barker, captain of the flat Robert Harrison, Stated that about three weeks ago he met the deceased in Birkenhead. It was raining heavily and she was very wet. In answer to his questions she said her name was Elizabeth Smith, and that some time previously a man named Wm. Smithhadbrought her from Chester to marry her, and they had lived together in lodgings. One morning he deserted her before she was awake, and she was quite destitute, and had not tasted food for three days. He took her on board his flat, and gave her some tea; she was ula.ble to eat. After a few days she complained of her chest, and he took her to a chemist in Birkenhead, who prescribed for her. They had not lived together as man and wife. He took her on board, so that she could °keep the cabin clean and mind for him. Before she died the deceased told him her real name was Elizabeth Lunt,., and that her parents lived in Grosvenor-court, Grosvenor- street, Chester. He telegraphed there on Thursday, but received no answer.—Dr. McLennan said he was called to the woman at three o'clirk on Thursday morning. She was sitting in a flat at the ' docks. She was in a dying state at that time, and in his opinion death had resulted from inflammation of the lungs and failure of the heart's action.—The jury returned a verilict of death from natural cautes.

BRUNNER, MOND, AND CO., LIMITED.—The report of the directors of Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, to be submitted to the shareholders at the fourteenth half-yearly.ordinary general meeting of the com- pany, to be held at the Law Association-rooms, 14, Ceok-street, Liverpool, on Monday, the 20th inst., states that the balance-sheet and profit and loss ac- count show a. balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended on the 31st December, 1887, of £89,111 19s 10di which, with the amount brought freward from the previous half-year, makes a total of £124,656 us 7d. The directors recommend the following dividends :—On the preference capital, at 7 per cent. per annum, £11,043 4s 7d: on the ordinary capital, at 25 per cent. per annum, £70,625. VERDlN:—Pro- bate has been granted of the will, dated 23rd Feb- ruary, 1880, of the late Mr. Robert Verdin, of BroCk- hurat, Northwich, salt proprietor and manufacturei, M.P. for the Northwich Division of Cheshire, who died, aged 52 years, on the 25th July, 1887, a few days before the intendeddedication of g, public park, baths, and an infirmary which he had presented to Northwich. The testator bequeaths £5,000, to his brother, Mr. Joseph Verdin; XlOO to his niece, Josephine Margaret, the daughter of his late brother, Mr. Thomas Verdin; £5,000 in trust for the•benefit of his sister, Mrs. Margaret Emily Cooke, her hus- band, Mr. Frederick Cooke, and their Children; £5,000 each in trust for the benefit of his brother, Mr. John Verdin, and his sister, Miss Mary Verdin, With remainder on the decease of each to hjs brothers, Mr. Joseph and Mr. William Henry Verdint whom he appoints as executors, by whom the value of the petsonal estate has been declared at £76,215 15s. 6d., and to whom the testator devises in equal shares all his real estate and bequeaths the residue of his personal estate, but directs that the Brock- burst estate, with the contents of the house, shall be offered first for sale at the price of £34,000 to his said brother, Mr. Joseph Verdin, and if refused by him, then to his said brother, Mr. W. PENKETH WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCLI.TION.—On Wednesday evening the mem- bers of this association herd and discussed a paper by Mr. John Peers on "The text or its expounders: Is it incumbent upon believers to teach, the text literally and verbally as it stands in the Revised Bible?" The essayist contended that the text, as found in the first 19 verses of the bible with the very definite announcement of a six days' crea- tion—each day with its evening and morning—and again intermingled with the commandments, mu at be accepted by all believers in it as a divine revela- tion, literally and without alteration; and that the expounder who ventures to alter the word day as there given into the indefinite word period or age. is arrogating to himself the power to express the rqind and will of God better than He Himself has' done it. The essayist concluded by summing, up the gist of his arguments as follows :—lf the text be of God it needs no altering: if it be not of God, it is not worth altering therefore it is either a sin or a folly to alter it. Messrs. It. Garnett (chairman). C. E. Parker, J. Dignum, J. Watson, C. Davison, and A. White took part in the discussion which fol- lowed. The meeting concluded, in the utual man- ner. WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.—A meeting of members of the committee of this club was held on Wednesday evening in the large room of the Corn Exehange, Warrington. Mr. T. Percival presided, and there was a moderate attendance. A discussion took place with regard to the charges for the car- riage of milk by the various railway companies.— The Chairmin said the charge had been reduced by some of the railway companies from a penny per gallon under a distance of 20 miles to a halfpenny, whilstthe London and North-Western Railway Com- pany had only reduced their charge by one farthing ner gallon.—Mr. J. L. Stelfox. honorary secretary, intimated that there was moray to be held a meetingpf the Northern Committee of .the London and North-Western Railway Company, and he suggested that a deputation should be appointed from the 'Warrington Farmers,' Club to attend that meeting. —This proposal was agreed to. It was also. resolved, on the proposition of Mr. tiarsh, seconded by Mr. James Davies, that the, members of Parliament for the district should be communicated with. A dis- cussion was then introduced by the Chairman deal- ing with the question of foreign beef and mutton. On the proposition of Mr. J. Davies, seconded by Mr. A. Bretherton, a resolution was passqd in favour of legislating for the protection of con- sumers and the English farmers alike, and that copies of this resolution be forwarded to Lord Salis- bury and Mr. Gladstone. It was further agreed to forward copies of the resolution to the neighbouring Chambers of Agriculture and Farmers' Clubs, ask- ing them to support the action of the Warrington Club.—This was the principal business.

WELSH CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES. In connection with this place of worship a sale of . .

work was opened in Lacey-street Wesleyin School, on Monday afternoon. The Rev. J. Thomas, D.D., of Liverpool, had been announced to perform the opening ceremony, but in his unavoidable absence this duty was undertaken lay Mr. J. Edwards, of Liverpool, treasuref to the Union of Welsh Congre- gational Churches of Liverpool, Manchester, and District. After a hymn had been sung, the Rev. R. Burdon reed a portion of scripture, and the Rev. E. Hall offered yp prayer. The Rev. D. Davies, the pastor, explained that the object of the bazaar was to reduce the debt of £335, which at present rested upon the chapel. Twelve months ago the debt amounted to .CAO, but by the last bazaar they held thy were enabled to clear off £125, and about the same time the Union Of Welsh Congregationao Churches of Liverpool, Manchester. and District gave them a donation of £lOO towards the same ob- ject. The debt .was thus reduced to its present dimensions. He spoke in terms of praise of the ad- mirable work done by the members of the church, and thanked both them and the friends outside for their kind helj..,—Mr.. Edwards then delivered an appropri4te speech. He wished the Widnes. friends every success and stated that the members of the Idenonaination in Liverpool were always ready to help them as one of the weaker causes. He then declared the bazaar open.—On the motion of the Rev. R. Yeattnan, seconded by the Rev. 3. Bryant, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Edwards ,for his presence —Mr. Edwards, in responding, pro- mised that if they would raise £75 by that bazaar he would add another £lO. (Applause.) -The fair saleswomen then commenced the sale of their wares, which were of the usual character. Stall No. 1 was in charge °Mrs William Williams, Miss Williams, Ottilland-street. Misses A,. Hughes, Maggie Hughes, Hackney. Dorothy Roberts, Maggie Baggering-, aid Ellen Hughes. No, 2. Mrs E. Thomas (Vine-street); Misses Alice Owen, Morgan, and E. Jones. No. 3, • 'Mrs Leyshon, Miss Maggie Williains (Vine-street), and Miss Thomas (Mersey-road.) The refreshment ' stall was attended to by Miss Thomas (Frederick- ; street), Mesdames David Jones, Edwards, Thomas , Williams, and Richards. Various entertainments- were provided for the amusement of visitors. . . _

Concerts were held in one of the classrooms, Mr. Duxbury and the Rev. J. Bryant alternately acting as chairman. Songs, recitations, Szc., were given by Misses Maggie Hughes' Maggie Hackney, and Owen; Messrs. G. Lacey and John Jones. Mr. E. Hunt performed a violin solo, and Mr. Joseph Jones, who officiated as ac- companist, gave a solo on the pianoforte. The proceeds of the day amounted to £25. The sale was continued on Tuesday. The Rev. J. Thomas, D.D., of Liverpool, performed the opening ceremony. He expressed his sympathy with Mr. Davies and the friends of Widnes in the efforts they were mak- ing: He had taken some interest in this little eause from its commencement, as he had something to do with its formation, and he thotight that the members had .done very well. They had battled hard with the debt, and had brought it down to a very low figure compara- tively. He congratulated them upon the previous day's suceess, and expressed the hope that that day's sale would be even more successful. (Applause). On the motion of the Rev. D. Davies, seconded by Mr. Evan Thomas, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Dr. Thomas for his services.

-A POISONOUS e.THOS,'HERN. Dr. McDougall moved, "That the owners of this pro- perty be requested to disconnect, within the next fort- night, the present system of heating the Boardroom. and the offices connected therewith.' Dr. McDougall des- scribed how the rooms were heated by a coil of double iron pipes, containing hot air, and said after he had attended one or two meetings he came to the conclusion that the members did so at great risk to their health.. In their own interests, and the interest of those over whom they had supervision, it was neeesaary that an efficient method of heating and ventilation should be adoptedb At present there was practically no ventila- tion.—Mr. S. C. Beckett seconded the resolution, and, on the suggestion of Mr. Lake, the resolution was altered to read as follows :—" That the owners of this property be requested to dis Connect, as soon as possible, the present system of heating the Boardroom and the offices con- nected therewith, and provide for the heating of such room by means of the ordinary open fires in the future." In agreeing to this form, Dr. McDo igall slid the resolution was not meant to be a menace to the.Bcard of Commis- sioners, but he wished, something to be done before the next Board meeting.—The motion was carried unani- mously. ---- • -- • ------

div.head: YPAR'S WORK.
div.p: A YPAR'S WORK.

The Clerk then read a report which showed that-there was elementary school accommodationler -994 boys,. 851 girls, and 916 infants, ancl the mixed schools would. ac-. commodate 436 children; total, 3,197. The Education Department considered that school seats should be pro- vided for one-sixth of the population. Assuming the population of Runcorn to be 18,000, the number of seats recpiired would be 3,000, so that on this basis of compu- tation Runcorn was at present well provided with ele- mentary school accommodation. The average attend- ance during the year had been 2,409, an increase. on the previous year of 125. The per centage of attendance last year was 76, previous year 74. An analysis of the attendance showed that in voluntary schools, which ac- commodated five-sixths of the children, the per centage was 79, while in the Board schools it was only 68. The low per centage in the Board schools was attributable in some degree to the irregular attendance of canal boat children. In 1877 the number on the rolls was 2;541, the average attendance 1,724, and the per centage 67. Last year the figures were 3,150, 2,409, and 76 respectively, the increase being gradual throughout the years included. During the past year the visitors had served 2;102 warn- ing notices, and 287 parents appeared before the Attend- ance Committee. The number of eases taken before the magistrates was only 16, prosecutions having been sus- pended during the quarter portion of the •ydar owing to a difficulty about costs, whichlad now been, arranged. The payment of school fees, which had been, a vexed question in many places, had been happily settled in Runcorn, by the Guardians having appointed the School Board visitors their inquiry officers. As to the grants earned from tit Government, Greenway-road Mixed School amounted to £ll9 8s 2d, Gvenway-road Girls' School £B9 14s, and Mill Brow Infants £65. The grant - per head in these schools was 16s sd, 17s 3d, and 13s respectively. The average grant per head throughout England and Wales in 1886 was, for boy and girls, 17s 91d, and infants 14s 80. The average passes in the Board's Mixed School were 83, and in the Girls' School 87. The average passes for England and Wales,were 85-79. With regarel to finances, the amount drawn from the rates was £950, being equivalent to a rate of 4id in the £l. In round figures, this amount may be said to have been expended as follows :-2372, repayment of loans with interest; £365, administrative expenses; £26, in- dustrial schools; £157, loss on school wnrking ; and £3O cash balance. During the year there were twelve ordinary meetings of the Board, and fourteen special meetings. There were also 33 committee meetings for various purposes.—The report was adopted, and ordered to be printed, on the proposition of Dr. McDougall, seconded by Mr. Beckett.

and Miss Horton; Messrs. Morris, Scott, and MR linger. Mr. Joseph Pollitt and Mr. T. Riley gave recitations in the Lancashire dialect, while Mr. T. Clegg gave a humorous address. ,
ATTACK ON BAILIFFS AT WIDNES: A
ROUGH NEIGHBOURHOOD.

f At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before , Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. George Pilkington, Wil- liam Bradshaw and Elizabeth Bradshaw, husband and wife, were charged with assaulting Daniel Dag- nail, assistant bailiff of the St. Helens County Court. Ann Kites, a married woman, was also charged with assaulting another bailiff named Thomas Rigby.— Mr. J. W. Knowles, who prosecuted, stated that on the 31st January Alexander Attwell, chief bailiff to the St. Helens Court, came to Widnes to levy exe- cutions, and he was attended by two assistants named Dagnall and Rigby. Ho gave a warrant to Dagnall to take possesmon of the house 44, Midwood- street, occupied by Bradshaw, and Dagnafl went there. He obtainled admittance and told Mrs. Bradshaw of his errand, whereupon she asked if anybody had seen him enter. He replied yes, and she said "Well, if they saw you come in they shan't see you go out." She called to her husband, who Was upstairs, that there was a baliff in the house, and added "Come down and help me to ekuck him out." She then snatched the warrant out of Da. nail's hand, and whilst he was endeavouring to regain possession, the husband came on the scene, and struck Dagnall a blip* on the side of the head that sent him sprawling on the floor. In the struggle, he managed to admit Rigby, who was waiting outside' and at that moment Mrs. Kites appeared and struck Rigby on the head, sending his hat flying, and it had not been re- covered. Bradshaw seized the poker, and was holding it 'in threatening attitude when Mr. Attwell came up and ' caused a ee‘sation of hostilities by his interference. Dagnall was bleeding from a wound on the head. Both men were severely maltreated and Rigby had his watch broken. Midwood-street was a place to which the bailiffs had a great objection to go, but theywere obliged to do their duty. Each time they made their appearance they were shouted at and hooted, and not unfrequently stones were thrown at them. Bailiffs, like police officers, must be protected. Witnesses proved this statement. Bradshaw said, hearing his wife scream, and then seeing a strante man "wrestling with her like a bear" he thought he was only doing his duty in knocking him off. Mrs. Bradshaw stated that she simply took the warrant to read the contents, and denied having struck a blow. Mrs. Kites also denied the charge. The Bench fined Bradshaw lOs and costs 16s 6d, Mrs. Bradshaw- 5s and costs 17s 6d, Mrs. Kites 2s 6d and costs 21s. This in- cluded advocate's fee.

The Mayor (Alderman Sut- ton) presided, and there were also present—Alder- man Pickmere, Alderman Davies (hon. secretary to the Infirmary), Major Litton, Mr. Ziba Armitage (hon. sec. to the Hospital Saturday and 'Sunday Funds), Mr. J. R. Buckton (hon. treasurer to the Infirmary), Mr. John Roberts (chairman 'of the Working-men's Committee), Mr. Thomas Roberts (hon. sec. to the Working-men's Committee), Messrs. John Griffiths, W. Fielden, Charles Bunch, D. Dun- can, John Oldham. Thomas Ince, S. Ross, William Whelan, William Roberts, Samuel Wilson, H. lies- son, William Payne, George Chubb, H. Morkill, Hy. Eyes,. John Pemberton, William Crosskill, &c. A. list of the contributions of employees during 1687, amounting in the aggregate to £368 5s 71d, was presen- ted, and upon the motion of Mr. •TORN GRIFFITHS, SeCOn- ded by Mr. Jose ROBERTS, the report was adopted.—Mr ARMITAGE moved that all the gentlemen present, with power to add to their number, form the General Com- mittee for the ensuing year.—Alderman PICKMERE secon- ded, and the proposal was agreed to.—Mr. ARMITAGE mentioned that he had invited. 112 firms to appoint re- presentatiAs, but only 40 out of that number had sent in names.—The following were appointed the Executive Committee for the ensuing year :—Messrs. John Roberts, W. A. Lloyd, Joseph Potter, W. Fielded, John Griffiths, Thomas Knight, J. Scattergood, Thomas Burton, J. Har- pley, J. Taylor, George Gill, J. H Waring, Thomas Wadsworth, Samuel Ross, H. Jevons, Charles Bunch, Henry Eyes, and William Crosskill. Mr. ARMI- TAGE proposed that Mr. John Roberts act as chairman of the Executive Committees, and Alderman Devms seconded the proposal. Mr. Mr. ROBERTS said he was ready to stand aside in order that new blood might be infused into the office. ("No, no.") He had held the position of chairman of the com- mittee since its formation in 11180. The committee had, since its institution; done good work. In the first,year they obtained subscriptions to the amount of £165 98 30, whereas, before that movement was set on foot, the total subscriptions from the workpeople in and out- side the borough of Warrington only amounted to £5O or £6O a year. At the time of which he spoke the Infirmary had a balance of about £2OO on the wrong side and the committee set to work to convert that debt in a substantial credit balance. In 1881 their subscriptions amounted to £339 8s 10d; in 1882 they had increased to £363 5s 11id; in, 1883, together with the proceeds of concert, they amounted to £422 4s 61d; in 1884, £397 13s ;in 1885, £.478 13s 6d; in 1886, £367 is 8d ; and In 1887, £368 5s ; making a total of £2,902 2s Oitd. (Applause.) That, he considered, was a very handsome sum of money for the working-men of Warrington to sub- scribe towards the Infirmary. (Applause.) The In- firmary was under the very best management, and he trusted that those firms in the town who were not yet on, the subscription list would very soon appear on it. The experience of the committee had been that those firms where the workpeople subscribed a halfpenny or a penny per week always subscribed more in the end than those who subscribed in a lump at the end of every six or twelve months. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously. Alderman DAvies remarked that during the past year, no doubt owing to the kindness and benevolence of the workingmen, the governing body had been enabled to • extend the usefulness of the institution. (Hear, hear.) Hitherto they had only employed one house-surgeon, but they now had two. reTala had also appointed a new dis- penser, and had inc the staff of nurses. He re- gretted to find that many of the workmen at some of the leading shops in Warrington contributed nothing towards the institution, and at other firms the total was some- thing like Is 4d. That was a reflection which he thought had only to be made known, and it would at once be' put right. It was simply negligence on the part of the . workmen. (Hear, hear.) It had been a great pleasure to him that day to support Mr. Armitage—(applause)— who. was the very backbone of that movement, and had contributed materially to the prosperity of the Infirmary —a prosperity which he felt sure would go on increas- ing. (Applause.)—Mr. J. R. BIICETON observed that ali theimprovements of which Alderman Davies had spoken cost money, and when the banking account catne to be written up on the 31st December, he found that they were about £2O in debt, so that where they would have been had it not been for the subscriptions of the work- ing-men he did not know. (Applause.)—Mr.W.FIELDMT proposed that the contributions be at the end. of May and November as before.—Mr. Gairerrits seconded, and the proposition was agreed to.—Alderman PICKMERE moved that a vote of thanks be accorded to the resident and honorary medical staffs of the Infirmary, observing valuable, services.._ that they theaytawftere greatly tlythienidr vebte, especially to•the hono- raryGRIFFITHS seconded, and the vote was accorded.—Alder- man DAVIES moved, and Mr. CROSSEILL seconded, the re-election of Mr. Ziba Armitage as hon. sec. to the Hos- pital Saturday and Sunday Funds.—AldermanPicemEßE, 'Mr. Joux ROBERTS, and Mr. GRierrrns supported the motion,which was carriedunanimously.--Mr. ARMITAGE, in returning thanks for his re-appointment, said it gave him pleasure to act in the capacity of secretary. (Au- plause.)—Major Linos proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for granting the use of the room, and for presi- ding at the meeting.—Mr. ARMITAGE seconded, and the vote was accorded.—The MAYOR, in ac''knowledging the compliment, said he might take that opportunity of say- ing that he gave his patronage the other day, to the Gaiety Theatre of Varieties. He did so on conaition that half the proceeds should' be given to the Infirmary, and he was pleased to tell them that he had received from that source the sum of £7, which he had pleasure in handing over to the treasurer. (Applause.) SO long as they could obtain any benefits of that sort he thought it was his duty, as well as the duty of everyone else, to as- sist as mucli as they possibly could. (Hear, hlw.)—The Meeting then ended.'

At noon on Thursday, Mr. John Jerram, a retired gentleman, liiing at Nottingham, who had been in fail- ing health for some time, blew out his brains by dis- charging the contents of a shotgun into his mouth. Early on Wednesday morning a fire broke Out in ,a rag store in Govanhill„ Glasgow, and spread ta some stables adjoining, belonging to a contractor named *Milian. The buildings were gutted, and 18 horses w6o burnt to. death. At Swansea, on Wednesday, an inquest was held on the body of Mary Zane Davies, a young woman whose throat was cut by her husband, David Davies, a sailor, the previous morning. A verdict of wilful murder was returned against the prisoner, who gave himself up ifta- ruediately after the crime,

RUGBY RULES. WIDNES Sr. MARY'S V. BLUNDELLSANDS.—ThiS match, was played at Blundellsands on Saturday, a good game resulting in a win for the home team by a goal and four minors to three minors. ST. HELENS RECREATION "A " Teissr v. WARRINGTON ST. PAUL'S.—Thi.s match was played at Warrington be- fore a small number of spectators. The Recs, had a poor team, while their opponents had a very strong team. The score was—Recreation three tries and two minors to St. Paul's one try and one minor. All the Rec.'s forwards played well. RUNCORN RECREATION V. FRODSHAM. OR Saturday the Recreation journeyed to Frodsham to play off their return fixture with the above-named club. They were poorly represented, being minus Jones and Moores, backs, and Worrall and Barker, forwards. T. Rogers was unable to play for Frodsham. The game, which was very evenly contested, resulted in a win for the Recreation by one goal and three mirrors, to Frodsham twat minor points. OWENS COLLEGE V. RUNCORN.—These clubs met at Run- corn, on Wednesday, and the game was witnessed by a good number of spectators. The home team were short of seven of their usual players, and the visitors were not fully represented. As the score indicates, Runcorn had the best of the play and did most of the pressing, but were unfortunately defeated by a.goal and two minors to a try and 10 minors Lydia secured the try for the visitors, and Broady for Runcorn. The teams were as follows :—Owens ColLsge „J. A. .Strick, back; J. M`Gowan, P. Escort, and M. B. James, three-quarters; W. Parlane and N. Green, halfbacks; H. T. Dreschfeld, K. P. Birley, H. Clarke, W. P. Montgomery,. R. Lyttle, E. Johnstone, J. Entwistle, A. Fleppenstall, and A. M‘Dougall, forwards. Runcorn: 3. Basendale, back; W. A. Riley, J. Woods, and T. H. Davies three- quarters • Huglies and G. Whitby, half backs'! W. Stubbs, W. H. Broady, J. Gaytor, W. Hughes, R. Dolan, J. Riley, J. Gattley, A. Hampson, and E. Andrews, for- wards. ' Wrnses V. TYLDESLEY.—The first teams of the above clubs contended for mastery, for the second time this year, on the Widnes Club ground on Saturday. There were about 3,000 persons present. Widnes was short of two of the advertised team, I, Gandy and J. Bingham, their places being taken by Wright and Gordon, whilst the visitors had their strongest team, including Berry, of the Kendal Hornets, who has recently joined them. The game was well contested, the final result being—Tyldes- ley four minors, Widnes two. For the home, team, Plumpton, Parkinson, Farrell, Barker, Wilkinson, Smith, Hardman, Kiddie, and Pennington played well, whilst the pick of the visitors' backs were Shaw,Fernley, Berry, and Pearson, and the whole of the forwards playecrwell. • Teams :—Widnes: S. Bbagharn, full back; Plimpton, Parkinson, and Farrell, three-quarter backs; Wilkinson and Barker, half backs; Smith (captain), Kiddie, Hard- man, Pennington, Woods, Barber, Hughes, Wright, and Gordon, forwards. Tyldesley : Pearson full back; Ken- yon, Shaw, and Fernley, three-quarterbacks ; Berry and Smith, half backs; Woodward, Ilampson,Sutcliffe, Hodg- ' kinson Healy, Brown, Leech, Hilton, and Warburton. forwards. RUNCORN (A) TEAM V. CHEETHA3f HILL INT.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Satur- day, before an enthusiastic crowd of spectators. The visitors arriving late, only two 25's could beplayed. The first portion of the game was a fine exhibition of Rugby football, being very fast and open, in which Brazendale. Crompton, and Hollingsworth for Runcorn showed up conspicuously, as did also Gresty for the visitors. The second portion of the game did not furnish anything of much note, being a series of scrimmages, in which the home team held the upperhand throughout. It would hardly be fair to mention any of the forwards indivi- dually, as they all played a grand combined game. Victory rested with Runcorn by one goal, one try, six minors, to one try. Teams :—Runcorn: Full back, P. Brazendale ; threequarters, W. A. Riley, Crompton, and E. Lunt; half backs' T. Whinyates and Hollingsworth; forwards, J. Gatley,T. Abrams, P. Riley, P. Bowyer, T. Cox, J. Ford, A. Hampson, H. Grounds, and A. Raffee. Cheetham Hill : Full back, Evans; threemiarters, Gresty, Parker, and Isherwood ; half backs, Spence and Fallows ; forwards, T. Ritchie (captain), Wood, Reynolds, Naylor, Fryer, cewbun, Trailnr; b.n4 Hitheock. ILffllconx v. NEW BRIGHToN.—These clubs met at Liscard, on Saturday, for their return fixture, about 500 spectators being.present: Runcorn having won the toes, F. W. Jones, as captain of the home team, started the WI!. Speakman returned into touch within the New Brighton half, where play was located for a while, and although a free kick was awarded New Brighton for off- side play, no progress was made. Runcorn kept in front of the New Brighton posts, and at length Speakman ran in easily. Woods was called up for the "place," and missed an easy chance of scoring the major point. The drop out found New Brighton on the half-way line, and interesting play ensued m the centre until Wainwright ran strongly along touch. R. Woodward stopped his career, and the New Brighton forwards again came down the field. Speakman relieved from a pass by Hughes, and New Brighton were under the necessity of touching down. Davies then put in a tricky run, and took play to the home line, another minor resulting. This brought about the interval, Runcorn leading by one try and four minors to one minor. On Runcorn 'restarting, play was quickly taken to, the home lines. After C. Woodward had relieved, Davies picked up, and ran behind the Brighton line. W. Hughes was entrusted with the place kick, which was in a difficult position, and he failed. For a short time the ball was kept in the New Brighton half, and on Paterson dribbling away, a temporary visit Was paid to the Run- corn end. From here hostilities were taken to the home line, and another try was added to the Runcorn score, Woods again failing at goal. Davies next ran finely on behalf of Runcorn and nearly scored. After a slight relief Whitby received possession, aml dashed over the New Brighton line, Woods' kick again resulting in failure. New Brighton tried hard to get away from the drop-out, but Runcorn pressed, and again the New Brighton tine was crossed, Speakman failing at goal. Towards the close a rush by the visiting forwards, conspicuous among whom were Wainwright, Gayter, Broady, W. Hughes, and Faulkner' again brought play unpleasantly near the home line, but danger was averted, and up to the call of time no further points were scored, Runcorn thus winning by five tries and four minors to one minor. Teams :—Runcorn' Woods, back; Speakman, Caw- ley, and Davies, three-quarter backs • Hughes and Vlitby, half-backs ; W. Hughes, E. Andrews, Broady, Faulkner, Gayter, Wainwright, Dolan, W. Stubbs. and F. Hancock, forwards. New Brighton: R. Wood- ward, back; W. H. Male, C. J. Luya, and W. J. Rigg, three-quarter backs, J. Dawson and C. Woodward, half-backs; 3. G. Gifford, H. Dodd, W. Dutton, H. Williams, 11. Paterson, B. J. Browne, J. M'Calman. A. Simpson, and F. W. Jones, forwards. WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON (" A " Tiams).—The return match between these teams was played at Broughton on Saturday, in fine weather. Warrington were short saf Antrobus, Appleton, Isherwood, and Molyneux, their places being taken by players from the 2nd team. The home captain won the toss, and Whittle kicked off for Warrington at 3-30 against a strong wind, and no return being made the visiting forwards dribbled to the home quarter flag, Lewis returning with a neat kick into touch. King put in a long kick, and Glendenning follow- ing up collared Jolley with the ball in the Warrington half, but the visiting forwards, headed by Eyes, Craghan Adamson, and Lloyd, again forced the home team on the defensive. Whittle passed to Evans, who kicked to San- son, but King secured and punted to Jolley, this player returning into touch. The Warrington forwards took the ball close to the line, where Whitt% got possession and passed nicely to Evans, this player landing a beauti- ful goal. Whiteley restarted, Daniels returning to King, who sent the ball into touch. The Warrington forwards again forced the home team on their line, Evans nearly getting over. Several scrimmages took place near the Broughton goal.line, Whittle ultimately getting ma pass to Evans, who, after' eluding several opponents, dropped another goal. Whiteley restarted, • Evans returning. Whittle next passed across the scrimmage to J. Bate, who put in a short run and kick, the home full back re- turning well into touch. Good passing between the Broughton backs was now indulged in, King kicking to Evans, who returned to 'Whiteley, this player making his mark; but the free kick was charged own, and from a scrimmage Whittle passed to Bate, who got nicely away and threw to Evans, the latter player grounding the ball over the line. J. Bate took the place kick, but failed to improve the point. Whiteley dropped out, Whittle re- turning into touch. The home forwards, headed by Ashton, Campbell, and Glendenning, made a raid on the Warrington stronghold, Jolley stopping their career near the 25 flag. Half time was now called, the score stand- ing—Warrington, two goals and one try, to Broughton nothing. Owing to -an injury to Sanson, Warrington played with 14 men daring the second half, J. Bate go- ing three-quarter back'and Jones taking his place at half. Whiteley re-started on behalf of Brouetton, Evans re- turning well. Lewis passed nicely to King,, who put in a long luck into touch. Warrington worked the ball into the home half, a godcl dribble by Eyes forcing the home full back\to touch down. Whittle next passed to Evans, who put in a high kick, and Smith mulling the ball, • Craghan dribbled over the line and gained a tly °no goal resulting from the place kick. Bate returned the kick out, and Eyes, Jones, and Holmes dribbled to the line, Clarke again touching down. Another minor was imme- diately afterwards added to the Warrington score by a combined dribble of the forwards. Whiteley now showed up with a strong run for the home team, being brought down by Holmes in the Warrington 25. The visiting for- wards relieved, and J. Bate put in a nice run, being, brought down by Smith near centre. Whittle here gave Daniels a wide pass. this player getting away with a rl shing run, and handing Whiteley off in tins style gained a splendid try. Jolley kicked a goal from a difficult position. 'Miteley dropped out, and Bate failing to return, the home players, headed by Glendenning and Mather, drib- bled the ball over the Warrington goal line, Bate saving by touching deem. No side was now calletl, leaving Warrington winners by three goals, two tries, and three minor points, to Broughton one minor point. Teams Warrington: Full back, Jolley • three-quarter backs, Daniels, Evans, and Sanson ; half backs, Whittle (cap-

tain), and J. Bate; forwards, Adamson Craghan, Eyes Thornley, Donohue, Jones, Lloyd, Bale, and Holmes. Broughton: Full back, Clarke; three-quarter backs, King, Whiteley, and Smith; half backs, 'Lewis and W. Jones; forwards, R. Campbell, Robertshaw, E. H. Smith, Mather, Clark, Glendenning, C. Pratt, J. Ashton, and H. Crpws. WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON.

This annual fmture was brought to a close at Wilde pool on Saturday, when fully 4,000 speetatons were pre- sent. The Broughton team are established favourites with the Warringtonians, and the enthusiasm that was displayed on Saturday whenever any good play was shown served to show that they had not lost any of that good favour with the well wishers of Rugby football in the Warrington district. When it became known that Flowers was not assisting his club, the excitement dropped considerably, and the visitors were pissed at additional disadvantage bytho absence of Kneen, though an able substitute was found in smith, the old Brough- ton full back, who excelled himself at that position on this occasion.

Jordan, as captain of Broughton, stepped into the arena at 3-35, and, no time being lost, the visiting cap- tain kicked off against the wind, and directly after starting Massey was obliged to kick dead after a danger- ous rush of the Broughton forwards. Frank Turner's drop-out found play in neutral ground, but Ashton (Broughton) pressed the home team "to their quarter flag. This was only momentary, for Barnes, tackling Jordan smartly. reheved to the centre flag. The game was of a very keen nature, both sets of forwards work- ing with great determination. No headway could be made with either team, and it was not until a grand dribble, headed by Frank Turner, that the Warrington- fans found themselves in Broughton quarters. Smith here got the leather away to-Barnes, but the latter as promptly returned, only to see it put into touch at half way. The Broughton men were now forced to act on the defensive and it was marvellous how they prevented the Warringt;mians from scoring a major point. Ran- dies, Dillon, and Davies were to the fore with a well. judged dribble, but the advantage gained was negatived by Prince rushing the leather back. Passing by the home backs was now indulged in, and a rush by the home team forced Jordan to save. The drop-out brought little relief, for again the " vrirepullers" pressed the visitors back. A grand effort by Tolson was backed up by pretty passing, in whish Jordan, Prince' and Ashton shone; but the advantage gained was lost by Martin mulling. Speakman now got in a good kick, and his companion at half helped this effort by a neat dribble to the Broughton line. Passing by the home team ended in Fair. Turner getting over, but on appeal this was dis- allowed, and a five yards scrimmage ordered. The oval was got out of danger by a smart run on the part of Martin, but Massey and Barnes put in some sterling work, and forced Smith to adopt the saving clause. Massey replied to Smith's drop out, and H. Ashton and Frank turner were to the fore by a smart dribble to Broughton quarter flag. Massey was applauded for some brilliant work, and Speakman here passed to Jol- ley, Martin saving the rush just in the nick of time. Smith again touched down, a performance that was repeated directly after. H. Ashton charged the drop out, but Jordan got the charge away. Neat play by Davies and Massey forced the Broughton men to again concede a minor. Smith dropped out, only to see Jolley making tracks for the Broughton lines, but half-time arrived with no major point scored, War- rington having five minors to their credit, whilstßrough- ton had one. The Warrington men were now playing against the wind, and Frank Turner restarted, Ashworth , returning. Hayward dribbled neatly to Warrington quarter flag, but Hayes, Ashton, and lair. Turner forced their opponents back. Smith replied to akickby Barnes, and after a rush of the home team forwards Prince saved. Slazenger restarted, and Prince was conspicuous by a capital ran to the Warrington quarter flag, and pretty exchange passing by Barnes and Massey almost ended in the latter getting in. Smith was again the mainstay of his side‘for with-a good kick he returned to half-way. Warren now showed up, and a mull by Nevins shortly after almost ended fatally for his side, Jolley being fOfe-ed to-- saire. Quick passing by Barrios and Massey was loudly applauded, and Tolson and Wall ran the leather out of danger. A good run and kiekby Jolley I again compelled the visitors to defend their line, and Massey had a shot at goal, the kick being charged down. Wall relieved gallantly to half-way, only to find an ob- stacle in Speakman. Jolley and Barnes again passed re- peatedly from one to the Other, and from some smart play;on the Broughton he Speakman gave Barnes a chance, but his drop at goal struck the cross-bar, and rebounded into play, Smith qavin„e. From now to the call of time the home team had the best of matters, but could gain no major point, and were unable to reverse the verdict of the verdict of the first match this season, the game remaining drawn, Warrington havinga majori- ty in minors by seven to two. The game was chiefly confined to the forwards, both sides showing to great advantage. On behalf of War- rington the brothers Turner, Dillon, Davies, and Hayes were the pick. Nevins was faulty at back, and of the three-quarters Massey and Barnes were best. Speakman was the best of the halves, Warren seeming to be off colour. Broughton were best represented by Smith, who played a splendid game at full back. He was ably as- sisted by Prince, Evans, Wall, and Tolson. The following were the teams :—Warrington :Full back, Nevins; three-quarter backs. Jolley, Battles, and Massey; half backs, Speakman and Warren; forwards, Ashton Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Dillon, Hayes, Littleviood, Povey, Davies, and Handled Broughton: full back, Smith; three-quarter backs Trince Jordan

, (captain,) Martin: half tacks, J. Ashton and Summer: forwards, Wormald, Evans, Wall, Tolson, Ashworth, Lodge, Lombard, Hayward, and Slazenger. Umpires: Messrs. Gilbert and Wyldes ; referee, Mr. R. Wilcock, West Lancashire Union.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The annual fixture with Broughton is evidently a popular one in Warrington. The attendance of specta- tors on tluf Wilderspool ground on Saturday afternoon was very large, and the game was watched with the keenest interest. The two teams were very evenly matched, though taken all round Warrington had the best of the game. In the forward department Brough- ton displayed particular smartness, their combined rushes being very effective, and on several occasions they carried the leather away at their toed. The home team were, hOwever, always equal to the occasion, and in spite of some fine play by Jordan and other of the Broughton backs, they showed a superiority behind. At 'Broughton the Warrington "A" team carried everything before it, and showed no sign of degeneracy on its grand form of the earlier part of the season. This team still bids fair to have a splendid record for the season, and had not some of its best players frequently been called upon to fill gaps in theranks of the first team, -who knows but what its series of victories might as yet have been unbroken.
