THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1888 • WATI.RINGTON TEMPVRAXCE ,PEntltA- ; TION. - MEETING IN THE „PUBLIC HALL. A meeting in support of the 'United Kingdom Alliance, and under the auspices of the Warrington Temperance Federation, was .held in the Public Hall, Warrington. on Tuesgay evening. There was la large audience. The Rev. S. Wilkinson occupied the chair, and he was supported on the platform by the Revs. Canon Barker (Rector of Marylebone, and Chaplain in Ordinary to the Queen), J. J. Langham' G. D. Wray, E. Phillips Varley, F. Lake Good, G. E. Young, E. Jackson, Priestley Prime, J. Warnock; Dr. Geary; Councillors Francis Dixon, Joseph Shaw-Green, H. Roberts; Sergeant Tudball ; Messrs. J. H. RAper (London), R. Garnett, John Walker, C. E. Parker, W. C. Copeland, William Roberts, Thomas Hardy (Liverpool), J. J. Sanderson. David Garnett, Edward Twiss, John Tofti David Houghton, John Gandy, Jos. Harrison, R. Roberts, E. Ford, C. Ashurst, William Smith, A. Coutts, R..E. Garnett. J". Wylie, Joseph Owen, William Twisk, W. Beswiek, H. Roscoller, J. Monks, Williani Chappell, Thomas Dale, John Drury, J. W. Hall, I. Mills, R. Storey, P. T. Winskill, G. Bayley, J. Tanner, G. Sambrook, G. Clay, Edwin Plinston, Thomas Prince, C. H. Pigot, and Isaac Barlow. Previous te the chair being taken, Mr. Frank Booth played several selections on the organ. The cHAIRMAN said he was very glad indeed to pre- face the few remarks he was going to make with that well-known expression of "Ladies and gentlemen," be- cause he was sure they were all delighted to welcome their sisters there that night to help them forward in the great cause of temperance. He believed that if they could only induce the women of England to take up that question—and they were certainly taking it up very warmly in Warrington—by God's help they would be able to do something in furtherance of the great cause of temperance. (Heal, hear.) He believed the temper- ance was one of the very greatest in which they could be engaged. It was a great subject, and a subject which could be treated in various ways and from various stand- points. He was not going to attempt to say anything on it that night, because ho felt in so doing he would be stealing the time of the deputation which was present. He believed that the society whose claims they had met together to advocate that night was a great and glorious society, and therefore he was sure that everyone would listen with patience and candour to the speeches to be delivered. In forwarding the temperance cause they were doing the work of God, and his blessing would rest upon their endeavours, however humble they might be. (Applause.) The Rev. J. J. LAwaium said apologies for non-atten- dance had been received from the Rev. Father Fo• ,lanaan, the Rev. J. Yonge (who was out of town), the Rev. Ed- ward Moore, and the Rev. W. Graham. He had that morning received a verbal apology from their old friend Mr. William Beamont, of Orford Hall. (Applause.) He had asked that the meeting • might be informed how ex- tremely sorry he was not to be present there that even- in.. He thoroughly sympathised with the objects of meeting, and gave expression to that sympathy in a most practical way by sending a sovereign towards the expenses of the meeting. (Applause.)

Ed t Op. tbey would not very lunch Mina that-- (renewed laughter)—with them, and he would tell his clearers why. One of the most eminent men in Englikrid, the Bishop of Durham, went to the House of Lords and asked them to sanction Sunday closing in Dur- ham; and the noble lords, after listening to the Bishop's most eloquent speech, went hoine, drunk their claret, and threw out his bill. (Laughter and "Shame.") He thought that was very disgraceful. (Hear, hear.) Why a few men should have the power to veto that which a whole country desired, and that, too, without argument or reason, he could not tell. (Hear, hear.) But. per- haps even they would some day be on the side of tem- perance. (Laughter.) His belief was that the rising generation was the hope of the temperance party. I No fewer than 1,800,000 • children belonged te Bands of Hope. (Applause.) Every third child who came out of the London Board Schools belonged to Band of Hope; and he looked upon that as one of the most hopeful signs for the future triumph of their cause. (Applause.) In conclusion Canon Barker urged the necessity for political action in order that those who ad- vocated the cause of temperance might achieve their ends. Warrington. he said, was an entity which could make its voice heard. Let them at the next election throw their force and power on tho side which would make for the moral and spiritual welfare of their fellows. (Loud applause). The motion was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously. The Rev. J. J. LANCIIIAM said that the motion he was about to propose to some might sound al having a some- what political aspect, and he had been told that the Warrington Temperance, Federation was a political or- ganization. He wished to give the assertion a most emphatic denial. Upon that platfonn were both Liberals and Conservatives. (hear, hear, and applause.) They felt very strongly on their own political sides, but he as- sured them that they felt most strongly on the import- ance of the temperance question, and that would band them together. (Applause.) They had been standing shoulder to shoulder in the past. Their organization had now existed for nearly a yrar, and they meant to stand shoulder to shoulder in the future, and to that end they had sunk differences of creed, as they might see by the representative platform, as well as differences of politics. But, he said, although they stood there as Liberals and Conservatives —as irate Liberals and Conservatives— they stood ashamed of both their parties, who had neg- lected what they ought to have done. (Hear, hoar, and applause.) In the future it was meant to make the tem- perance cause a realitY; and force their legislators tagive them an act, of justice. (Hear, hear.) The present licensing system was absolutely and entirely wrong—it 'was an act of tyranny. What right had the Legislature to impose upon them public-houses, which were admit- tedly a source of much crime, and produced paupers and criminals ;.and refuse them the right to say whether they would have them planted in their midst? But that was the lowest ground to take in support of the resolution. •As a Christian people they had a right to say whether they would have that demoralization in their midst or not, and he hoped that before long they Vrould not have the Number of drink shops that they had in their midst at present. (Applause.) He did not complain of the action of the magistrates: They had every reason to be thankful for what those gentlemen did last licensing day, and he hoped they would do in the future what they did then; what he did feel most strongly was that the magis- trates then had a very bad law to administer. He asked, was it justice that when a large petition was presented in the police court from the people most immediately con. cerned, it should not be looked at? The law was a very bad one, and the sooner it was altered the better it would be for the community. (Applause.) jole would at once submit the resolution, which read Ers follows "net this meeting; regretsthe apathy of successive Go- Yorimmats, which, a,dmittin,e.' the evils and miseries caused by that law-sanctioned system of temptation and corruption—the liquor traffic while they have put forward no remedial measures themselves, have refused facilities to those private members who were prepared, in accordance with pledges to their constituents, to pro- mote a measure of local option. This meeting further trusts that the direct poi lar veto, by which all localities throughout the United Kingdom will be enabled to pre- vent drink shops being forced upon them may speedily become the law of the land.", (Applause.)

The Rev. F. LAKE GOOD said it was with the greatest pleasure that he rose to move "That thismeetin,g, grate- fully recognizing the great advances made in every de- partment of the temperance reformation during the past 50 years, especially during the latter portion of that period, hereby Apresses its full assurance of the ulti- mate accomplishment of the beneficent aims of the movement, unde; the blessing of Almighty God, upon the persistent efforts of its earnest friends and generous supporters." (Applause.) That the., great temperance movement had made advances within the last 50 years was,, he thought, a self-evident fact. To his own know- ledge the temperance movement had made great pro- gress during the last five and twenty years, and had they not done so they should not have had so many per- sons present that night. They were determined to go on, come what would, and by the grace ef God they would do everything in their power to advance the *luso which they all had at heart. (Applause.) Mr. D. HOUGHTON in seconding the proposition said they had all sunk their religious differences and political thoughts to come upon one common platform for the promotion of the cause of temperance. He rejoiced as a Warringtonian and as the president of the Catholic League of the Cross that there had been a society formed amongst thorn that had brought them all together, no matter what might have been their political opinions or religious views, to make a united effort to destroy -an enemy that was ruining mankind. (Applause). Mr. Houghton alluded in complimentary terms to the services of Mr. Langhaan in connection with the Federation, and concluded by urging all local temperance associations to join the Federation. (Applause.) The Rev. Canon BARKER, on rising, had a very cordial reception. The resolution, he said, to his mind spoke of a principle, and inasmuch as a principle would always guide them in the future as to details,thete could be nothing much more important than speaking upon the pr:nciple containedinthe resolution. 'the principle contained in the resolution was a principle of expectancy and a principle of hope, and inasmuch as every life depended upon ex- pectancy and hope for its ultimate seccess, so the suc- cess of that and every movement depended upon ,the amount of expectancy and hope which had sprung ifi its bosom. (Applause.) That movement spoke of 50 years, and the first thing for them to know that night was that there was ground for encouragement and hope. He was well aware that the contest had been very long, that many and great sacrifices had been made, that there had been instances of retrogression' and also indications of loss of zeal ; he was aware that a movement like that had its vicissitudes like all other great social movements of our times, but the point which he wished to urge was that the progress of the movement was more remarkable than, the progress of any other movement in this age, and for this reason, that the opposition to their move- ment was of a different kind and different degree to any opposition which had yet beeri offered to any movement in the past. Their movement appealed to a set of sentiments and feelings wholly different from those which were appealed to in most of the movements which had characterised their age. Had they ever calculated the character of the opposition with which they met? It was unique in its way ; it was dis- guised opposition;. it was opposition dressed in the vesture of virtue ; it was opposition which wore the guise of Christian morality ; it was opposition which fell back for support upon the sacred book; it was opposi- tion which depended upon the sympathy of the r,elbpous classes. Had they realized all that? (Hear, hear.) Their opponents, and they were numerous, maintained that they were faddists ; that they were men of one idea; that they knew little of human nature else they would never attempt such a quixotic enterprise as that. To advance in the difficult mevement against the religious prejudices of' the people was indeed a great enterprise, and he regretted to say that there was a large portion of the Christian conunu- nity who were still opposed to the movement upon what they called principle. There were many who still main- tained that moderation was a higher virtue than total abstinence, and there were others who maintained that the Holy Scriptures did not support the total abstinence movement. It was that kind of opposition which was so strong; it was that kind of hostility which was so difficult to overcome. (Hear, hear.) The advocate of , the temperance , movement appealed to all that vras • highest, noblest, and most self-sacrificing in man ; they appealed to no selfish instinct, to no selfish motive. When, for instance, a person was advocating the aboli- tion of the Corn Laws, he had a tremendous leverage, because he could appeal to the selfish instincts of men by telling them that if they supported his views they would have cheaper bread and cheaper commodities. They could also see that in agitating for theabolition of slavery they could appeal to instincts which men could gratify without any personal sacrifice. But when they appealed to a man on their platform, what were they appealing to? They appealed to what was disinterested, unsel- fish. self-sacrificial, and eminently Christian. They said to a man, "Give up the drink," not because to drink was evil, but because drink might injure other men. They were told to give up the drink because it was a stumbling block to others. They were told to act on the highest law in religion, and take up the crossand follow Christ. But they as parsons knew that such an appeal often fell on barren ground. If the appeals were all answered they would have among the Christian communities such self-sacrificing cases of denial as would make the drink traffic in the country .an impossibility. His argument was that they must judge of the progress of the move- ment by the weight and power of the resistance opposed to it. Any man could win if his enemy was weak. Any man could win if his opponent was enfeebled; but if he overcame a force greater than his own, he said that that man did indeed achieve a victory, and it was almost a miracle. (Applause.) There were innumerable signs around them that they were winning. As proof of this the speaker referred to the decrease of drunkenness in what was called "society," and also the extraordinary change which had come over medical opinion of the country, and in connection with this he was told that every medical man in Warrington was in favour of total abstinence. (Applause.) Ha hoped that was true; for if it was it was an immense credit to Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Science likewise had undergone a complete change with regard to the proper uses of alcohol; and the Press, with which for power he believed there was nothing to be compared in the civilised world, now never thought of casting cold water on their movement. (Ap- plause.) The Press had not yet found out what Mr. Raper and his association had—the remedy, but the day vould come where they would find it advocating their principles and the chief means of carrying them to a triumphant issue. (Applause.) The House of Commons was a body which they all very much respected. They knew very well that it had not dene very much for the temperance cause yet, but the reception of the question there now was very different to what it was some years ago. (Applause.) It was a great thing to have got the House of Commons to vote for and. endorse the temper- . . _ _

Mr. Jonas WALKER said that he had very great pleasure in briefly seconding the resolution.' They would notice , that it remarked upon the apathy of successive Govern- ments as to their action on the temperance•question. He thought that if they looked back a few years they would feel that, while each government had been pledged more or less to do something in this matter, not one—whether Conservative or Liberal—had really , taken any action at all. The Governments, so far as they were concerned, were to blame, but they, the tem- perance people, were also to blame. They had done I something; they had brought the matter to a head, but they had not.put as much pressure on Governments as they should have done, and as they were capable of doing. • (Applause). He agreed with the other speakers in saying that in this matter.they were not party politi- cians; they were politicians in so far that they desired to influence our legislature, and he was ready to join hands and I say "We will not vote for any man who is not distinctly pledged on this question." He did not hesitate to say that both parties in 'Warrington had been seriously ne.g- ligent on this matter; but now that they were organis- ing in the shape of that Federation, he trusted that when ' the proper time cathe they would make their influence felt. (Hear, hear). They heard it said sometimes that people could not be made sober by Act of Parliament. But it seemed to some of them that there was a pos- sibility of making people drunk by 'Act of Parliament, if they considered what was done in connection with the groCers' licenses, and hew they had affected Warrington. It seemed to shew that the legislature could do a great deal in this matter, at least for evil. Statistics proved that in Warrington during the past ten years, whilst convictions for drunkenness had been decreasing so far as men were concerned, the women, on the other hand, had begun to drink more. Thus they had,the astounding and shameful fact that convictions for drunkenness dur- ing the past ten years amongst the female population of Warrington had increased no less than 100 per cent. In , face of statements like thathe thought that they were in that a position to say, at thelegislature had doneagreat deal that was evil. They must determine that a change should be made, and that the legislature should do a great deal for good. It was the duty of the State to make it easy to do right, and hard to do wrong, but bv putting a public-house at every street corner exactly the opposite was done. (Applause.) They must insist, therefore, upon local option, or the direct veto, being speedily made into law. If they get a good bill, let them have other meetings and insist that it should become law. If the House of Lords ventured to throw the bill out, let them set to work and throw out the House of Lords. (Applause). Mr. J. H. RAPER, who was well received, supported the resolution in an effective and humorous speech. What was wanted, Ile said, for Christian civilisation was total abstinence for the individual and total prohibition for the State. - On Saturday next the temperance people were to be face to face with Mr. Ritchie, who was going to meet them as well as the other skid, and he thought that it would be a great luxury to the Government as a wliole if they could all be present, and Canoh Barker would repeat what he had said to them that night. (Laughter and applause.) Be had listened to Canon Barker when he had been addressing Cabinet ministers' from the pulpit, and he prayed that the inspiration might come upon him—but it never came. All of them who preached to brewers would know exactly what he meant. There were times and seasons when the inspira- tion would not come. (Laughter.) Warrington was a part of the governing power of this country, and ought to do something. What did it do ? They had eight divisions in the House of Commons last session, and at no single division did Warrington vote right and in favour of temperance. But he was thankful to say it did not vote wrong. They had pretty nearly ceased to do evil, and he trusted that they might move forward to do well They must not make the mistake that the Go- uernment was something above them, for this country was now a self-governed" one, even more so than were the United States of America. The people formed the GovernMent, and any charge that they made against the Government they must take home to themselves. When they saw the evils of the drink traffic they must ask themselves to what extent they were contributing par- ties, and they must ask themselves how they voted at the last election. When they prayed "Lead us not into temptation," they must 'remember that they were parties to that temptation. , Very shortly they would have the Chancellor of the Exchequer presenting his Budget. The receipts per day for the drink traffic averaged from £60,000 to £BO,OOO for the whole of the year. The drink bill for the year ending December 31st, 1838, amounted to £122,905.000, and for the yedr ending 31st December, 1887, it would possibly come up to £124,000,000: That, however, was not by an increase of the population; but , the year which was called the national year ended on the 31st of March, and consequently, beihg Leap year, the extra day in February would be taken in, and he knew that the Chancellor of the Exchequer licked his . lips over that, because the revenue from this source , would consequently be; increased. They were a Chris- tian community, a Bible Society, missionaries to man- kind, they had 300,000 Sunday school teachers, and I nevertheless they were partners to the extent of £BO,OOO per day in a business which was creating ruin and . misery all round. Therefore, he was not in a condition ' to abuse many people in the matter. only he asked them ' very earnestly to give him the power to vote him- self out of the business. (Laughter and applause.) • Was it doing well, he asked, for the magistrates of War- rington to simply leave thepublic-houseswherethey were , and not grant any new licences ? It was round the old 1 houses that all the intemperance 'existed. They must ' demand that the people should on this question have the ' power of a direct veto. THE SHIP CANAL WORKS, AND HOW THEY WILL A FFECT WARRINGTON AND THE DISTRICT. NO. 4.—THE RUNCORN AND LATCHFORD CANAL, &c. Last week it was explained that, between Tom Paine's Bridge on the Chester-roadand Twenty-step Bridge on the Stretton and Northwich road at Stockton Heath, the centre line of the intended Ship Canal will twice pierce the present channel of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal. This, as we have already said, practically means that nearly the whole of the bed of the existing canal between the two bridges will be absorbed, in the wider chan- nel of the new canal. Near Twenty-step Bridge, however, the courses of the two' canals will again diverge, that of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal branching off in a north-easterly direction, as at present, and. that of the Ship Canal taking a "bee line "for the then inland port of Manchester. The stretch from Twenty-step bridge to the junc- tion with the Mersey opposite Howley will, 'it is expected, be all that will remain of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal 'after the Ship Canal project has boot carried out. The rest I of its course between Stockton Heath and Runcorn will be abandoned, and probably filled up. The junction between the remainffig portion of the Latchford Canal and the Ship Canal will be made at Stockton 'Heath, close to Twenty-step I Bridge, by a new cut, containing a lock, ind through this lock craft on the Ship Canal seeking to reach Howley and the upper parts of the Mersey, by means of the existing canal, will have to. pass, and, on the other hand, vessels from HOwleY wish- ing to enter the Ship Canal, will, of course, pass through the new lock in the opposite direction. It is provided that the Ship Canal Company are to main- tain at not less than its present width and depth, the part of the Latchford Canal between Stockton Heath and the Mersey, and the new lock near Twenty-step Bridge, is not to be less, as to depth, length, and width, than the present Latchford locks. l'ower is also granted to the Wilderspool Brewery Company (Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Com- pany, Limited) to at any time construct on land be- longing to them adjoining the remaining length of I the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, "such private' basins (with or without gates), lay-byes, wharves, and other works, with suitable entrances and ac- cess" from the canal "as they may desire, for the i accommodation, free of wharfage dues, of the brew- , ery company," its tenants, servants, &c. All works executed under these powers, however, so far as they affect the canal, are to be carried out accord- ing to plans approved by the Ship Canal Company's engineer, and under his superintendence. It should be mentioned that the section of the Act which gives the brewery company these powers applies not merely to the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, . but also to the Ship Canal, so that in the future, ;chic!' we are attempting to forecast, it is possible there may be on the banks of the Ship Canal, near Stock- ton Heath, lay-byes, wharves, &c., made for the convenience of the business of the brewery com- pany. SIR RICHARD BROOKE AND SIR GILBERT GREENALL PROTECTED. Seeing that so great a length of the Runcorn and Latchford Canal is to be abandoned, it may be of sonie interest to inquire as to what is to become of the disused portion. We do not know that the Ship Canal Company, to whom, of course, the canal now belongs, it having beenpart of the Bridgewater purchase, is bound down to any particular mode of dealing with the abandoned parts of the canal, but in all probability they will be filled up, and there can be no doubt that the excavation of the greater waterway will provide more than enough " spoil " to fill up the old channel to the level of the adjacent land. 'ln the section of the Ship Canal Act, 1885, "for the protection of Sir Richard Brooke, Baronet, and the Norton Priory estates," it is set forth that if any part of the Runcorn and Latchford canal, bounded on both sides by land Of Sir Richard Brooke, is not needed by the Ship Canal Company the company shall, if required by him, sell the same to Sir Richard Brooke, at a price to be settled, in 'case of„,dispute, by arbitration in the manner pro- vided by the Lands Clauses Acts. Before selling, however, the Company shall, if required by Sir Richard Brooke, and may if they themselves desire to do so, fill up the bed of the canal and make it and the adjoining towpath level with. the adjoining land, and fit for agriculture. • Sir Gilbert Greenall is "protected" with a clause almost iden- tical with regard to those parts of the canal which are bounded on both sides by his land;, and Mesys. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., have also sought' and obtained provision with respect to the option of purchasing the disused portions of the canal bor- dering on their property. Those parts of the aban- doned canal which abut on Sir Richard Brooke's and' Sir Gilbert Greenall's land may be filled up by the Canal Company before selling if they desire, but in the case of the Darts bordered by the lands of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., this can only be done it the latter firm do not .object in writing. It is further providei, at the instance of the Dares- bury Highway Board, that if the Ship Canal Com- pany acquire the Runcorn and Latchford Canal they shall at all times undertake all the obligations of the Bridgewater Company with respect to the main- tenance of the bridge known as " Bob's turn- bridge," near Moore, which carries a road across the canal; but in the event of their stopping up the canal, the Company may, in lieu of maintain- ing the turnbridge, construct, and for ever after maintain, to the reasonable satisfaction of the High- way Board a good and sufficient road not less than twenty feet in width across the site of the canal, in the position and On the same level as the present turnbridge. ORIGIN OF THE RUNCTIN AND -LATCHFORD CAN. It will be seen from what has been given above, that it is extremely probable that in a few years time the Runcorn and Latchford Canal will practi- cally cease to exist, as a feature of the country lying between Warrington and Run- corn. It may, therefore, not be out of place to take a brief glance back at the origin of a waterway i which n its history has served a useful purpose, but which like so many other things, is being superseded by the more effective instruments and appliances of modern times. In his interesting "Account of the Cheshire Township of Appleton since the Norman Conquest" our townsman, Mr. Beaumont, alludes in the following passage to the reasons for, and the period of, the construction of the canal. "That part of the bed of the river Mer- sey," he ,says, "which lies hi Appleton had been deepened and made more navigable for three-quar- ters of a century before 1824, by the company of proprietors of the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, under the powers of the Act of Parliament which they had obtained in 1720; and although by the making of the Bridgewater Canal the facilities of water arriage had been increased, and the river had in so far been relieved of some of its heavy bur- dens, yet it was still found that the great traffic be- tween Liverpool and Manchester had grown far faster that the existing modes of transport ; and there was aloud demand for more. The company having had their attention drawn to it, deternuned, as a means of meeting this demand, to cut a new canal from the Mersey at Rowley and Latchford through the township of Appleton, to join the river again at Runcorn, which, would have the twofold advantage of avoiding the neaps occurring twice a month in the river between Warrington and Run- corn, which stopped the traffic at those times, and of enabling fiats and barges to pass from Manchester to Liverpool without the necessity of loweringtheir mastele order to pass under Warrington Bridge. In the year 1794, the company having obtained the necessary Act to make such a canal, soon after- wards commenced the work; and it was finished in 1801, as appears by ,the date inscribed on the bridge called Tom Paine 5, in Appleton, which ob- tained its name from the writer of "The Age of Reason," who was then so unenviably notorious This canal, like that of the duke of Bridgewater,

was also made without locks, except at the two ends'', and, unlike that- it was crossed nowhere throughout its 'whole extent except in Appleton and Latchford, by any other than swing bridges, and so the bridges over the Bridgewater canal, which are such'obstructions in crossing, do not occur ,upon • this." In the "History of Runcorn," lately published, the author, Mr. Nickson, says, "The Mersey and Irwell navigation was navigable so long ago as 1720, but for sixty years the proprietors were losers by their venture. It was sold to the pro- prietors of the Mersey and Irwell Naviga- tion in 1780, who, observing the great in- crease of trade in Liverpool made great improve- 'meats. In 1800 they commenced the construction of a canal from Runcorn to Warrington in order to avoid the circuity of the river and che low tides. The canal, which cost £48,000, was completed in 1803. Commodious docks were built at the terminus at Runcorn in 1826, together with improved methods of communication with the Mersey at a cost of £60,000. In later years the whole of this important navigation was acquired by purchase by the Bridge- water Navigation Company, Limited, whose sub- scribed capital now amounts to £919,779." •

_ ROMAN REMAINS. Another matter of some interest to pejsons of an antiquarian turn of mind in connectipYwith the cutting of the projected canal-. through Stockton i Heath s the possibility, and it may indeed be said, the probability of the discovery of me relics of the ancient Roman station which one; stood in the neighbourhood. At both the cutting of the Bridge- water Canal in 1770 and that of the Run- corn and Latchford Canal, at the beginning of this century, were Roman remains found, I and on the latter occasion in considerable abundance. We are told by Mr. Beamont, in his "Account of the Roman Station at Wilders- pool," that in 1770 the find took place near Lum- brotk, when the articles found were so many and so curious, that they were collected in the neigh- bouring house of Mr. Ireland, where they formed al little museum." "This discovery," continues Mr. Beamont, "with an occasional finding of a Roman coin at Wilderpool, and more particularly the dis- covery of a number of relies by the late, Mr. Greenall in the course of building his great house there in the year 1787, aroused general suspicion in the neighbourhobd -that there had existed some- where near a station of the ancient masters of the winid. Not, however, until about 1800 did its true *value dawn upon the goneral belief, or receive any important confirmation, but in that year, in cutting the Old Quay Canal, for which an Act had been ob- tained in 1794, the workmen, in excavating a deep cutting through Wilderspool, came upbn the founda- tions of some extensive building buried deep be- neath the surface, which struck even their unprac- tised eyes as the work of no modern or native people; but, alas, some antiquary was again want- to notice what was discovered, to sketch the buildings, or leave a circumstantial account of the remains which might be handed dawn to our times'," Lana hope, in case the intended excavations,which will be both wider and deeper than those of 1800, result in -the turning up of ancient remains, that not only will the needful antiquary be at hand to take note of' them, but that they will find a safe and fitting resting place in our excellent local Museum, already So rich in curiosities of the kind.
(To be continued.)
EASTHAM.

Man are being rapidly put on at Eastham, and there are now fully a thousand hands engaged there. Two steam navvies are exclusively occupied cutting out the huge docks at Eastham, where the canal enters the Mer- sey. The Eastham section of the canal is by far the more advanced of the whole of the several sections between the Cheshire shore of the Mersey and Manchester. THE DAMAGE TO HIGHWAYS. At a meeting, on Monday, of the Wirrall (Cheshire) Highway Board, it was announced that if Mr. Walker, the contractor for the Manchester Ship Canal, did not pay the bill sent in, the ratepayers would be compelled to pay an additional rate of 3d in the pound. The clerk reported that he had taken out a summons against Mr. Walker for £199 for extra traffic incurred in November last, but as in the meantime a further expenditure had been in- curred during December of £421, it had been arranged that the summons for the November account should be adjourned, so that the whole case should be gone into at once, During January, the clerk added, a further ex- penditure of £4a had been incurred. •

• 500 HOUSES AT BARTON. AC the works at Irlam and Cadishead, anEnglish steam navvy and an American kind "grabber" have been got to work. The line of the Canal is being staked out inthe meadows at Salteye, Barton. By a mutual agreement between Sir H. de Trafford and Colonel Legh, a number of meadows at Barton are being laid out for building purposes, and it is said that it is paDposed to erect 500 houses thereon. The Eccles Local Board and the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority have passed plans for the erec- tion of at least 120 houses.

I, commend the interests of that great industry to your • attentive care, in the hope that means may be discovered for en- abling'it to meet more effectively the diffiulties under which it labours. _

Immediately on the conclusion of the reading of the Speech the Commons withdrew, and the sitting was sus- pended till the usual hour for the commencement of - business of the evening. The Lord Chancellor again took his seat at a. quarter after four o'clock., ' DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The Address in reply to the Queen's Speech was moved by ,the Earl of CRAWFOItD and BeLeAleltEd, who in the C 011 r 02 of his remarks " warned " the House that a grave feeling was arising in the country that means should be taken for the revision of ou; fiscal system.—Lord ARM. STRONG, who seconded thb Address, denied that the ' Liberal Unionists had identified themselves With a policy of coereion.--Earl. GRA.NVILLE criticised the polic* of the Government, and on foreign affairs pointedly drew the at- tention of the House to the recent statement of. Prince BISMARCK that at the Cortgress of Berlin Lords Beacons- field and Salisbury placed themselves in his' bands, and that he had succeeded in obtaining for Russia all that she required. On the Irish question, the noble Earl asked the Government if they thought that their policy waS succeeding. Its only effect had been to , Make popular heroes of the men who were imprisoned under the Crimes Act. The Government had come to the conclusion that they could govern Ireland by force; the Liberal Party were of the opposite opinion.-The Marquis of &Lissom(' In re' ply, denied that Lord Beaconsfield and himself had given way to alltheßussiandemandsat Berlin. Prince Bismarck had said that Germany had no interests in the East, but Great Britain had interests there, and a policy from which there Nees no idea of departing. Danger could , only arise from some illegal or adventurons action on the part of Russia, and they had the assuraece . of: the Russian GOvernmentthat no such action was intended. Referring to Ireland, he denied that the Ooveinment were coercing opinion.: They were only enforcing private rights, such as a Home Rule Cabinet, if it were ever instituted, would be compelled to enforce. The Address was agreed to, mid the House; adjourned.

div.head: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT.
• THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. HOUSE OF LORDS.-THußspey.

The third Session of "iti-t-NVelft-li--P-a-rlia-Ment, of the Queen was opened by Royal Commission, the Commis- sioners being the Lord Chancellor, the Earl of Lathom, the Earl of Rossyln, the Earl of kintore, and Viscount Cross. In the Houit;of Lords at the opening ceremony the number of ladies who on these occasions are admitted tO seats on the back benches both on the Opposition and Ministerial side was unusually large, and the Strangers' Gallery was filled:ladies being admitted as well, as gen- tlemen—there were only about 30 peers present. The Lord Chaiicellor took his seat on the Woolsack precisely at two o'clock, but immediately retired to the 'Prince's chamber and returned accompanied by the Lord Commissioners, who wore their full robes of scarlet and crimson. The Commissioners having taken their seats on a bench placed in front of the Throne, tile Usher of the Black Rod was directed to summon the Commons. The Speaker, attended by the Sergeant-at-Arms, and followed by a large number of members of the Lower House, shortly °afterwards appeared at the bar. The Lord Chancellor than announced that her Majesty, not seeing fit to be personally present, had caused a 'Commis- sion under the Great Seal to be issued for the opening of Parliament. The Commission having been read by the Hon. Slingsby Bethell, the reading clerk, the Lord Chan- cellor read the Queen's Speech as follows :
" THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. MY LORDS AND thENTIZMEN,-
I ccntinue to receive from all other Powers cordial assurances of their friendly sentiments, as well as of their earnest desire to, maintain the peace of the world.

My officers, in conjunction with those of the Emperor of Russia, have completed the demarcation of the Afghan boundary in conformity with the terms of the convention of last year. f trust that the work which has been brought to a conclusion may tend to remove the possi- bility of a misunderstanding between the two Towers in regard to their Asiatic possessions. • Animated by a desire to prevent the effusion of blood, I despatched a mission to the King of Abyssinia, with the hope of dissuading him from engaging in a war with Italy. I deeply ,regret that my efforts have not been sue. ces.sful:

The deliberations of the conference assembled at Wash- ington to adjust questions which have arisen between the Dominion of Canada and the United States are still in progress. The negotiations which were commenced in 1885 with respect to the regulation of the Suez Canal have been brought to a conclusion so far as the points of dif- ference between myself and the French Republic are concerned.
I have also entered into an agreement with the French Republic for. the protection of life and property in the group of the New Hebrides, by a joint naval com- mission._

A conference of delegates from the Powers interested in the sugar industry was summoned in London, in fife autumn, to consider the possibility of putting an entl to the injurious system of bounties, and they have made considerable progress towards the conclusion of a satis- factory arrangement. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE IF COMMONS," The estimates for the services of this year, which will be laid before you, have been framed with due regard to econotny. You will be asked to make provision for the improve- ments in the defence of the ports and coaling stations of my empire, Wttich have been rendered urgently necessary by the advance of military science. You will also be asked to sanction Oh arrangement for providing a special squadron for the protection of Aus- tralasian commerce, the cost of which will be partially borne by the colonies themselves. . MY IoORDS AND GENTLEMEN.— The measures which, at the. cost of great labour, you pasged during the last Session for the benefit of Ireland have been carefully carried into effect during the period which has since elated. The result of this legislation, so far as it has been tested by a short experience, has been satisfactory. Agrarian crime has diminished, and the power of coercive conspiracies has sensibly abated. 'Measures tending to develop the resources of Ireland and to facilitate an increase in the number of the proprietors osf the soil will be laid before you. Your attention will be invited to the subject of Local Government inEngland, and measures will be submitted to you for dealing with ft it combination with proposals for adjusting the relations between local ancl imperial finance, and for ,mitigating the burdens at present im- posed upon the ratepayers. The prospects of commerce are more hopeful than any to which I have been able to point for many years past,

MR. GLADSTONE'S RETERN.--Mr. Oladstone arrived at Dover on Wednesday, and was heartily welcomed by an enthusiastic crowd. On the way to London the train was stopped at Shorncliffe,' where an addr&s was pre- sented. In reply, Mr. Gladstone commented upon thp fact that in this country, almost altne among the coun- tries of Europe, the spectacle could be seen, of one nation holding down another by force. Even Russia would be' ashamed to say of Finland, what Englishmen said of Ire- land, that if a local Parliament were granted five millions would be too strong for thirty-two millions to manage. The people alone, however, could put an end to the way in which Ireland was being governed. During the even- ing 111,r. Gladstone had a conference in London with mein. bers of his late Government.

ST. PAUL'S ANNIT4I TEA PARTY, WARRINGTON.

On Monday evening the annual congregational tea party in connection with the parish of St. Paul's was held in the Public Hall. Between 600 and 700 members of the congregation and friends sat down to an excellent tea. In the course of the tea Ste.l Paul's brass band rendered an excellent selection of music. The entertainment which was aftprwards held was presided over by the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), in the absence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., who had been announced to attend. The fol- lowing is a list of the ladies and gentlemen who subscribed to the tea party :—The Lady Mary l'owys, the Hon. L. W. Powys, Sir G. Greenall, Bart., M.P., Lady Greenall, Sir A. B. Walker, Bart., the Mayoress; Mesdames R. Davis, Marson, W. Reid, D. W. Finney, Smethurst, F. Massey, Wilkinson, Clive, Pollitt, Ashurst, Morris, Milling, Jeans, Geddes, CrailP, J. Hepli erd, Ferguson, J. Pierpoint Braide, Proud, Perry, Chorley, J. T. Tunstall, Myle- ehreest, Bolton, Highley, Parsonage, J. Whittle, Ilankinson, Greenhough, H. Tofp, Badley, Hampson, Marshall, Chantry, G. Woods, E. Woods, G. Litton, W. Dutton, W. Gibson, Lazenby, Glover, J. A. Sut- ton, Eddowes, Hedgcock, Thompson, W. Lawless, Rathboxie, Boothroyd, and Senior; Misses Finney, Marson, Pierpoint (St. Austin's), Greening, Garland, Eddowes, and Burpws; Dr. Adams,; Messrs. IL Davies. Marson, Stubs, Tinsley, D. Jones, Kirkconnel, T. W.. Nelson and Co., Jolley, W. and J. Richardson, A. J. Jolley, Hutchinson, J. Crosileld and Sons, Smith (Bewsey-pad), and Copeland. The Mayon, in opening the proceedings, said that Pro- bably their member (Sir Gilbert Greenall) had not been able to put in an appearance that evening, as ho had much to do prior to his departure for London. The Rev. S. Wltanwsorr had only one matter to regret in connection with that annual tea party, and that was the absence of their dear friend Sir Gilbert Greenall. They were so accustomed to see his genial face and hear his kindly and friendly words that his absence wa.s very much felt. Sir Gilbert had always been a great per- sonal friend of his, and be had helped the parish in every way, and had he not felt unwell he would certainly haVe been with them that evening. (Applause.) The first thing he had to do on that occasion was to thank all connected with St. Paul's for the valuable help which had been rendered by them during the past year • in- cluding the churchwardens for their personal friendship and ready help in every good work, the sidesmen, lay representatives, and Sunday school teachers. Especial thanks were due to the superintendent of the boys' school, Mr. Alfred Jolley, and the able staff under him; to Mr. Lawless, superintendent of the girls' school; to Mr. Westwell, Mrs. Chorley, and other ladies, not for- getting their voluntary choir, which was second to none in Warrington. (Applause.) Its present excellent con- dition was due to a great extent to the popularity and regularity of attendance of the organist, Mr. Lytligoe. Thanks were also due to Mr. Parkinson, who assisted on Thursday evenings in connection with the choir. (Ap- plause.) He had not , much of an exciting character to mention to them that night, though the great event in connection. with the parish during the 'year was the opening of the Mis- sion Church of All Saints' Bewsey. The population in that district had increased very rapidly during the last few years, and it had been found necessary to es- tablish a mission. Formany years good work had been carried on conducted by laymen and clergyinen, and when the history of All Saints', Bewsey, was written the names of William Smith, Peter Sudlow, Miss Macken- zie, and Miss Westwell would be written in letters of gold. (Applause.) These ladies and gentlemen had worked hard, and their warmest thanks were due tok them for their loving labour. He had had one great anxibty, and that had been to provide church accommodation for the large population over Bewsey. As they' knew, during the past 15 years they had not been idle in connection I with church building work. They had during that time built St. Barnabas' Church, restored and improved St. Paul's, and the money which had been collected for the purpose amounted to between £6,000 and £7,000. That was a very large sum of money to collect, and when he began to collect for the new church at Bewsey he could assure them his heart failed him. Btit what happened? The jubitee year came, and God put it into the heart of their good friend Sir Gilbert Greenall to give them £BOO to supply the want which was felt in the neighbourhood, and now the church had been built, opened, and licensed as a place of ' religious worship. Having a building was one thing, but they must have a clergyman, and through the gene- rosity Of Lord Winmarleigh, the Hon. Leopold Powys, and Mr. Stubs—through their help entirely—they were able to have a clergyman to work in that part of the parish especially. (Applause.) They all knew the Rev. R. Phillips. They respected and loved him, and he felt sure Mr Phillips was doing a great work in Bewsey, and that God would bless his work and labour of love. (Ap- plause.) He had muctrpleasure in announcing that the Rev. J. J. Langham was going` to help them regularly at St. Paul's on Sundays. (Applause.) The entertainment'was of an excellent character, the selections by Mr. Downs' band inl particular being much admired. Songs were rendered by Miss Locker, Miss Oxley, and Messrs. Sherlock, Potter, Parr, Hill, and Par- kinson. Comic rend& ings by Mr. Greenwood were es- pecially successful, and were much enjoyed. A duet on the flute and clarionet by Messrs. Brimelow and Pendle- bury was a fine performance. Mn .L J. Lythgoe officia- ted as accompanist. - - • . After the entertainment Councillor JOHN PIEHPOINT proposed a vote of thanks to the Ladies' Tea Committee, the ladies in charge of the tea tables, and the band and vocalists, Mr. Downs' band receiving particular • com- mendation. Mr. D. W. FJNNEY seconded the motion, and proposed a vote of thanks to the mayor for presiding. This was seconded by the Rev. R. PHILLIPS, annoth propositions were earned by acclamation. • The MAYOR haying briefly replied, the proceedings en- ded. -

Next day her body was fonnd at the foot of a railway embankment in the locality, and examination showea that she had been criminally assaulted and then strangled. THE PROPOSED EXTENSION OF ST. PETER'S
PARISH.

_ Sir,—As a parishionei of the Rev. Mr. Wray, I think he will hud plenty to do—more than he does—in his pre- sent parish, without taking anything from the Parish Church. I have been living here ever since Mr. Wray came to Warrington, and before too, and yet he has never seen the inside of my house. I was for some time dangerously ill; Mr. Wray left me to pray for myself. My two youngest daughters were old gnouga to be con- firmed. They might have been heathens for anything Mr. Wray cared. If it had not been for on of the curateo of the Parish Church, who goes into the nooks and corners, and seems to get more kicks than half- pence for doing so, my two girls would not have been confirmed. I have sold hundreds of tickets for the tea parties and other things at St. Peter's, and given both time and money, and yet Mr Wray, whenever he has seen me, even in his own schools, has stood aloof as if I were his enemy. Let Mr. Wray mind his present parish better before trying to get more. He says he cannot get a site for a church in his present district. If he will call a meeting of his parishioners, we will soon find a good place for his new church in our own parish, without putting it half a mile from Horse- market-street, in which many of his principal parishion- ers reside.—Yours truly, 37, Lythgaes-lane, Warrington.
WILLIAM HUNT.
THE WARRINGTON CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

Sir,—! am not surprised that the success of the above society, with its 2,000 members (mostly fools of course) and a turnover of £l,OOO per week, has attracted the attention of a "Looker-on." When passing along San- key-street, he has seen the crowded shops at the Stores, and thought (prophetic soul) of his own empty establish- ment, and he has been filled with wrath and indigna- tion. The country house with its large garden built by imaginative brain for his declining years has fallen to the ground, and left him tempest-tost on the sea of com- petition. The society is increasing considerably every year. The workingman after trying other tradesp-lople and helping them to gala that independency for which a " Looker-on " seems to crave, sees that it is to his i -der- est to join the Co-operative Society and share in the profits which he helps to make. And notwithstanding the puny effort put forth by a " Looker-on " the society , will continue to prosper; and help the workingman to build up for himself an institution, which will 1 : a stronghold against the middleman who neither toils nor spins, yet gets far more than his share of the benefit. But, sir, the Society does not stop here. Buy :tig and selling is but the first ind lowest step in the great social movement which is destined at no distant date to revolutionise commerce and humanise society. Real co- operation means mutual assistance. If it means any- thing it means: the abolition of that keen and grasping competition in business which gives the lie to, and ren- ders obsolete, that venerable proverb which said that "honesty is the best policy." The very essence of real co-operation involves honest dealing between man And man, and if this principle is acted upon, it will tend to put down that fraud and adulteration to which many of the trading class are addicted. Yours, &c., A MEMBER.

div.head: lIOW THE RATEPAYEITS' MONEY IS SPENT.
div.p: lIOW THE RATEPAYEITS' MONEY IS SPENT.

Sir,—Having been laid up for the last five weeks, have not been able to follow up my investigations with regard to the costs and expenditure of the Longford and intercepting depots, as I should have liked, but reading the reports of the Council's proceedings; I am astonished to find Town Councillors so much at sea, and so easily put off when the question of the management of they places is raised. If we converse with most of them about the mat- ter, they seem quite bewildered and exclaim—" Its no use, we cannot get at it!" Why can they not? They are sent to the Council to represent us, and if they have to confess that they cannot, and are not allowed to penetrate into the secrets of the spending departments, and by this depriving the heavy burdened ratepayers 6! knowing how their money is spent, they had better stop at home. As it has not been noticed at the Council meeting on Tuesday evening last, as I expected it would, I wonder, Mr. Editor how many of the Town Councillors know about a little job which has just been transacted with regard to Long- ford'affairs. It has been fully represented tons that the latter place and the article it manufactures is *hat Mr. Alderman Crosfield would say "the best in the world." If so, then what has been the necessity lately of it requir- ing two full blown Aldermen and one borough surveyor to carry a parcel of the excreta from Longford all the way to London, to have it analysed, costing for travelling ex- penses alone between £l3 and £l4 of the ratepayers money? What is the object? And why lsould not a sample have been sent and returned after analysing? How many more nice little journeys are these officials to have before this stuff can be pronounced perfect? If the Town Councillors cannot "get at it," the ratepayers should insist upon knowing what is the cost and expen- diture of this department of the Town's affairs. I don't know whit the Ratepayers' Asanriation is doing, but everyone should join it, for it would pay the ratepayers to appoint a thoroughly qualified inspector of their own to look after the clique who have charge of this abomin- able expenditure! Bad enough for the manure to be sold at a loss in the best three months in the year, and the Council and the ratepayers to be told that it is to their advantage not to know the price, without throwing good money after had. A man can be too long in office.— Your's truly, WILLIAM DIGGLE _ _ . . . .
49, Wellington-street, Warrington, February-liKrigg.
THE IRISH QUESTION.-BY A PROTESTANT HOME- -- -
RULER.

-------- Sir,—Your issue of the 14th January has just reached me, in -which appears a letter, on the above subject, signed "Radical Unionist ; " which is intended as a reply to mine of the 7th ult. I have made it a rule neither to write, nor reply to anonymous letters, but I intend to break that rule in this instance, as I have ascertained that the writer is one of those briefiess bar- risters, who, tired of perambulating the Four Courts Ball, Dublin, has entered the service of the Irish Loyal and Patriotic Union. Speaking at a- meeting of the primrose League, in this city, this Radical Unionist referred to my letter and said Mr. Atkins was replied to in a Warrington paper, both forcibly and well." Your readers can judge. "Radical Unionist" doubts that there are such persons as " Protestant Home-Rulers" in Ireland. If he was present at the immense and enthusiastic meeting at the Leinster Hall, Dublin, on the 2nd inst., to welcome, and hear, the Marquis of Ripon and Mr. Morley, he would have seen Professors of Trinity College, clergy- men of the Church of Ireland, professional men of high standing, magistrates, merchants and traders, and repre- sentative men from all parts of Ireland, who were Pro- testant Home-Rulers. But, sir, it would not suit paid agents of the I.L.P.U. to admit that there were any Pro- testants in favour of Home Rule in Ireland. "Radical Unionist" seems to be lamentably ignorant of recent land legislation and of the "Plan of Cam- paign." The list of reductions which I gave were those of leaseholders, many of whom, in times past, were forced into taking leases, and who, until the act of last session, were debarred from getting their rents revised, no matter how unjust. What forced the Government to recognise the claims of the leaseholders? I say it was the " Plan ef Campaign," which also compelled them to allow "Judicial rents' to be revised. As some of your readers may not have read my pre- vious letters, permit me to state how the Plan of Cam- paign originated. Some time after a large number of the tenants had their rents judicially fixed, a gree fall in the prices of all agricultural produce took place, amounting on an average to 40 per cent.; which was never anticipated when the judicial rents were being fixed, which, coupled with a very dry season and short craps, made the judicial rents, rack rents, and which famers found it impossible to pay. For this state of things there was no legal redress; rents that were judicially revised were fixed for 18 years, and as for the unfortunate leaseholders, there was no redress for them, until the act of last sevion was passed. To meet such an emergency the tenants were advised to meet on each estate, and having carefully considered all the circum- stances, to decide on the abatement, which they would ask their landlords for. They were advised that their demands should be moderate and just, and if their landlord did not consent to give the required abatement

off the rent, or compromise the matter, the tenants should adopt the "Plan," by lodging their rents (less the abatement) in the hands of reliable trustees, until the landlord came to see the justice of their demands. This I am glad to say they are nearly all now•doing •' the owners of the Kingstone Estate, have accepted their tenants offer in its entiret7 ; which fully justified the action of Mr. William O'Bnen, M.P., who suffered three months torture in Tullamore gaol, to keep 600 leasehold tenants and their families (his constituents) from being turned out of house and home. Your readers must re- member that the Plan of Campaign was adopted long previous to the passing of the Land Act of last session and where any tenants have had their rents revised under that act, (on estates where the Plan was adopted), the reductions amply justify their adopting the Plan, and have shown that in most cusps the tenants demands were under the abatements given by the Comnsiesioners.

"Radical Uniorustfs other questions have been so often answered both on the platform and in the Press, that it is not necessary that I should do so; but there is one statement which I notice all the "paid agents" of the make, "that the increased sale of whiskey in Ireland amounts to about the same as the reduced rents come to." Now sir, I don't know if that state- ment is made in ignorance or with a deliberate intention to mislead your readers and make them believe that the Irish people spend all their money in drink, when it is well known that more than half the whiskey on which duty is paid in Ireland, is exported to England and con- sumed there.

In conclusion, I regret that "Radical Unionist" seems to have such a distinct liking for the utterance o 4 state- ments of a misleading character, and I cannot help say- ing that it would be more manly if he would put his real name to his communications as I am never ashamed to do.—Yours truly, Cork, February 4th, 1888.
RICHARD A. ATKINS, T.C. ___
THE SHOCKING SUICIDE AT WIN WICK.

On Saturday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner for South-West Lancashire, held an inquiry at' the Swan Inn, Winwick, relative to the circumstances of the death of William Blackledge (56), farmer, Winwick, who shot himself through the head last week.—The widow of the deceased, Elizabeth Black- ledge, said that on Tuesday evening in last week, when she went to bed, she left deceased sitting in a chair. She got Up several times during the night. About a quarter-past live on Wednesday raorning she went downstairs, and found her husband dead. He had acted in a very strange manner lately, and had been in a low and depressed state of mind.— Thomas Blackledge, son of the deceased, said he last I saw his father alive about 9-20 on Tuesday evening, when he was sitting in the kitchen. On that day he was wandering about. Witness thought he was not quite right. Next morning, between five and six o'clock, his mother called him. He found his father sitting in the chair in the kitchen, and saw a gun- shot wound in his head, and the gun produced between his legs. The gun was kept in a cupboard in the kitchen unloaded. On Monday night witness leaded the gun, I and left both caps on. On Wednesday morning he found one barrel had been fired.—By Mr. Worsley (who appeared for the relatives) : We have lately kept firearms out of his way.—By P.S. Commins We were afraid of my father, and my brother and I locked our bedroom door.—Ellen Porter said she knew the deceased, and saw him in the kitchen on Monday evening. He said to her, "Good night; I shall very likely not see you again." She did not see him again alive. She thought at the time he looked very strange. —John Blackeldge said on Wednesday morning he we,nt into the kitchen with his brother and found his father dead. The doors were fastened so that no one could get in. Witness heard the report of a gun shortly before they found him.—P.C. Parker, a constable stationed at Winwick, said he was informed of the occurrence about six o'clock on Wednesday morning. Ile went to the house and found the deceased sitting in an arm-chair in the kitchen quite dead. The top of the skull was blown completely away, and the wall opposite was strewn with brains and blood. The gun ViiS leaning on the muzzle between the deceased's legs, with the stock against the edge of a table. The left arm was leaning easily on the left thigh, and the right was on the table against which the gun leaned. The gun was in a position as if it haul been fired and then dropped. Witness found a mark afterwards on the table where the gun would probably have kicked. He saw nothing to suppose that anyone else had inflicted the injuries. One barrel of the gall was discharged and the other loaded. There was a cap on the nipple of the discharged barrel, and also one on the other. Both hammers were down.—After hearing this evidence, the jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased died from the effects of a gunshot wound inflicted by himself, being at the time of unsound mind.

div.head: CALIFORNIA AND BRITISH WOKEN.
div.p: CALIFORNIA AND BRITISH WOKEN.

There seems to be plenty of room for difference of opinion as to the advisability of emigrating to South California. The following letter constitutes vstrong protest on the subjeg from one who ought to know

attention has been called to the efforts of Mrs. Margaret E. Parker to induce "needy gentlewomen" to emigrate to California, with a view to their bettering their condition by becoming "lady helps," or, in other words, domestic servants. I cannot find words strong enough to condetrur this scheme. A number of Mrs. Parker's unfortunate emigrants have come to me for as- sistance, which I have felt compelled to extend to them to save them from starvation. California is the last plaee in the civ;lised world that an English lady should come to unless she has the means to go away inhe does not like it. lam infcrnied that Mrs. Alice Westwood, lof San Francisco, his written to a Manchester paper 'protesting against needy English ladies being sent out in I this war. Though I have not seen Mrs. Westwood's letter I have no hesitation in endorsing it if it contains a efficiently strong protest to this effect. In my consular report for 1885, I stated, with rt-fer- ence to domestic servants, as follows :—" Domestic ser- vants who are willing to do the work that two or three servants would be employed to do inEngland can readily get employment at from £5 to £8 per month and board. Two English servants who are receiving £6 per month each called at my office to-day to ascertain if I knew anyone who was returning to England who would pay their fare in exchange for services en route. Apologising for trespassing so much on your valuable space, I am, sir, faithfully yours, WC. HITE MORTIXER, British Vice-Consul. Temple Block, Los Angeles, California, Jan. 11 1888. _ _ . .

Mrs. Parker' Ei reply is as follows:— Sir,—My attention has been directed to a letter by Mr. White Mortimer, of Los Angeles, condemning my scheme for helpinffithe women of this country to homes in Cali- fornia, and stating that he has been compelled to help some who were sent out by me. His letter is dated January 11th. At that time only nire of my women ..tiad arrived, all of whom were engaged thefirst day, and the "Liverpool Mercury " of January 11 contains a lot- tor from Miss Jones, of Liverpool, in which she says, "We are all comfortably settled; no one whom you may send need have the slightest fear or hesitation about coming here. We have met with wholehearted kindness from all parties, &c." On the same date, Jan. 11th, a larger party sailed by the Celtic. Two young ladies were desired by their friends to cable a single word as soon as settled. One cabled the word "Splendid," the other "Delighted." Could anything better refutethe statements of Mr. Mort- imer. He must have mistaken these applicants for'some of my protegies. It is not at all probable they would have gone to Mr. Moitimer when an efficient committee of Christian ladies exists purposely to receive and help them. Personally, lam not dis'airbed by this letter. I know the possibilities which lie before the women there. But I am sorry for those who are influenced by Mr. Mor- timer's letter. MARGARET E. PARKER.

---„--. P.S.—I am told that this gentleman has depreciated even the climate of California, wh:ch has a world-wide celebrity. There are some people who will not be con- tented in Heaven itself. M. E. P. [lt will be noticed that one party had reached California, and had been there a short time when the Vice-Consul wrote, Can it be that, after Miss Jones wrote, some of those who were reported as "comfortably settled." were so far unsettled as to apply to Mr. Mortimer, or is that gentleman under a misapprehension as to the applicants? This is a point which can be determined only by further in- formation.—ED. Ex.]
