div.head: OUR LONDON _LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON _LETTER.
LONDON. TEUBSDAT NIGHT. •

There were many circumstances which combined to make the opening of Parliament to-day a lively event. There was the news carefully kept back, and then blurted forth with almost brutal frankness. of the critical state of the Crown Prince's health, and the imminence of an operation peremptorily under- taken to save his life. Then there was the announce- ment of the retirement of Lord Dufferin from the Viceroyalty of India, and the Consequent changes. This last event, like the true state of the Crown Prince's health, has been known in certain circles for a considerable time, and for reasons 4,ef renoe has been kept a secret. Some time ago the Duf- feria secret partially broke out in the announce- ment that Lord Stanley of Preston was going to succeed Lord Landsdowne in the Governor-General- ship of Canada. Enquiring about this at the time I was assured that it was all true about Lord Stan- ley. But there was no whisper of Lord Lands- downe's sudden transference from the snows of Ottowa to the sultry clime of India. It was sur- mised in the quarter where information was likely to be found that Lord Landsdowne was coming home to join the reconstructed Cabinet. This may possibly have been the intention at the period I am speaking of, which was shortly after Christmas Day. However it be, it is now finally settled that Lord Landsdowne goes to India, Lordßtanley of Preston to Canada, and that Lord Dufferin retires, finally it is said, ,from the high position in which he has so long and so brilliantly moved. These things were talked about a good deal in the animated crowd that has swarmed about the lob- bies and corridors of the House' of Commons since noon to-day. But there were other things of closer interest to keep up the excitement. The attendance of members of the House of Commons on an open- ing day is always excessive. To-day it was added to by the urgent " Whip " sent out by Ministers affrighted by the report that in the very earliest moments of the new session the Irish members, held down by the throat during the recess, were to have their innings. Then there was the liughes- Hallett scandal, with respect to which an explosion is momentarily expected. It is an awkward thing for the hero of Rochester to have as a fellow mem- ber the brother of the girl he ruined. Captain Selwyn, as has been shown throughout the miserable transaction, is a man not to be tritled'with.. He was narrowly watched as he walked about the lobby this afternoon, and finally took his seat on the back bench, nothing less being expected than that if Colonel Hughes-Hallett turned up he would take him by the throat and shake him in the face of the House. It will be understood that these personal matters, combined with the real importance of the political programme put forth by the Government in the Queen's Speech, made the opening day un- usually full of life and movement. Among the early corners was Mr. Chaplin, per- haps anxious to show that there is no truth in the rumour that, failing to obtain recognition of his value in home politics, he was about to bury him- self in the 'wilds of South Australia. Mr. Chaplin ' has by thie time diecovered that he made a great mistake when the present Gisi-ernment was formed. He was then offered the post of President of the Local Government Board, but vrithouqa seat in the Cabinet. This he felt was a recompense below his merit, and a dignity beneath his notice. He there- fore declined, and it was handed over to Mr. Rit- chie. This is a matter upon which all concerned with Local Government are to be congratulated, since Mr. Ritchie makes a much better Minister than Mr. Chaplin would have done. But as things have worked out, Mr. Chaplin's chagrin must be profound. Local Government has come to be the question of primeat importance in the Ministerial programme, and the stone which the builder re- jected has become the chief corner stone. Mr. Ritchie has been promoted so a seat in the Cabinet, and has charge of the measure upon which the attention of the House of Commons will be concen- trated during the session, and upon which the for- tunes of the Ministry rest. Mr. Gladstone, as he sat on the Front Opposition Bench talking eagerly to Mr. John Morley (who, by the way, still shows traces of his severe illness) and to Sir William Harcourt, seemed in excellent health, and was evidently in the highest spirits. As usual, he takes a sanguine view of the future, and believes that everything is going well for the cause he has at heart. That as quite true. But it is also true that things are going very slowly, and that it is diffi- cult, accidents apart, to see where the pace can be increased. The continual dropping of water weareth away the stone, and the gain of successive seats at bye-elections, and the return of wanderers to the fold will in time wear away the working majority of ninety with which on this opening day ot the session a Conservative Government, thanks to the co-operation of some so-called Liberals, jubilantly face the future. Of the altered feeling in the coun- try as compared with that prevalent at the general election in 1886, there can be no doubt in any reason- able mind. It is written in the returns of the bye- elections, and not less forcibly in the influences brought to bear upon certain gentlemen who find their constituents will not stand their arraying themselves in Conservatide uniform. As compared with this time last year, the Conservative majority has been reduced by twelve votes. Simple arithme- tical computation will show that at that rate Con- servatives will be able to keep in office for the full statutory term of the existence of a Parliament. That, to tell the truth, is just what they mean to do, and since, whether by abstention or by petulantly voting the wrong way, the Liberal majority in 1886 I permitted the Conservatives to come into power, they must bear the injurious infliction with what grace is possible to them. I think there is nowhere more pleasant reading than the Paris papers occasionally supply when they invent little stories descriptive of social life in England: One never knows which to admire more, their ardazing insight, or their grotesque ignorance. I find the following in the " Gaulois," really a respectable and important daily paper published in Paris: "Sir William Draggs , hailed a cab at Brighton about a year ago, and told the driver to take him to the pier, off which Sir Draggs (sic) had his yacht. He told the cabman to wait for him, meaning to cruise about off Brighton for an hour or two, but, changing his mind, he determined to go around the world. The cabman waited and waited; and finding that his " fare " (this word is prinfed in the native tongue, by way of showing the historian's familiarity with everything anglaise), did not come back, he obtained leave from the Municipality- to erect a shelter for himself and horse. Here hes waited for more than a twelve- month, when the other day Sir Drage 'returned with his yacht, and was not at all surprised to find the cabman vdaiting for him. "How much do I owe you ?" he said, and 111)011 the cabman handing him a bill for £6OO, he tore a cheque out of his book, filled it up for the amount, and told the man to drive him to his hotel." This is delightful. But the crowning touch, the full blaze of genius, is reserved for the final sentence. "To illustrate We extortionate' character of cabmen," says the " Gaulois," "the man asked Sir -Draggs for his fare from the pier to the hotel." .Mr. Blunt has, I hear, asked that he might have a copy of the works of Shelley as companion in his cbnfinement. The request has, of course, been re- fused, Mr. Blunt's sentence not permitting the gild- ing of his term of imprisonment by the presence of books.' I wonder whether, in asking for Shelley, Mr. Blunt had in mind some curious points of re- semblance between himself and the poet? It is, I fancy, forgotton or not generally known, that Shelley at one period of his life had his soul stirred to the lowest depths by the cdndition of the Irish people. It was early in the century, when the question of Catholic Emancipation filled the place now occupied by Home Rule. Shelley was a hot

div.head: BAZAAR AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: BAZAAR AT STOCKTON HEATH.

A. very successful bazaar was held in Ebenezer Chapel, Stockton Heath, on Wednesday and Thurs- day. It was opened on the afternoon of Wednes- day by Mr. W. J. Horton, of Warrington, and at the ceremony there were present, amongst others, the Rev. G E. Young, the Rev. W. H. Brookes, Mr. E. Dallow, Mrs. Horton, Mrs. Byron (Altrincham), Mrs. J. Shaw Green, Mrs. and Miss Hedgecock, Mr. R. Miller, Mr. W. Arnold, and Mr. John Miller. At the commencement of the proceedings, the Rev.G.E.Young, in the course of a few remarks, said that he looked upon Ebenezer Chapel as a great centre of power, and as a great effort to promote the glory of God, and the general good interests of the neighbourhood. There was a rapidly increasing population, which, he supposed,would be more and more increased as the work of constructing the Ship Canal progressed. The friends of Ebenezer Chapel did not wish to oppose any other religious deno- mination, but they thought that there was Plenty of work for all to do. Remarks were also Tiede by the Rev W. H. Brookes, who said that there were all sorts of preachers—some professing one form of faith, and others another—but still, notwithstanding the differences they might have as regarded theological views, be believed that the aim of every preacher who went to the chapel was to do good, and he believed that good *as being done. The bazaar vs then declared open by Mr. W. J. Horton, and, on the motion of Mr. E. Dallow, seconded by Mr. R. Miller, a vote of thanks was apcorded to the Revs. G. E. Young and W. H. Brookes, and to Mr. W. J. Horton, for their presence and assistance. The sale, by which it was hoped to raise about £65, towards defray- ing a debt on the chapel of £l5O, was then commenced. The stall-holders were as follow :—(1) Mrs. Miller and Miss Worrall ; (2) Mrs. Dallow and Miss Horton; (3; Mrs. Arnold and Miss Woodier (4) Misses Bowcock Arnold, and A. Horton.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from Faye 6.)
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from Faye 6.)
THELWALL AND LYMM,

Work has been vigorously continued this week on the section of the canal lying between Morris Brook farm and the river at Theiwall, on which ground was broken last week. As yet the labour of excavation is being carried on without the aid of machinery, no rails having been laid down or steam navvies erected, but, owing to the number of men employed the soil, is being very rapidly . dieplaced, and the emoankments of "Spoil "alongside the intended limits of the canal are quickly assuming formidable dimensions. Timber and other apparatus are still being accumulated in the adjoining fields, though as yet no temporary huts or workshops seem to have been erected, Across the river from Thelwall, ground has been broken during the week, and work there is being very actively prosecuted. Communication between the two banks of the river is maintained by means of a raft worked by ropes through pulleys. In the neighbour- 'hood of Lymm there is still a considerable number of men engaged, and preparations are being made for the laying of rails, Sze. In 'this locality some differences seem to have occurred with the workmen, the terms on whicb "piece work" was offered to be let not having been considered satisfactory, and at the end of last week a number of the men struck work. An agreement was, however, soon come to, and operations are now in full swing.

div.head: LATCHFORD_ AND WALTON.
div.p: LATCHFORD_ AND WALTON.

A number of engines and other machinery have, dur- ing the week, been sent from Latchford siding to differ- ent sections • and a fine new locomotive called the Brooklands has arrived. A great quantity of timber, metal, and other material now covers the wharf near the railway bridge over the Old Quay Canal. kis expected that a commencement will shortly be made near Tom Pain's Bridge, Stockton Heath, land having been se- cured here as well as near Morley Common. At Lower Walton, on the east side of the railway, men have been got to work and a quantity of timber has arrived. At Acton Grange another locomotive is busy taking the sand to the tip near the wood. Ant American steam navvy has arrived at Ball's Wharf, and will, in a few days be got to work in the cutting near Bell House- lane.

RUNCORN, NORTON, &c. The work on these sections is progressing very favour- ably under the superintendence of Mr. Gregson, who is the agent for the sections between Runcorn and War- rington. At Moore, the German navvy, which started operations 10 days ago, and a sketch of which appeared in this journal last Saturday, is fulfilling its purpose in a satisfactory fashion. At the Big Field, at Norton, the workshops and offices are now occupied, and are dis- tinguished by the title of depot. In the vicinity, Nat nearer towards Moore, Messrs. Kirkham and Co. have commenced the construction of a bungalow to servo as Mr. Gregson's private residence. The building is to be similar in cOnstrirtion to those in use in South Africa. Although but one storey high, it will contain a dining-room, drawing-room. three bed- rooms, larder, and kitchen, and will be fitted with every convenience. The bungalow is to be roofed with ornamental tiles, and, as it 'will be shaded on one side by a plantation of trees, it will form one of the most picturesque buildings on the Ship Canal system. From his new residence Mr. Greg- soh will command a view of three or four miles in extent towards Warrington, so that each morningbefore he com- mences his arduous laboursrhe will be able to take a bird's eye view of a considerable section of the Canal under his charge. On the marsh at the other side of the Canal, Messrs. Kirkham are also about to build a locomotive shed. At present a large staff of navvies are busily employed there excavating and they have made a most interesting discovery. They have opened out to the light, a large deposit of peat of the finest quality, estimated to amount to some hundreds of tons. It is intended to cut the peat into blocks, anduse it instead of coal for various purposes. This marsh, it may be well to repeat, is to have deposited upon it the soil and clay from the excavations of the canal; and there will be formed what is technically known as a " spoil bank." ITo make this bank no less than 3,000 millions of tons of clay will pass over the bridge erected by Messrs. Kirkham. This one fact gives someiclea of the immensity of the undertaking. At Norton, it is interesting to note, occurs sand of the deepest cutting on the whole length from Manchester to Eastham. The spot -Where the American navvies are now at work is dignified with the name of Hill, but it would be more correct to say that it is rising ground. Here, before the level of the canal is reached, clay and any other material that may be encountered will have to' be excavated to a depth of no less than 80 feet. Even this depth is exceeded when Runcorn is approached. Near the works of Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele the cut- ting will be 70 feet deep. On the rising ground at Norton just mentioned it is intended to erect two reservoirs or water tanks, with a capacity of about 20,000 gallons each. From these huge tanks, pipes will be laid to the depot, and to any other place where water is required. It is anticipated that there will not be any scarcity of the precious fluid. A capital stream which, it is said, does not become dry in the most droughty of seasons, runs through the land, and, from the commencement of the operations, water has been obtained from this source. Rand pumps have hitherto been used, but now a watef station has been formed, and powerful pulsometer pumps, worked by steam, have been fitted up. These pumps are capable of lifting 20,000 gallons per hour, to a height of 25 feet. • _ _

On this section at Weston Point a number of Messrs. Kirkham and Co.'s men are busily:occupied in erecting store-rooms, blacksmith's shop, engineering shop, engine i shed, and six huts for the labourers to live n. The huts are to be two stories in height. The offices which have been constructed are ready for occupation and it is expected that the staff will take charge of the premises next week. Already a steam saw mill is hard at work. We hear on good authority that the construction of what are to be known as tke river Weaver sluices will be com- menced in the course of a few weeks.

FALL DOW:MATZ/S.—Ellen Derrick, aged 56,wh0 lived with. her husband, Philip Derrick, fish dealer, at 63, Duke-street, St. Helens, went out on Tuesday morn- ing for the purpose of coUecting some debts. About three o'clock in the afternoon she returned, but there wag no one irethe house. Some little time afterwards a neighbour heard a noise, and on going in found Mrs. Derrick lying at the foot of the stairs with her neck broken, and almost dead. She was lifted up, but death ensued almost immediately. Deceased had evidently fallen down the stairs.—Mr. Brigbouse held an inquest on the body of the decea4d at the Town Hall, on Wed- nesday.—Mary Wilson, daughter of the deceased, said she was in the next door neighbour's house, and heard her mother go into the house, and shortly afterwards, there being a noise, she went in and saw thl,deceased lying at the foot of the stairs.—Ellen Cravitr.aid she heard the deceased going upstairs and talking very loud. —Mr. John Rimmer, grocer, said he saw the deceased pass his house that afternoon. She appeared to be very drunk.—Mrs. Oakes deposed that Mrs. Derrick was dead when found at the foot of the stairs.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and recommended tb,at a handrail should be fixed along the stairs.

div.head: OUR: FINANCIAL LETTER
div.p: OUR: FINANCIAL LETTER
[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.I 23, Old Bmad-stieet, E.C.

The, record on the Stock Exchange during the past week has been a most unsatisfactory and depressing one during a period which has become proverbial for un- certainty and• disappointment engendered by hope deferred. The closing days of last week witnessed a gradual but steady fall in prices in nearly every class of security. This fall continued without abatement into the present week, and was suspended only in anticipa- tion of the peaceful utterances which Prince Bismarck was expected to make. Pending the arrival of this speech speculation remained at a stand still, and on the receipt of a summary of this speech a favourable inter- pretation was put on it, and prices were put up. The hopeful feeling was carried on until the morning of the next day, and then hopefulness began to evaporate. Unce then a steady and persistent fall in prices has occifved, which at the time of writing has reached its clitaax. The grave reports as to the serious condition of the Crown Prince, and the absence of anything .like re-assurance in the Queen's Speech, have further helped the depres- sion. The general belief on the Stock Exchange is tbic war cannot long be illYstponed. Whether this be so oi not, the pubiic keep firmly aloof from all dealings, with the natural consequence that, if only from want of sup- port, prices drift downwards. Foreign stocks are es- pecially flat. Home Rails are almost without feature, but what movement there is continues to be anything but satis- factory; Southern rails especially. Deferred stocks are particularly flat; the latest reports of heavy lines in Paris, and of Rio Tintos and other mines causing quite a scare in those shares. North-Westerns and other ' heavy lines also are depressed, while Scotch lines show no improvement ; Caledonians, in spite of the favour- able traffic returns at the past week, being particularly dull.

Mining securities, which continue to occupy chief attention at the present moment, show no probability Of an immediate improvement. There have been some active dealings in copper, but at the time of writing prices are lower than they have been this year, and in the present unsatisfactory position we think that the bears have undoubtedly the best of the outlook. An attempt has been made to galvanise some life into the 14isbon-Berlyn Mining Company on the reports which are about to be pub ished. It would be well for specula- tors not to be led away by statements, however favour- able they may appear. Regarding this mine, long since nearly all the capital was exhausted, and the possibility of anything like a substantial rise, to say nothing of a possible dividend, is so remote that it would bedangerous to touch it under any circumstances. It will beiemem- bered that this mine was the last public appearance of Mr. Albert Grant as a promoter, and the association of his name with this scheme is not likely to add to the con- fidence of the public. In diamond mines there has been some active demand. De Beers having been very firm, had a rise of 2 during the week, but the present premium at which these shares stand is almost prohibitive; consequently it would be well for speculators to look to the chief mines like St. Augustine, where there is a possibility of a rise and little or no risk of a fall at present prices. In other mines Con- solidated Esmeralda are likely to be one of the first to feel the effect of any upward movement should confi- dence be inspired as to the future. 1 Generall,r, it would be well for the investing public to remain quiet; at any rate, not to be " bulls "at the present moment, otherwise the possibilities are they will be on the wrong side pf the hedge. It is an axiom on the Stock Exchange that the public are always "bull," professional dealers are the "bears," arid in nine cases out of ten the "bears "get all the profit.

It is stated that Mr. Oliver- Heywood; of Clare- mont, Pendleton, will be the ' next High Sheriff of Lan- cashire. Tuesday. next has been fixed for the nomination and the following Friday for the polling in the borough of Southwark. The Fife and Clackmannan miners resolved on Friday to stop 'work to-day? This resolution affects six , thou- sand men. A young unmarried woman, named Alice Middleton, was remanded at Rotherham on Friday ,on a charge ot murdering her female child. The Central News understands that Lord Stanley of Preston will proceed to Canada next May to take up his new duties as Governor-General. The Queen of Sweden, Prince Oscar of Sweden' Miss Muncke, and suite arrived at Victoria Station, London, shortly after seven o'clock last evening. A heavy snowstorm visited Wick on Friday morning, and caused the engineof the southern mail train to leave ithe rails near Georgemas. The passengers proceeded via Thurso. REMEMBER Iffrramismowx.--The Lord Chief Justice of Ireland and Justices Harrison and Murphy, on Friday quashed the verdict of the coroner's jury at Mitchels- town, which found the constabulary guilty of murder on the ground of partiality of the proceedings and coroner's misconduct. Mr. Pyne, M.P., was arrested last evening as he was about to enter the House of Commons. The detectives were also lying in wait for Mr. Crilhooley ; but he man- aged to get in the House unobserved He is being watched, and will probably be arrested whente leaves the House. EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE.—At Ferndale, Rhondda Val- ley, on Friday, a married man named David Evans went to the back yard of his home, and shortly afterwards his corpse minus the head and one arm was discovered on the ground. The deceased must have placed dynamite on his head and then fired the explosive by striking it with some instrument held in his hand. LAST° NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. MiscELLANzons.--Earl DELAwsnit gave notice to call attention to the agricultural depression, and Lord Non- mon to the working of the Technical Instruction (Scot- land) Act tills to amend the law of thstress for rent, to consolidate county court acts, and to amend copy- hold acts were rc-.d a first time. Earl GRANVILLE drew attention to various statements made last night by the Marquis of Salisbury, who replied, showing ,that the noble Earl had misquoted him The sitting wag almost formal, and the House adjourned early. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. QUESTIONS.—Mr. Rimcnif, in reply to Mr. Howarth, said the Government did not intend bringing in a bill to preventimmigmtionof foreign paupers into England.—Sir .J. FERGUSON, replying to Mr. Picton said all engage- ments made with the Ameer of Afglianistati had been made known to the House. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The adjourned debate on the address was resumed by Mr. MUNDELLA, who pointed out that no intimation had yet been given that the information required by Mr. Gladstone as to the work4ng of the Crimes Act would be given. He asked for figures and returns on the sub- ject. Mr. A. BALFOUR then entered on a defence of the action of the Government since the passing of the Crimes Act. He then proceeded to comment on the telegram sent by Mr. Gladstone "Remember Mitchelstown' and accused the right hon. gentleman of going about the country making speeches to iinflame the minds of the people against the police who had died in the execution of their duty.—[Mr. GLADSTONE in a most energetic tone said there was not a syllable of truth for the assertion of the right hon. gentleman. (Cheers.)]—Mr. Balfour said he would leave it to the House whether the interpretation he had had put upon was unfounded. (Cheers.) He then proceeded to condemn the speeches that had been made by other members. Lord Spencer, he insisted, had proceeded against more prisoners for that crime than the present Government had done. He strongly con- tended that the amount of crime was generally decreas- ing in Ireland, and quoted statistics to prove that fact. He promised to lay the statistics on the table. k Mr. JOHN MORLEY thought the temper exhibited by the Trish Chief Secretary showed the way in which the Crimes Act was being administered in Ireland. He denied that the Irish Secretary had in the slightest degree shown what was called coercive conspiracies had been weakened in their proceedings by a single step taken under the Crimes Act. He condemned the way the Crimes Act had been administered, and insisted it had added fresh danger to that which was already dangerous. He contended that the figures quoted were fallacious, and was of opinion that the decrease of crime had been occasioned by the feeling of hope that now tilled the minds of the people of Ireland. Mr. WADDY took 6xception to the Irish policy of the Government, and Mr. MARE STEwART urged on the Go- vernment the duty of seeing what .could be done to remedy the depression that existed in rgriculture. Mr. E. HARRINGTON, With at the commencement of his speech was called to order by: the Speaker for using of- fensive words towards the Irish Chief Secretary, intima- ted his intention of continuing to act as he had hitherto done until the undoubted rights of the Irish people were conceded. Mr. W. A. HUNTER complained of the absence of all reference to distress prevaillng amongst Scotch Crofters, and Mr. C. FENWICH wished something done to reform mining royalty rents. [LEFT SITTING.]

ST. HELENS CAFE AND RECREATION COMPANY.—The an- nual meeting of the shareholders of this company was held on Monday night id their principal rooms, the Mar- ket Tavern, Marketplace. Mr./C. Sharpies (chairman of directors) presiAtd, and amongst those present were Aldermen Harrison and, Cook; Mtissrs. H. Martin, F. France, W. Middlehurst, W, Loader, J. Gandy, George , Hatchman, T. Sherlock, M. Bayley, S. Boyden, and A. Griffin (sec.). The annual report showed the result of last year's working to be fairly satisfactory, although the amount of business transacted has not been so large as in previous years. The net profits of the company for the year amount to £l3l 3s 9d, which together with the balance of £l2 2s 9 brought from the previous year, made a total sum of £143 5s lid available for dividend. The directors.recommend that a dividend of £lO per cent, per annum on the called-up c'apital be paid, which, with interest on that portion of thal capital which has been subscribed in anticipatioff of calls, will absorb the sum bf £lOl 9s. The report was adonted, and Messrs. C. Sharpies, Alderman Harrison, H. A. Biimey, and Alder- man Cook, were re-elected directors., Mr. Jesse Boy- den said the society was called .a recitation society, and he suggested that a gyinnasium be established out of the £7OO which the company had in hand. There was no discussion on the subject, and a vote of thanks to ,the chairman and directors, concluded the pro- ceedings.
